english: My bow Gandiva slips from my hand and my skin is burning. I cannot stand steady, and my mind seems to be reeling.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna begins to argue against the battle, seeing no good in killing his relatives.
devanagari:
निमित्तानि च पश्यामि विपरीतानि केशव ।
न च श्रेयोऽनुपश्यामि हत्वा स्वजनमाहवे ॥
iast:
nimittāni ca paśyāmi viparītāni keśava |
na ca śreyo'nupaśyāmi hatvā svajanamāhave ||
english: Krishna, I see bad omens, and I see no good in killing my own people in battle.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: In despair, Arjuna says that victory, kingdom and even life mean nothing to him; Krishna answers this despair from chapter 2.
devanagari:
न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण न च राज्यं सुखानि च ।
किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा ॥
iast:
na kāṅkṣe vijayaṃ kṛṣṇa na ca rājyaṃ sukhāni ca |
kiṃ no rājyena govinda kiṃ bhogairjīvitena vā ||
english: Krishna, I do not want victory, or a kingdom, or pleasures. What use to us is a kingdom, or enjoyment, or even life?
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna reflects that the people for whom he wanted a kingdom are the very people he would have to kill.
devanagari:
येषामर्थे काङ्क्षितं नो राज्यं भोगाः सुखानि च ।
त इमेऽवस्थिता युद्धे प्राणांस्त्यक्त्वा धनानि च ॥
iast:
yeṣāmarthe kāṅkṣitaṃ no rājyaṃ bhogāḥ sukhāni ca |
ta ime'vasthitā yuddhe prāṇāṃstyaktvā dhanāni ca ||
english: The very people for whose sake we wanted a kingdom, enjoyment and pleasures stand here in battle, ready to give up their lives and wealth:
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna lists the relatives he sees standing ready for battle.
devanagari:
आचार्याः पितरः पुत्रास्तथैव च पितामहाः ।
मातुलाः श्वशुराः पौत्राः श्यालाः संबन्धिनस्तथा ॥
iast:
ācāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrāstathaiva ca pitāmahāḥ |
mātulāḥ śvaśurāḥ pautrāḥ śyālāḥ saṃbandhinastathā ||
english: teachers, fathers, sons and grandfathers, uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna declares he will not kill his relatives even to save his own life, a conclusion Krishna goes on to reject.
devanagari:
एतान्न हन्तुमिच्छामि घ्नतोऽपि मधुसूदन ।
अपि त्रैलोक्यराज्यस्य हेतोः किं नु महीकृते ॥
iast:
etānna hantumicchāmi ghnato'pi madhusūdana |
api trailokyarājyasya hetoḥ kiṃ nu mahīkṛte ||
english: I do not want to kill them, Krishna, even if they kill me, not even to rule the three worlds, let alone this earth.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna argues that killing his cousins, even though they are aggressors, would bring only sin.
devanagari:
निहत्य धार्तराष्ट्रान्नः का प्रीतिः स्याज्जनार्दन ।
पापमेवाश्रयेदस्मान्हत्वैतानाततायिनः ॥
iast:
nihatya dhārtarāṣṭrānnaḥ kā prītiḥ syājjanārdana |
pāpamevāśrayedasmānhatvaitānātatāyinaḥ ||
english: What joy could we have from killing the sons of Dhritarashtra, Krishna? Only sin would come to us from killing these aggressors.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna concludes that killing his own relatives could never bring happiness.
devanagari:
तस्मान्नार्हा वयं हन्तुं धार्तराष्ट्रान्स्वबान्धवान् ।
स्वजनं हि कथं हत्वा सुखिनः स्याम माधव ॥
iast:
tasmānnārhā vayaṃ hantuṃ dhārtarāṣṭrānsvabāndhavān |
svajanaṃ hi kathaṃ hatvā sukhinaḥ syāma mādhava ||
english: So it is not right for us to kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, our own relatives. How could we be happy after killing our own people, Krishna?
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna argues that destroying a family is a grave wrong, even if his cousins, blinded by greed, cannot see it.
devanagari:
यद्यप्येते न पश्यन्ति लोभोपहतचेतसः ।
कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं मित्रद्रोहे च पातकम् ॥
iast:
yadyapyete na paśyanti lobhopahatacetasaḥ |
kulakṣayakṛtaṃ doṣaṃ mitradrohe ca pātakam ||
english: Even if they, their minds overcome by greed, do not see the wrong in destroying a family, or the sin in betraying friends,
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna argues that he and his brothers, unlike their cousins, can see the wrong and should turn away from it.
devanagari:
कथं न ज्ञेयमस्माभिः पापादस्मान्निवर्तितुम् ।
कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं प्रपश्यद्भिर्जनार्दन ॥
iast:
kathaṃ na jñeyamasmābhiḥ pāpādasmānnivartitum |
kulakṣayakṛtaṃ doṣaṃ prapaśyadbhirjanārdana ||
english: why should we not know to turn back from this sin, Krishna, when we can clearly see the wrong in destroying a family?
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna begins a chain of consequences (1.40-1.44): war will destroy families and with them their traditions.
devanagari:
कुलक्षये प्रणश्यन्ति कुलधर्माः सनातनाः ।
धर्मे नष्टे कुलं कृत्स्नमधर्मोऽभिभवत्युत ॥
iast:
kulakṣaye praṇaśyanti kuladharmāḥ sanātanāḥ |
dharme naṣṭe kulaṃ kṛtsnamadharmo'bhibhavatyuta ||
english: When a family is destroyed, its timeless family traditions perish; and when that dharma is lost, lawlessness overtakes the whole family.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Continuing his chain of consequences, Arjuna says lawlessness corrupts a family's women and leads to the mixing of varnas.
devanagari:
अधर्माभिभवात्कृष्ण प्रदुष्यन्ति कुलस्त्रियः ।
स्त्रीषु दुष्टासु वार्ष्णेय जायते वर्णसंकरः ॥
iast:
adharmābhibhavātkṛṣṇa praduṣyanti kulastriyaḥ |
strīṣu duṣṭāsu vārṣṇeya jāyate varṇasaṃkaraḥ ||
english: When lawlessness prevails, Krishna, the women of the family become corrupt; and when the women are corrupt, the varnas become mixed.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna argues that the mixing of varnas sends both the family and its destroyers to hell, as the rites for ancestors stop.
devanagari:
संकरो नरकायैव कुलघ्नानां कुलस्य च ।
पतन्ति पितरो ह्येषां लुप्तपिण्डोदकक्रियाः ॥
iast:
saṃkaro narakāyaiva kulaghnānāṃ kulasya ca |
patanti pitaro hyeṣāṃ luptapiṇḍodakakriyāḥ ||
english: This mixing drags the family and those who destroyed it down to hell, for their ancestors fall, deprived of their offerings of rice and water.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna concludes that destroying families wipes out the ancient duties of caste and family.
devanagari:
दोषैरेतैः कुलघ्नानां वर्णसंकरकारकैः ।
उत्साद्यन्ते जातिधर्माः कुलधर्माश्च शाश्वताः ॥
iast:
doṣairetaiḥ kulaghnānāṃ varṇasaṃkarakārakaiḥ |
utsādyante jātidharmāḥ kuladharmāśca śāśvatāḥ ||
english: Through these wrongs of those who destroy families, which cause the mixing of varnas, the timeless duties of caste and family are wiped out.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna ends his chain of consequences with what he has heard about the fate of people who lose their family traditions.
devanagari:
उत्सन्नकुलधर्माणां मनुष्याणां जनार्दन ।
नरकेऽनियतं वासो भवतीत्यनुशुश्रुम ॥
iast:
utsannakuladharmāṇāṃ manuṣyāṇāṃ janārdana |
narake'niyataṃ vāso bhavatītyanuśuśruma ||
english: We have heard, Krishna, that people whose family traditions have been destroyed live in hell for an endless time.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna laments that greed for a kingdom has brought him and his brothers to the edge of a great sin.
devanagari:
अहो बत महत्पापं कर्तुं व्यवसिता वयम् ।
यद्राज्यसुखलोभेन हन्तुं स्वजनमुद्यताः ॥
iast:
aho bata mahatpāpaṃ kartuṃ vyavasitā vayam |
yadrājyasukhalobhena hantuṃ svajanamudyatāḥ ||
english: Alas! We are set on committing a great sin, ready to kill our own people out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: In despair, Arjuna says he would rather be killed without resisting, a despair Krishna rejects in chapter 2.
devanagari:
यदि मामप्रतीकारमशस्त्रं शस्त्रपाणयः ।
धार्तराष्ट्रा रणे हन्युस्तन्मे क्षेमतरं भवेत् ॥
iast:
yadi māmapratīkāramaśastraṃ śastrapāṇayaḥ |
dhārtarāṣṭrā raṇe hanyustanme kṣemataraṃ bhavet ||
english: It would be better for me if the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapons in hand, killed me in battle while I stood unarmed and did not resist."
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Sanjaya
context: Sanjaya reports that Arjuna, overwhelmed with grief, puts down his bow and sits down in his chariot, ending chapter 1.
devanagari:
एवमुक्त्वार्जुनः संख्ये रथोपस्थ उपाविशत् ।
विसृज्य सशरं चापं शोकसंविग्नमानसः ॥
iast:
evamuktvārjunaḥ saṃkhye rathopastha upāviśat |
visṛjya saśaraṃ cāpaṃ śokasaṃvignamānasaḥ ||
english: Having said this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of his chariot, casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed with grief.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Sanjaya
context: Sanjaya describes Arjuna in tears and despair as Krishna begins to speak, opening the teaching of chapter 2.
devanagari:
तं तथा कृपयाविष्टमश्रुपूर्णाकुलेक्षणम् ।
विषीदन्तमिदं वाक्यमुवाच मधुसूदनः ॥
iast:
taṃ tathā kṛpayāviṣṭamaśrupūrṇākulekṣaṇam |
viṣīdantamidaṃ vākyamuvāca madhusūdanaḥ ||
english: To him, overcome with compassion, his eyes troubled and filled with tears, sinking in despair, Krishna spoke these words.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna's first words in the Gita: he challenges Arjuna's despair at the critical moment as unworthy of him.
devanagari:
कुतस्त्वा कश्मलमिदं विषमे समुपस्थितम् ।
अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुन ॥
iast:
kutastvā kaśmalamidaṃ viṣame samupasthitam |
anāryajuṣṭamasvargyamakīrtikaramarjuna ||
english: Arjuna, where has this faintness of heart come from at this critical moment? It is not the way of a noble person; it does not lead to heaven, and it brings disgrace.

school_notes.note: Summarises 2.1-2.3: Krishna rebukes Arjuna's grief as out of place, unknown to the wise, a bar to the higher worlds, a cause of disgrace, petty and born of weakness of heart, and tells him to drop it and rise to fight.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna urges Arjuna to shake off his weakness and stand up to fight.
devanagari:
क्लैब्यं मा स्म गमः पार्थ नैतत्त्वय्युपपद्यते ।
क्षुद्रं हृदयदौर्बल्यं त्यक्त्वोत्तिष्ठ परन्तप ॥
iast:
klaibyaṃ mā sma gamaḥ pārtha naitattvayyupapadyate |
kṣudraṃ hṛdayadaurbalyaṃ tyaktvottiṣṭha parantapa ||
english: Son of Pritha, do not give in to unmanliness; it does not suit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and stand up, scorcher of enemies.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna answers Krishna's rebuke: he cannot bring himself to fight the elders he reveres.
devanagari:
कथं भीष्ममहं संख्ये द्रोणं च मधुसूदन ।
इषुभिः प्रति योत्स्यामि पूजार्हावरिसूदन ॥
iast:
kathaṃ bhīṣmamahaṃ saṃkhye droṇaṃ ca madhusūdana |
iṣubhiḥ prati yotsyāmi pūjārhāvarisūdana ||
english: Krishna, how can I fight back with arrows in battle against Bhishma and Drona? They deserve my reverence, destroyer of enemies.

school_notes.note: Arjuna, still shaken by love, compassion and fear of doing wrong, fails to grasp Krishna's helpful words and asks how he could kill revered elders like Bhishma and Drona, then enjoy pleasures stained with their blood (2.4-2.5).

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna argues that a beggar's life would be better than enjoying a kingdom won by killing his teachers.
devanagari:
गुरूनहत्वा हि महानुभावान् श्रेयो भोक्तुं भैक्ष्यमपीह लोके ।
हत्वार्थकामांस्तु गुरूनिहैव भुञ्जीय भोगान् रुधिरप्रदिग्धान् ॥
iast:
gurūnahatvā hi mahānubhāvān śreyo bhoktuṃ bhaikṣyamapīha loke |
hatvārthakāmāṃstu gurūnihaiva bhuñjīya bhogān rudhirapradigdhān ||
english: It would be better to live in this world even by begging than to kill these noble teachers. If I killed my teachers, however much they seek gain, I would enjoy here only pleasures stained with blood.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna admits he cannot tell whether winning or losing would be worse, since victory means killing his own kin.
devanagari:
न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयो यद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः ।
यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषाम- स्तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः ॥
iast:
na caitadvidmaḥ kataranno garīyo yadvā jayema yadi vā no jayeyuḥ |
yāneva hatvā na jijīviṣāma- ste'vasthitāḥ pramukhe dhārtarāṣṭrāḥ ||
english: Nor do we know which is better for us: that we defeat them, or that they defeat us. The sons of Dhritarashtra stand before us; if we killed them, we would not even wish to live.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna, confused about what is right, asks Krishna to teach him and becomes his disciple, which sets up the teaching that follows.
devanagari:
कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावः पृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसम्मूढचेताः ।
यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्चितं ब्रूहि तन्मे शिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम् ॥
iast:
kārpaṇyadoṣopahatasvabhāvaḥ pṛcchāmi tvāṃ dharmasammūḍhacetāḥ |
yacchreyaḥ syānniścitaṃ brūhi tanme śiṣyaste'haṃ śādhi māṃ tvāṃ prapannam ||
english: My nature is overcome by a pitiful weakness, and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me clearly what is better. I am your student; I have come to you for refuge. Teach me.

school_notes.note: Summarises 2.6-2.8: Arjuna reasons that being killed by the Kauravas would be better than an unrighteous victory; then, utterly helpless, he takes refuge at Krishna's feet and asks, as his disciple, to be told what is truly good for him.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna explains that no kingdom, not even rule over the gods, could take away his grief.
devanagari:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद् यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् ।
अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धं राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम् ॥
iast:
na hi prapaśyāmi mamāpanudyād yacchokamucchoṣaṇamindriyāṇām |
avāpya bhūmāvasapatnamṛddhaṃ rājyaṃ surāṇāmapi cādhipatyam ||
english: I see nothing that could drive away this grief that dries up my senses, even if I won an unrivalled, prosperous kingdom on earth, or even lordship over the gods.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Sanjaya
context: Sanjaya reports that Arjuna, having asked for guidance, declares he will not fight and falls silent.
devanagari:
एवमुक्त्वा हृषीकेशं गुडाकेशः परन्तप ।
न योत्स्य इति गोविन्दमुक्त्वा तूष्णीं बभूव ह ॥
iast:
evamuktvā hṛṣīkeśaṃ guḍākeśaḥ parantapa |
na yotsya iti govindamuktvā tūṣṇīṃ babhūva ha ||
english: Having spoken this way to Krishna, Arjuna said to him, "I will not fight," O king, and fell silent.

school_notes.note: Krishna saw that Arjuna, overcome by misplaced love and compassion, now took a warrior's highest duty for wrongdoing and had come to him for refuge. Knowing this delusion would not end without knowledge of the self, and of selfless duty as the way to it, Krishna began teaching that knowledge.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Sanjaya
context: Sanjaya describes Krishna, smiling between the two armies, about to begin his teaching.
devanagari:
तमुवाच हृषीकेशः प्रहसन्निव भारत ।
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये विषीदन्तमिदं वचः ॥
iast:
tamuvāca hṛṣīkeśaḥ prahasanniva bhārata |
senayorubhayormadhye viṣīdantamidaṃ vacaḥ ||
english: Then, O king, between the two armies, Krishna, as if smiling, spoke these words to the despairing Arjuna.

school_notes.note: Śaṅkara's commentary begins here. He reads 1.2-2.9 as showing where grief and delusion, the seeds of worldly existence, come from: Arjuna's sense of 'I' and 'mine' towards kingdom, teachers, sons, friends and relatives.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna begins his teaching: Arjuna's grief rests on a misunderstanding of what a person truly is (2.11-2.30).
devanagari:
अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे ।
गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः ॥
iast:
aśocyānanvaśocastvaṃ prajñāvādāṃśca bhāṣase |
gatāsūnagatāsūṃśca nānuśocanti paṇḍitāḥ ||
english: You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, and yet you speak words that sound wise. The wise grieve neither for the dead nor for the living.

school_notes.note: Bhishma, Drona and the others are not to be grieved for: they lived rightly, and in their true nature they are eternal. Arjuna shows folly and learning at once, like someone deranged.
Arjuna's arguments, such as ancestors falling when rites stop (1.42), come from taking the body for the self. Those who know the true nature of the body and of the self grieve for neither.
Krishna speaks to Arjuna caught in a net of delusion about his relatives; the 'wise-sounding words' are arguments of Arjuna's own devising.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna's first argument against grief: the self of every person, his own included, has always existed and always will.
devanagari:
न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः ।
न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम् ॥
iast:
na tvevāhaṃ jātu nāsaṃ na tvaṃ neme janādhipāḥ |
na caiva na bhaviṣyāmaḥ sarve vayamataḥ param ||
english: There was never a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these kings; and none of us will ever cease to exist in the future.

school_notes.note: Each of us exists as the self in all three times, unaffected as bodies arise and perish, as space is unaffected by pots. The plural 'we' follows the different bodies; it does not mean there are many selves.

Just as the Lord of all is eternal, so are the individual selves, Arjuna and these kings. Because Krishna says 'I, you, these, all of us' while teaching the highest truth, the distinction between the Lord and the selves, and among the selves, is real.
Krishna cites his own eternity, well known from the Upanishads, as an example: just as I am eternal, so are you and these kings.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna compares death to the changes of a single lifetime to show that the self continues.
devanagari:
देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा ।
तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति ॥
iast:
dehino'sminyathā dehe kaumāraṃ yauvanaṃ jarā |
tathā dehāntaraprāptirdhīrastatra na muhyati ||
english: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes into another body. A steady person is not confused by this.

school_notes.note: The self does not perish when childhood ends or come into being when youth begins; it passes unchanged through these states, and in the same way into another body.
Just as no one grieves that the self has perished when it moves from childhood to youth in one body, the wise do not grieve when it moves to another body.
The self is the one who experiences childhood and the other stages, which the inert body cannot do; as it continues through these, so it continues into another body.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna turns to the sensations of pain and pleasure, urging Arjuna to bear them because they pass.
devanagari:
मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः ।
आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत ॥
iast:
mātrāsparśāstu kaunteya śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkhadāḥ |
āgamāpāyino'nityāstāṃstitikṣasva bhārata ||
english: Contact with the objects of the senses, son of Kunti, brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These come and go; they do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

school_notes.note: The 'contacts' are the meeting of the senses with sound and other objects, which give cold, heat, pleasure and pain; since they come and go, they should be borne.
Bear them with fortitude until your prescribed duty, such as this battle, is complete. They can be borne because they come and go, and they cease altogether when the karma that binds is exhausted.
Pain and pleasure do not belong to the self by nature, since they come and go; if they did, they would persist even in deep sleep.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says that the person who stays steady in pain and pleasure is fit for liberation.
devanagari:
यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ ।
समदुःखसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते ॥
iast:
yaṃ hi na vyathayantyete puruṣaṃ puruṣarṣabha |
samaduḥkhasukhaṃ dhīraṃ so'mṛtatvāya kalpate ||
english: The steady person whom these do not shake, best of men, who stays the same in pain and pleasure, is fit for immortality.

school_notes.note: One who is neither elated nor dejected by pleasure and pain, because they see the eternal self, is able to attain immortality, that is, liberation.
Only one who bears unavoidable pain as if it were pleasure, while doing their duty without seeking its fruit, attains immortality; not someone who cannot bear pain.
States the purpose of endurance: the person who keeps pain and pleasure equal, through steadiness, is not troubled by sense contacts.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna distinguishes what is real, and never ceases, from what is unreal, as the basis for his teaching on the self.
devanagari:
नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः ।
उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः ॥
iast:
nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ |
ubhayorapi dṛṣṭo'ntastvanayostattvadarśibhiḥ ||
english: The unreal never comes into being; the real never ceases to be. Those who see the truth have reached the final understanding of both.

school_notes.note: Heat, cold and every other effect are unreal: no effect is found apart from its cause, as a pot is nothing apart from clay. Only the real, Brahman, truly is.
The body, being perishable, has unreality as its nature; the conscious self, being imperishable, has reality as its nature. This is the settled conclusion of those who see the truth about both.
Neither the cause of the world (prakṛti, here called 'unreal') nor Brahman ('the real') ever ceases to exist; citing the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, he holds that prakṛti, the soul and time are eternal.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the self that pervades everything as beyond destruction.
devanagari:
अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम् ।
विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित्कर्तुमर्हति ॥
iast:
avināśi tu tadviddhi yena sarvamidaṃ tatam |
vināśamavyayasyāsya na kaścitkartumarhati ||
english: Know that what pervades all this is indestructible. No one can destroy the imperishable.

school_notes.note: What pervades the whole world, as space pervades pots, is Brahman, called 'the real'; having no parts, it neither grows nor declines, so nothing can destroy it.
The self pervades all non-conscious things and is subtler than all of them. Weapons, fire and the like destroy only what they can pervade, so nothing can destroy the self.
What is unlimited in space is eternal; it cannot be destroyed even by something like a curse.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna contrasts perishable bodies with the imperishable self and draws the conclusion that Arjuna should fight.
devanagari:
अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ताः शरीरिणः ।
अनाशिनोऽप्रमेयस्य तस्माद्युध्यस्व भारत ॥
iast:
antavanta ime dehā nityasyoktāḥ śarīriṇaḥ |
anāśino'prameyasya tasmādyudhyasva bhārata ||
english: These bodies of the eternal, indestructible, immeasurable embodied self are said to come to an end. So fight, Arjuna.

school_notes.note: 'Fight' is not a command to fight: Arjuna was already engaged in battle and had stopped only because of grief and delusion. The word merely removes that obstacle, since the Gita aims to remove grief and delusion, not to prompt action.
Bodies are built up to experience the fruits of karma and perish when that karma ends. The self is imperishable because it is never known as an object, only ever as the knower.
The self does not perish with the body as a reflection vanishes with its mirror, because it resembles the immeasurable Lord.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna argues that the true self neither kills nor is killed, answering Arjuna's horror at killing his kin.
devanagari:
य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम् ।
उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते ॥
iast:
ya enaṃ vetti hantāraṃ yaścainaṃ manyate hatam |
ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyaṃ hanti na hanyate ||
english: Whoever thinks this self is a killer, and whoever thinks it is killed, neither of them understands. It does not kill, and it is not killed.

school_notes.note: Those who think 'I kill' or 'I am killed' mistake the body for the self; the self is neither the doer nor the object of killing.

Because the self is eternal, it neither causes death nor dies. 'Killing' means separating a self from its body, so scripture's command not to harm any being still forbids every such separation scripture does not sanction.
Ordinary talk of killing is mistaken: the self neither kills nor is killed. Like a reflection, it acts only through the actions of the original, the Lord.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna's first answer to Arjuna's grief over killing his teachers and kin: the true self is not the body and does not die with it (2.11-2.30).
devanagari:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिन्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः ।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
iast:
na jāyate mriyate vā kadācinnāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ |
ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṃ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre ||
english: The self is never born and never dies. It did not come into being, and it will never stop being. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.

school_notes.note: Reads the verse as denying, one by one, all six changes that worldly things undergo (birth, existence, growth, change, decline, destruction). The self has no parts, so it can neither decline nor grow; it is entirely free of change.

Birth and death belong to the non-conscious body and never touch the self, even in the bodies of great beings that arise and dissolve with each cosmic cycle. 'Ancient' means the self is old yet always fresh.
Says the teaching also has Vedic mantra support, and that the self is unborn and eternal because it resembles the Lord in nature. He glosses 'ancient' (purāṇa) as 'that which animates the body'.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna draws out what knowing the indestructible self means for Arjuna's fear of killing.
devanagari:
वेदाविनाशिनं नित्यं य एनमजमव्ययम् ।
कथं स पुरुषः पार्थ कं घातयति हन्ति कम् ॥
iast:
vedāvināśinaṃ nityaṃ ya enamajamavyayam |
kathaṃ sa puruṣaḥ pārtha kaṃ ghātayati hanti kam ||
english: Son of Pritha, how can a person who knows this self to be indestructible, eternal, unborn and unchanging kill anyone, or cause anyone to be killed?

school_notes.note: The question is rhetorical: one who knows the self to be changeless does not, in any way, kill anyone or cause anyone to kill.
Grieving 'I am killing them' comes from not knowing the true nature of the self; with eternal selves, only their separation from bodies takes place.
Glosses 'indestructible' as free of destruction from outside causes, or free of defects, and 'eternal' as free of destruction by its own nature.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives his best-known image of rebirth: the self changes bodies as a person changes clothes.
devanagari:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि ।
तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णान्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही ॥
iast:
vāsāṃsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya navāni gṛhṇāti naro'parāṇi |
tathā śarīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇānyanyāni saṃyāti navāni dehī ||
english: As a person throws away worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self throws away worn-out bodies and enters new ones.

school_notes.note: Like the person who changes clothes, the self remains unchanged as it leaves old bodies and takes on new ones.
Scripture teaches that those who give up the body in a righteous war gain a better one, so this is cause for joy, like exchanging worn clothes for fine new ones.
An illustration to help one experience the self as distinct from the body.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the self as beyond the reach of weapons and the elements.
devanagari:
नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः ।
न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः ॥
iast:
nainaṃ chindanti śastrāṇi nainaṃ dahati pāvakaḥ |
na cainaṃ kledayantyāpo na śoṣayati mārutaḥ ||
english: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it.

school_notes.note: Having no parts, the self cannot be divided by weapons, burned to ash, loosened by water or dried out by wind.
The self pervades all the elements and is subtler than them, so they cannot pervade it; and cutting, burning, wetting and drying work only on what they pervade.
Even something that does not perish of itself might seem destructible by some special cause; this verse rules out such causes for the self.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna continues describing the self as untouched by any physical force, eternal and unchanging.
devanagari:
अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च ।
नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातनः ॥
iast:
acchedyo'yamadāhyo'yamakledyo'śoṣya eva ca |
nityaḥ sarvagataḥ sthāṇuracalo'yaṃ sanātanaḥ ||
english: It cannot be cut, burned, wetted or dried. It is eternal, present everywhere, stable, unmoving and timeless.

school_notes.note: Because the elements that destroy one another cannot destroy the self, it is eternal; being eternal, it is everywhere; being everywhere, it is stable and unmoving; and it is timeless, not produced by any cause.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna concludes that, knowing the self to be unmanifest and unchanging, Arjuna has no reason to grieve.
devanagari:
अव्यक्तोऽयमचिन्त्योऽयमविकार्योऽयमुच्यते ।
तस्मादेवं विदित्वैनं नानुशोचितुमर्हसि ॥
iast:
avyakto'yamacintyo'yamavikāryo'yamucyate |
tasmādevaṃ viditvainaṃ nānuśocitumarhasi ||
english: It is called unmanifest, beyond thought and unchanging. So, knowing it to be like this, you should not grieve.

school_notes.note: The self is not an object of any sense, so it is unmanifest and beyond thought; having no parts, it does not change the way milk turns into curd.

The self is not revealed by the means that reveal things that can be cut, and, being unlike everything else, cannot even be conceived in their terms; so it cannot change, and there is no reason to grieve for it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna makes a second argument: even if the self were born and died with each body, grief would still be misplaced.
devanagari:
अथ चैनं नित्यजातं नित्यं वा मन्यसे मृतम् ।
तथापि त्वं महाबाहो नैवं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥
iast:
atha cainaṃ nityajātaṃ nityaṃ vā manyase mṛtam |
tathāpi tvaṃ mahābāho naivaṃ śocitumarhasi ||
english: And even if you think of the self as constantly being born and constantly dying, even then, mighty-armed one, you should not grieve like this.

school_notes.note: Even granting the popular view that the self is born and dies with each body, grief is wrong, since what is born must die and what dies must be born.
Even if you take the self to be just the body, you should not grieve so much, because birth and destruction are unavoidable for a body that changes by nature.
Answers the objection that even if the self is eternal, birth and death, as joining and leaving a body, still happen.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna continues the second argument: what is born must die, so grief over the unavoidable is misplaced.
devanagari:
जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च ।
तस्मादपरिहार्येऽर्थे न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥
iast:
jātasya hi dhruvo mṛtyurdhruvaṃ janma mṛtasya ca |
tasmādaparihārye'rthe na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi ||
english: Death is certain for whoever is born, and birth is certain for whoever dies. So you should not grieve over what cannot be avoided.

school_notes.note: Birth and death are bound to each other and cannot be avoided, so grieving over them is unfitting.
Arising and perishing are only states of a substance that always exists, as threads in a certain arrangement are called cloth; so what is destroyed is born again.
There is no cause for grief, because birth and death are fixed.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna observes that beings come from the unseen and return to it, appearing only in between.
devanagari:
अव्यक्तादीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत ।
अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना ॥
iast:
avyaktādīni bhūtāni vyaktamadhyāni bhārata |
avyaktanidhanānyeva tatra kā paridevanā ||
english: Beings are unmanifest at their beginning, manifest in their middle, Arjuna, and unmanifest again at their end. What is there to lament in that?

school_notes.note: Sons, friends and others come from the unseen before birth and return to the unseen after death; he quotes a saying that the one who came from the unseen and went back to it was neither yours nor you his.
Even on the view that the self is the body, beings simply pass through unseen, seen and unseen states, so there is no cause for lament.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna acknowledges how hard it is to grasp the self: even those who hear of it rarely understand.
devanagari:
आश्चर्यवत्पश्यति कश्चिदेनमाश्चर्यवद्वदति तथैव चान्यः ।
आश्चर्यवच्चैनमन्यः शृणोति श्रुत्वाप्येनं वेद न चैव कश्चित् ॥
iast:
āścaryavatpaśyati kaścidenamāścaryavadvadati tathaiva cānyaḥ |
āścaryavaccainamanyaḥ śṛṇoti śrutvāpyenaṃ veda na caiva kaścit ||
english: Some see this self as a wonder; another speaks of it as a wonder; another hears of it as a wonder; and even after hearing of it, no one truly knows it.

school_notes.note: The self is hard to understand: one who truly sees it, speaks of it or hears of it is a rarity, one among many thousands.

Among countless beings, only someone whose sins have been worn away by great austerity sees this self, which is unlike everything else; and even among seers, speakers and hearers, true seeing, speaking and hearing are rare.
The self is hard to see because it resembles the Lord and is subtle, so the one who sees it is a wonder.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna sums up his first line of argument (2.11-2.30): the self in every body cannot be killed, so grief is unfounded.
devanagari:
देही नित्यमवध्योऽयं देहे सर्वस्य भारत ।
तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥
iast:
dehī nityamavadhyo'yaṃ dehe sarvasya bhārata |
tasmātsarvāṇi bhūtāni na tvaṃ śocitumarhasi ||
english: The self that dwells in every body is eternal and can never be killed, Arjuna. So you should not grieve for any being.

school_notes.note: Even when the body of any being is killed, the self within it cannot be, so do not grieve for Bhishma and the others.

All beings, from gods to plants, differ in form but are alike and eternal in their true nature; inequality and impermanence belong only to bodies. So grieve for none of them, not only for Bhishma and the others.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna's second line of argument begins: apart from the nature of the self, a warrior's own duty calls him to fight a just war.
devanagari:
स्वधर्ममपि चावेक्ष्य न विकम्पितुमर्हसि ।
धर्म्याद्धि युद्धाच्छ्रेयोऽन्यत्क्षत्रियस्य न विद्यते ॥
iast:
svadharmamapi cāvekṣya na vikampitumarhasi |
dharmyāddhi yuddhācchreyo'nyatkṣatriyasya na vidyate ||
english: And looking at your own duty, you should not waver; for a warrior, there is nothing better than a war fought for what is right.

school_notes.note: A warrior's own duty is to fight; this war, waged to win the land for the sake of dharma and to protect the people, is entirely in keeping with dharma.
Although battle involves killing, it is a warrior's own duty, like a prescribed Vedic rite; nothing is better for a warrior than a war waged justly. He cites 18.43 on the warrior's nature.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the battle Arjuna faces as, by the warrior ethic of his time, a rare opportunity.
devanagari:
यदृच्छया चोपपन्नं स्वर्गद्वारमपावृतम् ।
सुखिनः क्षत्रियाः पार्थ लभन्ते युद्धमीदृशम् ॥
iast:
yadṛcchayā copapannaṃ svargadvāramapāvṛtam |
sukhinaḥ kṣatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddhamīdṛśam ||
english: Fortunate are the warriors, son of Pritha, who find a war like this, come of its own accord: an open door to heaven.

school_notes.note: Unsought, the war has come to them as an open gate to heaven; are the warriors who gain such a war not fortunate?
Only warriors with merit gain, without effort, such an unobstructed war, which is a means to supreme happiness.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna warns Arjuna that refusing to fight this righteous battle would mean abandoning his duty and honour.
devanagari:
अथ चेत्त्वमिमं धर्म्यं संग्रामं न करिष्यसि ।
ततः स्वधर्मं कीर्तिं च हित्वा पापमवाप्स्यसि ॥
iast:
atha cettvamimaṃ dharmyaṃ saṃgrāmaṃ na kariṣyasi |
tataḥ svadharmaṃ kīrtiṃ ca hitvā pāpamavāpsyasi ||
english: But if you do not fight this righteous battle, you will give up your duty and your honour, and you will incur sin.

school_notes.note: By not fighting, you lose your duty and the fame you won in encounters such as the one with Mahādeva, and gain only sin.
If, out of delusion, you do not fight the battle already begun, you lose the supreme happiness and fame that victory brings and incur great sin.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna appeals to Arjuna's sense of honour, warning of lasting disgrace if he withdraws.
devanagari:
अकीर्तिं चापि भूतानि कथयिष्यन्ति तेऽव्ययाम् ।
सम्भावितस्य चाकीर्तिर्मरणादतिरिच्यते ॥
iast:
akīrtiṃ cāpi bhūtāni kathayiṣyanti te'vyayām |
sambhāvitasya cākīrtirmaraṇādatiricyate ||
english: People will tell of your disgrace for ever, and for someone who has been honoured, disgrace is worse than death.

school_notes.note: For someone honoured for virtues such as righteousness and courage, death is better than disgrace.
Disgrace from failing in courage is worse than death for one honoured for valour; for you, death would be better than such disgrace.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna warns that the other warriors will put Arjuna's withdrawal down to fear, not compassion.
devanagari:
भयाद्रणादुपरतं मंस्यन्ते त्वां महारथाः ।
येषां च त्वं बहुमतो भूत्वा यास्यसि लाघवम् ॥
iast:
bhayādraṇāduparataṃ maṃsyante tvāṃ mahārathāḥ |
yeṣāṃ ca tvaṃ bahumato bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam ||
english: The great warriors will think you pulled back from battle out of fear, and those who once thought highly of you will think little of you.

school_notes.note: Duryodhana and the others will think you withdrew out of fear of Karna and the rest, not out of compassion.
Brave enemies cannot imagine a warrior quitting battle out of love for his relatives, so Karna, Duryodhana and the others will put it down to fear.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna adds that Arjuna's enemies will mock his courage, a pain worse than any other.
devanagari:
अवाच्यवादांश्च बहून्वदिष्यन्ति तवाहिताः ।
निन्दन्तस्तव सामर्थ्यं ततो दुःखतरं नु किम् ॥
iast:
avācyavādāṃśca bahūnvadiṣyanti tavāhitāḥ |
nindantastava sāmarthyaṃ tato duḥkhataraṃ nu kim ||
english: Your enemies will say many things that should never be said, mocking your strength. What could be more painful than that?

school_notes.note: Your enemies will scorn the prowess you showed in battles such as the one against the Nivātakavacas; no pain is worse than that scorn.
Your enemies will say you could not stand a moment before brave men like them; you yourself would think death better than hearing that.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna's second line of argument (2.31-2.38): apart from the nature of the self, Arjuna's own duty as a warrior calls him to fight a righteous war.
devanagari:
हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम् ।
तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौन्तेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चयः ॥
iast:
hato vā prāpsyasi svargaṃ jitvā vā bhokṣyase mahīm |
tasmāduttiṣṭha kaunteya yuddhāya kṛtaniścayaḥ ||
english: If you are killed, you will reach heaven; if you win, you will enjoy the earth. So stand up, son of Kunti, resolved to fight.

school_notes.note: Takes the verse at face value: either outcome is a gain, so Arjuna should rise with the firm resolve 'I will defeat the enemy or die'.
Reads it as about a righteous war (dharma-yuddha) fought without seeking its fruits. Such duty is itself a means to the highest good, liberation, so the effort to fight is undertaken for that end.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna closes his argument from duty: fight with an even mind towards pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat.
devanagari:
सुखदुःखे समे कृत्वा लाभालाभौ जयाजयौ ।
ततो युद्धाय युज्यस्व नैवं पापमवाप्स्यसि ॥
iast:
sukhaduḥkhe same kṛtvā lābhālābhau jayājayau |
tato yuddhāya yujyasva naivaṃ pāpamavāpsyasi ||
english: Treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as the same, prepare yourself for battle. Then you will incur no sin.

school_notes.note: Treat them alike, without attachment or aversion, and fight. This advice is incidental: the arguments from a warrior's duty (2.31-2.37) were worldly reasoning to dispel grief, not the main point, which is the vision of the highest truth.

Knowing the eternal self beyond the body, and unmoved by the pain, gain or defeat war brings, begin the battle without aiming at heaven, simply as what must be done. Then you will not fall into 'sin', the painful cycle of rebirth, but be freed from it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna turns from knowledge of the self (Sankhya) to the discipline of action (yoga), the theme of 2.39-2.53.
devanagari:
एषा तेऽभिहिता सांख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां शृणु ।
बुद्ध्या युक्तो यया पार्थ कर्मबन्धं प्रहास्यसि ॥
iast:
eṣā te'bhihitā sāṃkhye buddhiryoge tvimāṃ śṛṇu |
buddhyā yukto yayā pārtha karmabandhaṃ prahāsyasi ||
english: This is the understanding I have taught you in terms of Sankhya. Now hear it in terms of yoga: joined with this understanding, son of Pritha, you will throw off the bondage of action.

school_notes.note: Sankhya here is discernment of the highest truth, which directly removes the causes of grief and delusion; yoga is the means to it: action without attachment, done as worship of the Lord, and meditation.
Sankhya is the truth of the self grasped by the intellect, taught in 2.12-2.30; yoga is the understanding with which one performs action, grounded in that knowledge, as a means to liberation.
Sankhya means knowledge of the pure self and yoga means the means to it, citing Vyāsa and the Bhāgavata; the separate Sankhya and Yoga schools are not what is meant.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna reassures Arjuna that on the path of selfless action, no effort is ever lost.
devanagari:
नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते ।
स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात् ॥
iast:
nehābhikramanāśo'sti pratyavāyo na vidyate |
svalpamapyasya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt ||
english: On this path no effort is wasted and no harm comes from falling short. Even a little of this practice protects a person from great fear.

school_notes.note: Unlike farming, a start on this path never goes to waste, and unlike an unfinished course of medicine, an incomplete practice does no harm; even a little protects from the great fear of birth and death.
Karma yoga, even begun and broken off, is not fruitless and brings no penalty; even a small part protects from the fear of rebirth. He links this to 6.40.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna contrasts a resolute, single-minded purpose with the scattered aims of the irresolute.
devanagari:
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिरेकेह कुरुनन्दन ।
बहुशाखा ह्यनन्ताश्च बुद्धयोऽव्यवसायिनाम् ॥
iast:
vyavasāyātmikā buddhirekeha kurunandana |
bahuśākhā hyanantāśca buddhayo'vyavasāyinām ||
english: On this path, Arjuna, the resolute mind is single-pointed; but the thoughts of the irresolute are many-branched and endless.

school_notes.note: The resolute understanding, born of right knowledge, is one, and it overcomes the endless contrary notions that keep worldly existence going.
Action for liberation rests on firm conviction about the true self, so the mind is single; action for desired rewards needs no such conviction, and its aims branch out endlessly.
Answers the worry that so many differing views make commitment hard: views rightly settled by sound reasoning are in fact one.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna contrasts the resolute mind with people who treat Vedic ritual only as a way to heaven and its rewards (2.42-2.44).
devanagari:
यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः ।
वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः ॥
iast:
yāmimāṃ puṣpitāṃ vācaṃ pravadantyavipaścitaḥ |
vedavādaratāḥ pārtha nānyadastīti vādinaḥ ||
english: The unwise, son of Pritha, who delight in the letter of the Vedas and claim there is nothing more, speak flowery words

school_notes.note: The undiscerning, delighting in Vedic passages that praise rewards, say there is nothing beyond rites that bring heaven, cattle and the like; their words are like a tree in flower, pleasant to hear.
People of little understanding, attached to Vedic promises of heaven, speak words that are all flower and no fruit, attractive at first; they think nothing surpasses heaven.
Not only non-Vedic views are irresolute: some Vedic interpreters also say rites yield only heaven. Compared with liberation, their words are mere flowers.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna continues describing those who value Vedic ritual only for the pleasures and power it promises.
devanagari:
कामात्मानः स्वर्गपरा जन्मकर्मफलप्रदाम् ।
क्रियाविशेषबहुलां भोगैश्वर्यगतिं प्रति ॥
iast:
kāmātmānaḥ svargaparā janmakarmaphalapradām |
kriyāviśeṣabahulāṃ bhogaiśvaryagatiṃ prati ||
english: full of desire, intent on heaven, offering rebirth as the reward of action, and crowded with special rites for gaining pleasure and power.

school_notes.note: Full of desire and holding heaven as the highest goal, they speak words that promise rebirth as the fruit of action and abound in special rites aimed at pleasure and power.
They claim the Vedas aim only at gaining enjoyment and power.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna concludes that people carried away by desire for pleasure and power cannot develop a steady, resolute mind.
devanagari:
भोगैश्वर्यप्रसक्तानां तयापहृतचेतसाम् ।
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिः समाधौ न विधीयते ॥
iast:
bhogaiśvaryaprasaktānāṃ tayāpahṛtacetasām |
vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ samādhau na vidhīyate ||
english: Those who cling to pleasure and power, their minds carried away by such words, do not develop the resolute understanding that rests in deep concentration.

school_notes.note: In those devoted to pleasure and power, whose discernment is covered over by such words, resolute understanding, whether of Sankhya or yoga, does not arise in the mind.
In such people the conviction about the true self, on which action for liberation depends, never arises; so a seeker of liberation should avoid rites done for desired rewards.
Their understanding does not settle in concentration on the Lord, which comes from rightly established knowledge and is the means to liberation.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna urges Arjuna to look beyond the rewards promised by Vedic ritual and rise above the three gunas, the qualities of nature.
devanagari:
त्रैगुण्यविषया वेदा निस्त्रैगुण्यो भवार्जुन ।
निर्द्वन्द्वो नित्यसत्त्वस्थो निर्योगक्षेम आत्मवान् ॥
iast:
traiguṇyaviṣayā vedā nistraiguṇyo bhavārjuna |
nirdvandvo nityasattvastho niryogakṣema ātmavān ||
english: The Vedas deal with the three gunas. Rise above the three gunas, Arjuna: be free of the pairs of opposites, always grounded in purity, unconcerned with getting and keeping, and centred in the self.

school_notes.note: The Vedas have worldly existence, the realm of the three gunas, as their subject; you should be free of desire, beyond the opposites, always in sattva, and unconcerned with gaining or keeping things.
Out of great care, the Vedas teach what is good for people dominated by each of the gunas; Arjuna should rise above that and grow in sattva alone.
Because the Vedas speak indirectly, they seem to be about heaven and other rewards tied to the gunas; do not be misled by that apparent sense. The Vedas themselves are not being rejected.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna compares the Vedas' rewards to a well beside a flood: for one who knows the truth, they add nothing.
devanagari:
यावानर्थ उदपाने सर्वतः संप्लुतोदके ।
तावान्सर्वेषु वेदेषु ब्राह्मणस्य विजानतः ॥
iast:
yāvānartha udapāne sarvataḥ saṃplutodake |
tāvānsarveṣu vedeṣu brāhmaṇasya vijānataḥ ||
english: As much use as there is in a small well when water is flooding everywhere, so much is there in all the Vedas for a brahmin who truly knows.

school_notes.note: Just as every use of wells and ponds is contained in a great flood of water, the fruit of all Vedic rites is contained in the knowledge of the brahmin, here a renunciant who knows the highest truth.
As a thirsty person takes from a full reservoir only what they need to drink, a Vedic seeker of liberation takes from the Vedas only what leads to liberation.
Whatever fruit all the Vedas give is included in the fruit of the one who knows; 'brahmin' here means one with direct knowledge of Brahman.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna turns from the nature of the self to how to act: with a steady mind, doing one's work without clinging to results (2.39-2.53).
devanagari:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन ।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥
iast:
karmaṇyevādhikāraste mā phaleṣu kadācana |
mā karmaphalaheturbhūrmā te saṅgo'stvakarmaṇi ||
english: Your right is to the work alone, never to its results. Do not let the results be your motive, and do not become attached to doing nothing.

school_notes.note: Arjuna's entitlement is to action, not yet to the path of pure knowledge. Never thirst for results, because acting from that thirst makes one a cause of further birth; but this must not become a liking for inaction either.

Work done for its fruit binds; work done without desire for fruit, as worship of the Lord, leads to liberation. One should also reflect that one is not the sole doer: agency rests with the guṇas or with the Lord.

The ban on acting for results applies even to the wise, and all the more to others, since results do not depend on oneself alone. Scripture's promises of rewards are only an inducement, like sweetening medicine.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna defines yoga as evenness of mind, acting without attachment to success or failure.
devanagari:
योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनंजय ।
सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते ॥
iast:
yogasthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā dhanaṃjaya |
siddhyasiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṃ yoga ucyate ||
english: Established in yoga, do your work, Arjuna, giving up attachment and staying the same in success and failure. This evenness of mind is called yoga.

school_notes.note: Act only for the Lord's sake, giving up even the attachment 'may the Lord be pleased with me'. Success here is the purity of mind that leads to knowledge; staying even in success and failure is itself the yoga.
Give up attachment to kingdom and kin and do your work, such as fighting, even-minded about victory or defeat; yoga here is this evenness, a settled mind.
Clarifies the previous verse: yoga is the means; giving up fondness for results makes one even in success and failure.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna contrasts action driven by results with action guided by an even, clear understanding.
devanagari:
दूरेण ह्यवरं कर्म बुद्धियोगाद्धनंजय ।
बुद्धौ शरणमन्विच्छ कृपणाः फलहेतवः ॥
iast:
dūreṇa hyavaraṃ karma buddhiyogāddhanaṃjaya |
buddhau śaraṇamanviccha kṛpaṇāḥ phalahetavaḥ ||
english: Action done for its results is far inferior to the discipline of understanding, Arjuna. Seek refuge in that understanding; those whose motive is the result are pitiable.

school_notes.note: Action done for results is far inferior, since it causes birth and death. Take refuge in the understanding of evenness, or in the knowledge it ripens into; those who act for results are wretched.
Action with this discipline removes all worldly suffering and leads to liberation; action without it leads to the endless suffering of rebirth.
The discipline of understanding is the means to knowledge; take your stand in knowledge. 'Those whose motive is the result' act for the fruit.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that acting with an even mind frees a person from the binding effects of good and bad deeds.
devanagari:
बुद्धियुक्तो जहातीह उभे सुकृतदुष्कृते ।
तस्माद्योगाय युज्यस्व योगः कर्मसु कौशलम् ॥
iast:
buddhiyukto jahātīha ubhe sukṛtaduṣkṛte |
tasmādyogāya yujyasva yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam ||
english: One joined with this understanding leaves behind both good and bad deeds, here in this life. So devote yourself to yoga: yoga is skill in action.

school_notes.note: Joined with even understanding, one sheds both merit and demerit through purity of mind and knowledge. Skill in action is doing one's own duty with the mind offered to the Lord, even-minded in success and failure.
Acting with this understanding, one sheds the endless merit and demerit, piled up since beginningless time, that cause bondage. This discipline in action is 'skill': it takes great capacity.
The knower gives up only the unwanted fruits of good deeds, such as another human birth, not the great fruit of worship; he cites the Upanishads to show that a knower's good karma is not lost.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes where selfless action leads: freedom from rebirth and a state beyond suffering.
devanagari:
कर्मजं बुद्धियुक्ता हि फलं त्यक्त्वा मनीषिणः ।
जन्मबन्धविनिर्मुक्ताः पदं गच्छन्त्यनामयम् ॥
iast:
karmajaṃ buddhiyuktā hi phalaṃ tyaktvā manīṣiṇaḥ |
janmabandhavinirmuktāḥ padaṃ gacchantyanāmayam ||
english: The wise, joined with this understanding, give up the fruit that action brings; freed from the bondage of rebirth, they reach the state beyond all suffering.

school_notes.note: Giving up the fruit of action, good or bad births, through even understanding, the wise are freed from the bondage of birth even while living, and reach Viṣṇu's highest state, liberation.
Acting while giving up the fruit, they are freed from the bondage of birth and reach the state free of suffering, as all the Upanishads teach.
The method: give up the fruit by offering it to the Lord without desire. This yoga of action is a means to knowledge, and knowledge is the means to liberation.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna tells Arjuna that once his mind clears, he will no longer be swayed by the many promises of ritual and teaching.
devanagari:
यदा ते मोहकलिलं बुद्धिर्व्यतितरिष्यति ।
तदा गन्तासि निर्वेदं श्रोतव्यस्य श्रुतस्य च ॥
iast:
yadā te mohakalilaṃ buddhirvyatitariṣyati |
tadā gantāsi nirvedaṃ śrotavyasya śrutasya ca ||
english: When your understanding crosses beyond the thicket of delusion, you will become indifferent to what you have heard and to what you have yet to hear.

school_notes.note: When your mind passes beyond the confusion that blurs self and non-self, you will gain dispassion, and what has been heard and what remains to be heard will seem fruitless.

When your mind, cleansed by acting this way, passes beyond the delusion that clings to petty rewards, you will turn away of yourself from the rewards you have heard of and those you have yet to hear of.
Answers how long a seeker must keep acting this way: until 'nirveda', which he reads not as disgust but as complete attainment.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the goal of this discipline: a mind steady and settled, no longer pulled in different directions.
devanagari:
श्रुतिविप्रतिपन्ना ते यदा स्थास्यति निश्चला ।
समाधावचला बुद्धिस्तदा योगमवाप्स्यसि ॥
iast:
śrutivipratipannā te yadā sthāsyati niścalā |
samādhāvacalā buddhistadā yogamavāpsyasi ||
english: When your understanding, unsettled by all you have heard, stands firm and unmoving in deep concentration, then you will attain yoga.

school_notes.note: Your mind, distracted by the many Vedic teachings on means and ends, will reach yoga when it becomes still and settles, unwavering, in the self.

When the understanding gained from hearing me settles steadily in a mind purified by unattached action, you will attain yoga, the vision of the self. Action grounded in knowledge leads to steady wisdom.

When the mind, once confused by the Vedas, stands firm through knowledge that accords with their true meaning, unshaken even by contrary words, and rests in bliss through direct vision of Brahman, the means is accomplished.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna asks Krishna to describe the person of steady wisdom, opening the portrait in 2.55-2.72.
devanagari:
स्थितप्रज्ञस्य का भाषा समाधिस्थस्य केशव ।
स्थितधीः किं प्रभाषेत किमासीत व्रजेत किम् ॥
iast:
sthitaprajñasya kā bhāṣā samādhisthasya keśava |
sthitadhīḥ kiṃ prabhāṣeta kimāsīta vrajeta kim ||
english: Krishna, how would you describe a person of steady wisdom, settled in deep concentration? How does someone of steady mind speak, how do they sit, how do they move?

school_notes.note: Arjuna asks for the marks of one whose wisdom, 'I am the supreme Brahman', is firmly established.
Arjuna asks what words describe such a person's nature and how such a person acts, since describing their conduct also reveals their nature.
'Description' (bhāṣā) means the distinguishing mark: Arjuna asks for the marks of one whose knowledge is steady.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna begins his portrait of the person of steady wisdom: free of cravings and content within.
devanagari:
प्रजहाति यदा कामान्सर्वान्पार्थ मनोगतान् ।
आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते ॥
iast:
prajahāti yadā kāmānsarvānpārtha manogatān |
ātmanyevātmanā tuṣṭaḥ sthitaprajñastadocyate ||
english: Son of Pritha, when a person gives up every desire that enters the mind and is content in the self, by the self, that person is said to be of steady wisdom.

school_notes.note: When one gives up all desires and, independent of outward gains, is content in the inner self, one is called steady in wisdom.
Content in the self through a mind resting on the self alone, one lets go of every other desire; this is the peak of steadiness in knowledge.
Through remaining past karma even the wise may keep slight desires, as sages like Śuka did, so 'all desires' means practically all.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna continues: the person of steady wisdom is not shaken by sorrow and is free of craving, fear and anger.
devanagari:
दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः ।
वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते ॥
iast:
duḥkheṣvanudvignamanāḥ sukheṣu vigataspṛhaḥ |
vītarāgabhayakrodhaḥ sthitadhīrmunirucyate ||
english: One whose mind is not shaken by sorrows, who does not crave pleasures, and who is free of passion, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.

school_notes.note: Unshaken when sorrows come, without craving when pleasures come, and free of passion, fear and anger: such a person is a sage, a renunciant of steady wisdom.

Not distressed at losing what is dear, not longing for pleasant things even when they are near, and free of craving, of fear of loss, and of anger, which is one's own mind's reaction to someone who causes pain.
These marks of the wise are also the means for the one seeking knowledge.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna adds that the steady person meets good and bad fortune without elation or resentment.
devanagari:
यः सर्वत्रानभिस्नेहस्तत्तत्प्राप्य शुभाशुभम् ।
नाभिनन्दति न द्वेष्टि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
iast:
yaḥ sarvatrānabhisnehastattatprāpya śubhāśubham |
nābhinandati na dveṣṭi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||
english: One who is without attachment anywhere, who neither rejoices at good fortune nor resents misfortune, has wisdom that is firmly established.

school_notes.note: Without attachment even to body and life, neither delighted by good nor resentful of bad, such a person has wisdom born of discernment, firmly established.
Indifferent towards what is dear, neither delighted nor resentful at gaining or losing it: this too is steady wisdom, at a lower stage than the last.
Because they are unattached everywhere, they neither delight nor resent on meeting good or bad.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives the image of the tortoise for mastery over the senses.
devanagari:
यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः ।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
iast:
yadā saṃharate cāyaṃ kūrmo'ṅgānīva sarvaśaḥ |
indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyastasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||
english: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs, a person withdraws the senses completely from their objects, that person's wisdom is firmly established.

school_notes.note: As a tortoise draws in its limbs out of fear, one devoted to knowledge draws the senses back from all their objects.

The moment the senses reach for their objects, such a person withdraws them like a tortoise and fixes the mind on the self. He reads 2.55-2.58 as four stages of steadiness in knowledge, each leading to the one before it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that simply avoiding sense objects does not remove the craving for them; only seeing the highest does.
devanagari:
विषया विनिवर्तन्ते निराहारस्य देहिनः ।
रसवर्जं रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते ॥
iast:
viṣayā vinivartante nirāhārasya dehinaḥ |
rasavarjaṃ raso'pyasya paraṃ dṛṣṭvā nivartate ||
english: When an embodied person stops feeding the senses, their objects fall away, but the taste for them remains; even that taste fades once the supreme is seen.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna warns that the senses can overpower even a wise person who is making an effort.
devanagari:
यततो ह्यपि कौन्तेय पुरुषस्य विपश्चितः ।
इन्द्रियाणि प्रमाथीनि हरन्ति प्रसभं मनः ॥
iast:
yatato hyapi kaunteya puruṣasya vipaścitaḥ |
indriyāṇi pramāthīni haranti prasabhaṃ manaḥ ||
english: Even when a wise person is striving, son of Kunti, the turbulent senses forcibly carry the mind away.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives the remedy: restrain the senses and fix the mind on him.
devanagari:
तानि सर्वाणि संयम्य युक्त आसीत मत्परः ।
वशे हि यस्येन्द्रियाणि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
iast:
tāni sarvāṇi saṃyamya yukta āsīta matparaḥ |
vaśe hi yasyendriyāṇi tasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||
english: Having restrained them all, one should sit disciplined, intent on me. One whose senses are under control has wisdom that is firmly established.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna traces how brooding on sense objects leads step by step to anger (2.62-2.63).
devanagari:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते ।
सङ्गात्संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
iast:
dhyāyato viṣayānpuṃsaḥ saṅgasteṣūpajāyate |
saṅgātsaṃjāyate kāmaḥ kāmātkrodho'bhijāyate ||
english: When a person dwells on the objects of the senses, attachment to them arises; from attachment comes desire, and from desire comes anger.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna completes the chain from brooding to ruin: anger clouds judgement until reason itself is lost.
devanagari:
क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः ।
स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥
iast:
krodhādbhavati saṃmohaḥ saṃmohātsmṛtivibhramaḥ |
smṛtibhraṃśādbuddhināśo buddhināśātpraṇaśyati ||
english: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, confused memory; from confused memory, the loss of reason; and when reason is lost, a person is ruined.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna shows the alternative to the chain of craving: living among sense objects without attraction or aversion brings calm.
devanagari:
रागद्वेषवियुक्तैस्तु विषयानिन्द्रियैश्चरन् ।
आत्मवश्यैर्विधेयात्मा प्रसादमधिगच्छति ॥
iast:
rāgadveṣaviyuktaistu viṣayānindriyaiścaran |
ātmavaśyairvidheyātmā prasādamadhigacchati ||
english: But one who moves among the objects of the senses with senses free of attraction and aversion, under the self's control, with a disciplined mind, attains inner calm.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes what inner calm brings: the end of sorrow and a steady mind.
devanagari:
प्रसादे सर्वदुःखानां हानिरस्योपजायते ।
प्रसन्नचेतसो ह्याशु बुद्धिः पर्यवतिष्ठते ॥
iast:
prasāde sarvaduḥkhānāṃ hānirasyopajāyate |
prasannacetaso hyāśu buddhiḥ paryavatiṣṭhate ||
english: In that calm, all sorrows come to an end; for the understanding of one whose mind is calm soon becomes steady.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains why discipline matters: without it there is no clarity, no peace, and so no happiness.
devanagari:
नास्ति बुद्धिरयुक्तस्य न चायुक्तस्य भावना ।
न चाभावयतः शान्तिरशान्तस्य कुतः सुखम् ॥
iast:
nāsti buddhirayuktasya na cāyuktasya bhāvanā |
na cābhāvayataḥ śāntiraśāntasya kutaḥ sukham ||
english: One who is undisciplined has no understanding and no power of contemplation; without contemplation there is no peace, and without peace, how can there be happiness?
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives the image of a boat blown off course to show how the senses can sweep away judgement.
devanagari:
इन्द्रियाणां हि चरतां यन्मनोऽनु विधीयते ।
तदस्य हरति प्रज्ञां वायुर्नावमिवाम्भसि ॥
iast:
indriyāṇāṃ hi caratāṃ yanmano'nu vidhīyate |
tadasya harati prajñāṃ vāyurnāvamivāmbhasi ||
english: When the mind follows the wandering senses, it carries away a person's wisdom, as the wind carries away a boat on the water.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna concludes his teaching on the senses: mastery over them is the mark of steady wisdom.
devanagari:
तस्माद्यस्य महाबाहो निगृहीतानि सर्वशः ।
इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता ॥
iast:
tasmādyasya mahābāho nigṛhītāni sarvaśaḥ |
indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyastasya prajñā pratiṣṭhitā ||
english: So, mighty-armed one, a person whose senses are completely held back from their objects has wisdom that is firmly established.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna contrasts the outlook of the sage with that of ordinary people: what one sees as real, the other does not.
devanagari:
या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी ।
यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः ॥
iast:
yā niśā sarvabhūtānāṃ tasyāṃ jāgarti saṃyamī |
yasyāṃ jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśā paśyato muneḥ ||
english: What is night for all beings is the time of waking for the self-controlled; and when other beings are awake, that is night for the sage who truly sees.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna compares the person of steady wisdom to the ocean, which rivers keep filling without disturbing it.
devanagari:
आपूर्यमाणमचलप्रतिष्ठं समुद्रमापः प्रविशन्ति यद्वत् ।
तद्वत्कामा यं प्रविशन्ति सर्वे स शान्तिमाप्नोति न कामकामी ॥
iast:
āpūryamāṇamacalapratiṣṭhaṃ samudramāpaḥ praviśanti yadvat |
tadvatkāmā yaṃ praviśanti sarve sa śāntimāpnoti na kāmakāmī ||
english: As waters flow into the ocean, which is always being filled yet stays still within its bounds, so the person into whom all desires flow in this way finds peace; not the one who chases desires.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna sums up the person of steady wisdom: free of craving, possessiveness and ego, and at peace.
devanagari:
विहाय कामान्यः सर्वान् पुमांश्चरति निःस्पृहः ।
निर्ममो निरहंकारः स शान्तिमधिगच्छति ॥
iast:
vihāya kāmānyaḥ sarvān pumāṃścarati niḥspṛhaḥ |
nirmamo nirahaṃkāraḥ sa śāntimadhigacchati ||
english: A person who gives up all desires and lives free of longing, without any sense of 'mine' and without ego, attains peace.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna closes chapter 2: steady wisdom is the state of Brahman, which leads to final peace even at the hour of death.
devanagari:
एषा ब्राह्मी स्थितिः पार्थ नैनां प्राप्य विमुह्यति ।
स्थित्वास्यामन्तकालेऽपि ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृच्छति ॥
iast:
eṣā brāhmī sthitiḥ pārtha naināṃ prāpya vimuhyati |
sthitvāsyāmantakāle'pi brahmanirvāṇamṛcchati ||
english: This is the state of Brahman, son of Pritha. Having reached it, a person is never deluded again; remaining in it even at the hour of death, they attain the peace of Brahman.
licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna, confused by Krishna's praise of understanding over action, asks why he must still fight, opening chapter 3 on action.
devanagari:
ज्यायसी चेत्कर्मणस्ते मता बुद्धिर्जनार्दन ।
तत्किं कर्मणि घोरे मां नियोजयसि केशव ॥
iast:
jyāyasī cetkarmaṇaste matā buddhirjanārdana |
tatkiṃ karmaṇi ghore māṃ niyojayasi keśava ||
english: Krishna, if you think that understanding is better than action, then why do you urge me into this terrible action?

school_notes.note: Arjuna's question shows that knowledge and action are not meant to be combined in one person: if they were a single combined means, he could not have set understanding apart as better than action.
Steadiness in knowledge, reached by withdrawing all the senses, was said to be the means of seeing the self; so Arjuna asks why Krishna urges him into action, its opposite.
Chapter 2 taught the self and the means to knowledge; chapter 3 rejects inaction and enjoins action as a means to knowledge. Arjuna asks why, if knowledge is far better (2.49), he is urged into war.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna asks Krishna for one clear teaching, since praise of both knowledge and action has confused him.
devanagari:
व्यामिश्रेणेव वाक्येन बुद्धिं मोहयसीव मे ।
तदेकं वद निश्चित्य येन श्रेयोऽहमाप्नुयाम् ॥
iast:
vyāmiśreṇeva vākyena buddhiṃ mohayasīva me |
tadekaṃ vada niścitya yena śreyo'hamāpnuyām ||
english: With words that seem mixed, you seem to confuse my mind. So tell me, decisively, the one thing by which I may reach what is best.

school_notes.note: Krishna speaks clearly, but to Arjuna's limited understanding the words seem mixed: the one who came to remove his confusion seems to add to it.
Telling him to act, the opposite of the knowledge that withdraws the senses, seems contradictory, so Arjuna asks for one unmixed teaching he can follow.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna answers that there are two paths, knowledge and action, suited to different people.
devanagari:
लोकेऽस्मिन्द्विविधा निष्ठा पुरा प्रोक्ता मयानघ ।
ज्ञानयोगेन सांख्यानां कर्मयोगेन योगिनाम् ॥
iast:
loke'smindvividhā niṣṭhā purā proktā mayānagha |
jñānayogena sāṃkhyānāṃ karmayogena yoginām ||
english: As I said before, sinless one, there are two paths in this world: the path of knowledge for people of contemplation, and the path of action for people of action.

school_notes.note: At the beginning of creation the Lord taught two paths to those qualified for scripture: the path of knowledge for those who discern the highest truth, and the path of action for those engaged in action.
Not everyone who longs for liberation is at once fit for the path of knowledge; action done without desire for its fruit, as worship of the Supreme Person, prepares them for it.
Some, like Sanaka, give up household duties and rest in knowledge; others, like Janaka, keep their duties and still rest in knowledge. Knowledge is greater, but Arjuna is qualified for action.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that simply avoiding action does not lead to freedom or perfection.
devanagari:
न कर्मणामनारम्भान्नैष्कर्म्यं पुरुषोऽश्नुते ।
न च संन्यसनादेव सिद्धिं समधिगच्छति ॥
iast:
na karmaṇāmanārambhānnaiṣkarmyaṃ puruṣo'śnute |
na ca saṃnyasanādeva siddhiṃ samadhigacchati ||
english: A person does not reach freedom from action by not starting to act, nor attain perfection by renunciation alone.

school_notes.note: Rites such as sacrifice destroy past sin, purify the mind and so lead to knowledge; one does not gain actionlessness just by not acting.
Without doing prescribed action, one does not reach steadiness in knowledge; nor does abandoning action already begun bring it.
Liberation is not won by not doing actions such as war; knowledge alone is its means. If inaction freed us, plants would be liberated.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna points out that no one can stop acting, because nature itself drives all activity.
devanagari:
न हि कश्चित्क्षणमपि जातु तिष्ठत्यकर्मकृत् ।
कार्यते ह्यवशः कर्म सर्वः प्रकृतिजैर्गुणैः ॥
iast:
na hi kaścitkṣaṇamapi jātu tiṣṭhatyakarmakṛt |
kāryate hyavaśaḥ karma sarvaḥ prakṛtijairguṇaiḥ ||
english: No one can remain even for a moment without acting; everyone is driven to act, helplessly, by the qualities born of nature.

school_notes.note: Every being without knowledge is made to act by the three gunas of nature; the path of action is for the unknowing, since the wise are set apart.
Even someone resolved to do nothing is driven to act by the gunas, grown strong through past karma; so destroy past sin through karma yoga and master the gunas.
Actions cannot be given up entirely.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna warns against outward renunciation while the mind still dwells on pleasures.
devanagari:
कर्मेन्द्रियाणि संयम्य य आस्ते मनसा स्मरन् ।
इन्द्रियार्थान्विमूढात्मा मिथ्याचारः स उच्यते ॥
iast:
karmendriyāṇi saṃyamya ya āste manasā smaran |
indriyārthānvimūḍhātmā mithyācāraḥ sa ucyate ||
english: One who holds back the organs of action but sits dwelling in the mind on the objects of the senses is deluded, and is called a hypocrite.

school_notes.note: Holding back the hands and other organs while thinking of sense objects, such a person has a deluded mind and is called false, even sinful, in conduct.
Someone whose sins are not yet destroyed sets out for self-knowledge with an untamed mind and keeps thinking of sense objects; intending one thing and doing another, they are ruined.
Still, one should give up what one can; it is the mind that drives action.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna contrasts the false renouncer with one who acts in the world with self-control and without attachment.
devanagari:
यस्त्विन्द्रियाणि मनसा नियम्यारभतेऽर्जुन ।
कर्मेन्द्रियैः कर्मयोगमसक्तः स विशिष्यते ॥
iast:
yastvindriyāṇi manasā niyamyārabhate'rjuna |
karmendriyaiḥ karmayogamasaktaḥ sa viśiṣyate ||
english: But one who controls the senses with the mind, Arjuna, and without attachment engages the organs of action in the path of action, stands out.
