school_notes.note: One who, unattached and not seeking results, takes up the path of action with the organs of action is superior to the false renouncer.
Such a person is less likely to slip, and so stands above even one devoted to the path of knowledge.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna urges Arjuna to do his duty, since action is better than inaction and life itself depends on it.
devanagari:
नियतं कुरु कर्म त्वं कर्म ज्यायो ह्यकर्मणः ।
शरीरयात्रापि च ते न प्रसिद्ध्येदकर्मणः ॥
iast:
niyataṃ kuru karma tvaṃ karma jyāyo hyakarmaṇaḥ |
śarīrayātrāpi ca te na prasiddhyedakarmaṇaḥ ||
english: Do the work that is yours to do, for action is better than inaction; without action, you could not even keep your body alive.

school_notes.note: Do the regular duty scripture assigns you; action is better than not acting, since without it even your body could not be kept going.
Action comes naturally to one bound up with nature, so it is easier and less prone to lapses; action is better even than the path of knowledge, which is what 'inaction' means here.
Do the duty suited to your station and stage of life.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna introduces sacrifice (yajña): action done as an offering does not bind a person.
devanagari:
यज्ञार्थात्कर्मणोऽन्यत्र लोकोऽयं कर्मबन्धनः ।
तदर्थं कर्म कौन्तेय मुक्तसङ्गः समाचर ॥
iast:
yajñārthātkarmaṇo'nyatra loko'yaṃ karmabandhanaḥ |
tadarthaṃ karma kaunteya muktasaṅgaḥ samācara ||
english: This world is bound by action, except for action done as sacrifice. So, son of Kunti, act for that purpose, free of attachment.

school_notes.note: Citing the Veda's 'sacrifice is Viṣṇu', action done for the Lord does not bind; any other action does.
Earning wealth and other work done for sacrifice and the like does not bind; work done for one's own ends does. So act for sacrifice, free of attachment to personal gain.
Action is said to bind, but action done for Viṣṇu, who is sacrifice, without attachment, does not.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna recounts the creation story in which the creator gives sacrifice to humanity as the source of prosperity (3.10-3.16).
devanagari:
सहयज्ञाः प्रजाः सृष्ट्वा पुरोवाच प्रजापतिः ।
अनेन प्रसविष्यध्वमेष वोऽस्त्विष्टकामधुक् ॥
iast:
sahayajñāḥ prajāḥ sṛṣṭvā purovāca prajāpatiḥ |
anena prasaviṣyadhvameṣa vo'stviṣṭakāmadhuk ||
english: In the beginning, the Lord of creatures created people together with sacrifice and said: "By this you will prosper; let this be the cow that grants your wishes.

school_notes.note: Prajāpati, the creator, brought forth beings along with sacrifice and told them to grow by it, since it would yield all they desire.
Takes 'Lord of creatures' to mean Nārāyaṇa, Lord of all, who out of compassion created beings lost in matter, together with sacrifice, so they could reach their goals.

speaker: Krishna
context: The creator's teaching continues: gods and humans sustain each other through sacrifice.
devanagari:
देवान्भावयतानेन ते देवा भावयन्तु वः ।
परस्परं भावयन्तः श्रेयः परमवाप्स्यथ ॥
iast:
devānbhāvayatānena te devā bhāvayantu vaḥ |
parasparaṃ bhāvayantaḥ śreyaḥ paramavāpsyatha ||
english: With this, nourish the gods, and let the gods nourish you; nourishing one another, you will reach the highest good.

school_notes.note: Nourish Indra and the other gods with sacrifice, and they will nourish you with rain; so you will reach the highest good, liberation through knowledge, or else heaven.
The gods are Krishna's body and have him as their self; worshipped through sacrifice, they sustain you, and so you reach liberation. He cites 9.24.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna warns that enjoying life's gifts without giving back is a kind of theft.
devanagari:
इष्टान्भोगान्हि वो देवा दास्यन्ते यज्ञभाविताः ।
तैर्दत्तानप्रदायैभ्यो यो भुङ्क्ते स्तेन एव सः ॥
iast:
iṣṭānbhogānhi vo devā dāsyante yajñabhāvitāḥ |
tairdattānapradāyaibhyo yo bhuṅkte stena eva saḥ ||
english: Nourished by sacrifice, the gods will give you the pleasures you desire." Whoever enjoys their gifts without offering anything back to them is simply a thief.

school_notes.note: Whoever enjoys the gods' gifts without repaying that debt by offering to them, feeding only their own body and senses, is a thief.
The gods, pleased by sacrifice, give what is needed for further worship; whoever uses their gifts only for themselves is a thief.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna contrasts those who share what they have with those who live only for themselves.
devanagari:
यज्ञशिष्टाशिनः सन्तो मुच्यन्ते सर्वकिल्बिषैः ।
भुञ्जते ते त्वघं पापा ये पचन्त्यात्मकारणात् ॥
iast:
yajñaśiṣṭāśinaḥ santo mucyante sarvakilbiṣaiḥ |
bhuñjate te tvaghaṃ pāpā ye pacantyātmakāraṇāt ||
english: The good, who eat what remains after sacrifice, are freed from all wrongs; but the wicked, who cook only for themselves, eat sin.

school_notes.note: Those who eat the remains of sacrifice are freed from all sins, including the unavoidable harm done in running a household, such as at the hearth; those who cook only for themselves eat sin.
Those who prepare food as worship of the Supreme and live on what remains are freed of the sins that block the vision of the self.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the cycle that links food, rain, sacrifice and action (3.14-3.16).
devanagari:
अन्नाद्भवन्ति भूतानि पर्जन्यादन्नसम्भवः ।
यज्ञाद्भवति पर्जन्यो यज्ञः कर्मसमुद्भवः ॥
iast:
annādbhavanti bhūtāni parjanyādannasambhavaḥ |
yajñādbhavati parjanyo yajñaḥ karmasamudbhavaḥ ||
english: Beings come from food; food comes from rain; rain comes from sacrifice; and sacrifice comes from action.

school_notes.note: Quoting Manu: an offering in the fire reaches the sun, the sun brings rain, rain brings food, and food brings beings; sacrifice arises from the action of priest and patron.
That beings come from food and food from rain is plain to all; that rain comes from sacrifice is known from scripture.
Parjanya, the deity of the rain-cloud cycle, arises from sacrifice; he also cites Manu.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna traces action back to Brahman and the Imperishable, showing that sacrifice is rooted in the divine.
devanagari:
कर्म ब्रह्मोद्भवं विद्धि ब्रह्माक्षरसमुद्भवम् ।
तस्मात्सर्वगतं ब्रह्म नित्यं यज्ञे प्रतिष्ठितम् ॥
iast:
karma brahmodbhavaṃ viddhi brahmākṣarasamudbhavam |
tasmātsarvagataṃ brahma nityaṃ yajñe pratiṣṭhitam ||
english: Know that action arises from Brahman, and Brahman arises from the Imperishable. So the all-pervading Brahman is always established in sacrifice.

school_notes.note: 'Brahman' here is the Veda, which reveals what action is; the Veda comes from the Imperishable, the Supreme Self, like breath from a person, and so is always established in sacrifice.
'Brahman' here means prakṛti in the form of the body, as in 14.3; so action arises from the body, which is a transformation of prakṛti.
Action arises from Brahman, the Lord, who causes all good action, since inert things cannot act on their own.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna concludes that refusing one's part in this cycle of giving makes a life empty.
devanagari:
एवं प्रवर्तितं चक्रं नानुवर्तयतीह यः ।
अघायुरिन्द्रियारामो मोघं पार्थ स जीवति ॥
iast:
evaṃ pravartitaṃ cakraṃ nānuvartayatīha yaḥ |
aghāyurindriyārāmo moghaṃ pārtha sa jīvati ||
english: Whoever does not keep turning the wheel set in motion in this way, son of Pritha, lives in vain, a sinful life of pleasing the senses.

school_notes.note: One qualified for action who does not follow the wheel of Veda and sacrifice set going by the Lord lives a sinful life, given over to the senses, in vain.
The wheel: food yields living bodies, bodies act, action yields sacrifice, sacrifice brings rain, rain brings food. One on the path of action who does not keep it turning lives in vain.
Whoever does not keep the world's wheel turning harms it, so their life is lived for sin.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the exception: someone fully content in the self has no duty left to fulfil (3.17-3.18).
devanagari:
यस्त्वात्मरतिरेव स्यादात्मतृप्तश्च मानवः ।
आत्मन्येव च सन्तुष्टस्तस्य कार्यं न विद्यते ॥
iast:
yastvātmaratireva syādātmatṛptaśca mānavaḥ |
ātmanyeva ca santuṣṭastasya kāryaṃ na vidyate ||
english: But for one who delights in the self alone, is satisfied by the self, and is content in the self alone, there is nothing that must be done.

school_notes.note: Such a person, a renunciant devoted to knowledge of the self, finds delight and contentment within rather than in outer things, and has no duty left.
One who by nature delights in the self, needing neither the path of knowledge nor of action, has nothing to do to see the self, since they always already see it.
Distinguishes delight, satisfaction and contentment, all arising from seeing the Supreme Self.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna continues: the one content in the self gains nothing from action and loses nothing by not acting.
devanagari:
नैव तस्य कृतेनार्थो नाकृतेनेह कश्चन ।
न चास्य सर्वभूतेषु कश्चिदर्थव्यपाश्रयः ॥
iast:
naiva tasya kṛtenārtho nākṛteneha kaścana |
na cāsya sarvabhūteṣu kaścidarthavyapāśrayaḥ ||
english: Such a person has nothing to gain in this world by acting and nothing to lose by not acting, and depends on no being for anything.

school_notes.note: Delighting in the Supreme Self, they gain nothing by acting and incur no fault by not acting, and they need nothing from any being, from Brahmā down to the smallest thing.
They need no means to see the self, and nothing in the elements serves them as either goal or means.
Such a person gains nothing from action beyond their delight in the self, and incurs no fault by omitting rites such as the twilight prayer.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna draws the practical conclusion for Arjuna: keep acting, but without attachment.
devanagari:
तस्मादसक्तः सततं कार्यं कर्म समाचर ।
असक्तो ह्याचरन्कर्म परमाप्नोति पूरुषः ॥
iast:
tasmādasaktaḥ satataṃ kāryaṃ karma samācara |
asakto hyācarankarma paramāpnoti pūruṣaḥ ||
english: So, without attachment, always do the work that should be done; for by acting without attachment a person reaches the highest.

school_notes.note: Without attachment, always do your regular duty; acting for the Lord, one reaches liberation through purity of mind.
Keep acting, unattached and aware that you are not the doer, until you reach the self; one reaches the self through karma yoga itself.
Only in the highest absorption is there nothing to do, so keep acting.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna cites King Janaka as an example and introduces acting for the welfare of the world.
devanagari:
कर्मणैव हि संसिद्धिमास्थिता जनकादयः ।
लोकसंग्रहमेवापि संपश्यन्कर्तुमर्हसि ॥
iast:
karmaṇaiva hi saṃsiddhimāsthitā janakādayaḥ |
lokasaṃgrahamevāpi saṃpaśyankartumarhasi ||
english: It was through action that Janaka and others reached perfection. You should act, too, if only with an eye to holding the world together.

school_notes.note: If kings like Janaka had full knowledge, they kept acting for the world's welfare; if not, they reached liberation as action purified their minds.
Even those fit for the path of knowledge do better with karma yoga, which is why royal sages like Janaka, foremost among the wise, reached the self through it.
Janaka and others acted while already having knowledge, as the Mahābhārata shows; action is a means to knowledge.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains why leaders must act well: others follow their example.
devanagari:
यद्यदाचरति श्रेष्ठस्तत्तदेवेतरो जनः ।
स यत्प्रमाणं कुरुते लोकस्तदनुवर्तते ॥
iast:
yadyadācarati śreṣṭhastattadevetaro janaḥ |
sa yatpramāṇaṃ kurute lokastadanuvartate ||
english: Whatever a leading person does, others do too; whatever standard they set, the world follows.

school_notes.note: Whatever the eminent do, their followers do too; whatever they treat as authoritative, in worldly or Vedic matters, others accept.
One renowned for knowing and practising scripture sets the pattern others copy, so such a person must fully carry out the duties of their station for the world's sake.
Whatever words and conduct such a person treats as authoritative, others follow.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives himself as the example: though he needs nothing, he still acts (3.22-3.24).
devanagari:
न मे पार्थास्ति कर्तव्यं त्रिषु लोकेषु किंचन ।
नानवाप्तमवाप्तव्यं वर्त एव च कर्मणि ॥
iast:
na me pārthāsti kartavyaṃ triṣu lokeṣu kiṃcana |
nānavāptamavāptavyaṃ varta eva ca karmaṇi ||
english: Son of Pritha, there is nothing in the three worlds that I must do, nothing I lack or need to gain; and yet I keep on acting.

school_notes.note: Nothing remains for me to gain, and yet I continue in action.
I, the Lord of all, whose every wish is fulfilled and who takes form as god or human at will, have nothing to do; yet I act to protect the world.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that if he stopped acting, people everywhere would follow his example.
devanagari:
यदि ह्यहं न वर्तेयं जातु कर्मण्यतन्द्रितः ।
मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः ॥
iast:
yadi hyahaṃ na varteyaṃ jātu karmaṇyatandritaḥ |
mama vartmānuvartante manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ ||
english: For if I ever failed to engage in action tirelessly, son of Pritha, people everywhere would follow my path.

school_notes.note: If I did not act, people would follow me, the foremost, in every way.
Born by my own will in the house of Vasudeva, foremost of the virtuous, if I neglected my family's duties, the virtuous would take that as the rule and follow it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains what would happen if he stopped acting: the world, following his example, would fall into ruin.
devanagari:
उत्सीदेयुरिमे लोका न कुर्यां कर्म चेदहम् ।
संकरस्य च कर्ता स्यामुपहन्यामिमाः प्रजाः ॥
iast:
utsīdeyurime lokā na kuryāṃ karma cedaham |
saṃkarasya ca kartā syāmupahanyāmimāḥ prajāḥ ||
english: If I did not act, these worlds would fall into ruin; I would be the cause of confusion, and I would destroy these people.

school_notes.note: Without the action that sustains the world, the worlds would perish; I would cause confusion and so harm the very people I act to help, which would not befit the Lord.
If I neglected my family's duties, the virtuous, who rely on my example, would perish by failing to keep the scriptural ways; the same holds for Arjuna, a leader among the virtuous.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna tells the wise to act as diligently as others do, but without attachment, for the good of the world.
devanagari:
सक्ताः कर्मण्यविद्वांसो यथा कुर्वन्ति भारत ।
कुर्याद्विद्वांस्तथासक्तश्चिकीर्षुर्लोकसंग्रहम् ॥
iast:
saktāḥ karmaṇyavidvāṃso yathā kurvanti bhārata |
kuryādvidvāṃstathāsaktaścikīrṣurlokasaṃgraham ||
english: Just as the unwise act out of attachment to their work, Arjuna, so the wise should act without attachment, wishing to hold the world together.

school_notes.note: As the unwise act, attached to the fruit, so the wise should act, but unattached, wanting only the world's welfare.
Just as those not yet fit for the path of knowledge practise karma yoga, the wise, though fit for knowledge, should act unattached, protecting the world by their example.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna advises the wise not to unsettle others' commitment to their work, but to lead by example.
devanagari:
न बुद्धिभेदं जनयेदज्ञानां कर्मसङ्गिनाम् ।
जोषयेत्सर्वकर्माणि विद्वान्युक्तः समाचरन् ॥
iast:
na buddhibhedaṃ janayedajñānāṃ karmasaṅginām |
joṣayetsarvakarmāṇi vidvānyuktaḥ samācaran ||
english: The wise should not unsettle the minds of the unknowing who are attached to action; acting with discipline themselves, they should encourage others in all their work.

school_notes.note: The wise should not shake the conviction of those attached to action ('I must do this and enjoy its fruit'), but should do those same actions themselves and so lead others to do them.
Do not suggest to seekers bound to action that there is another way to see the self; rather, even if fit for knowledge, practise karma yoga yourself and show others its worth.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that the sense of being the doer comes from ego, while nature's qualities actually act (3.27-3.29).
devanagari:
प्रकृतेः क्रियमाणानि गुणैः कर्माणि सर्वशः ।
अहंकारविमूढात्मा कर्ताहमिति मन्यते ॥
iast:
prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ |
ahaṃkāravimūḍhātmā kartāhamiti manyate ||
english: All actions are carried out by the gunas of nature, but one deluded by ego thinks, "I am the doer."

school_notes.note: Prakṛti is the balance of the three gunas; all actions are done by its products, body and senses. One whose mind is confused by ego, identifying with body and senses, thinks 'I do this'.
Ego (ahaṅkāra) means taking prakṛti, which is not the 'I', to be 'I'; not knowing the self, one thinks 'I am the doer' of what the gunas do.
The 'gunas of nature' here are the senses and the like; the self, like a reflection, has no action of its own.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes how one who understands the workings of nature stays unattached to action.
devanagari:
तत्त्ववित्तु महाबाहो गुणकर्मविभागयोः ।
गुणा गुणेषु वर्तन्त इति मत्वा न सज्जते ॥
iast:
tattvavittu mahābāho guṇakarmavibhāgayoḥ |
guṇā guṇeṣu vartanta iti matvā na sajjate ||
english: But one who knows the truth about how the gunas and their actions are distinct, mighty-armed one, thinks, "The gunas are acting on the gunas," and does not become attached.

school_notes.note: Knowing that it is the senses (gunas as instruments) that act on their objects (gunas as objects), not the self, such a person does not become attached.
Knowing that sattva and the other gunas work in their own effects, one does not cling to the thought 'I am the doer'.
The gunas are the senses and the like, acting among their objects.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna repeats his advice that the wise should not unsettle those who are still attached to their work.
devanagari:
प्रकृतेर्गुणसंमूढाः सज्जन्ते गुणकर्मसु ।
तानकृत्स्नविदो मन्दान्कृत्स्नविन्न विचालयेत् ॥
iast:
prakṛterguṇasaṃmūḍhāḥ sajjante guṇakarmasu |
tānakṛtsnavido mandānkṛtsnavinna vicālayet ||
english: Those deluded by the gunas of nature become attached to the workings of the gunas. One who knows the whole should not unsettle these slow people of partial knowledge.

school_notes.note: Those attached to action for its results, seeing only the fruit, should not be unsettled by the one who knows the self.
Those of partial knowledge, entangled in nature, cling to action and are not yet fit for the path of knowledge; the one who knows fully should not unsettle them by standing in that path himself.
'Gunas' here means the senses; attachment to objects comes from identifying with the senses.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna sums up his teaching on action: offer every act to him and fight without anxiety.
devanagari:
मयि सर्वाणि कर्माणि संन्यस्याध्यात्मचेतसा ।
निराशीर्निर्ममो भूत्वा युध्यस्व विगतज्वरः ॥
iast:
mayi sarvāṇi karmāṇi saṃnyasyādhyātmacetasā |
nirāśīrnirmamo bhūtvā yudhyasva vigatajvaraḥ ||
english: Surrendering all actions to me, with your mind on the self, free of desire and of any sense of 'mine', fight, with your fever of distress gone.

school_notes.note: Offer all actions to me, Vāsudeva, the all-knowing Lord, thinking 'I act for the Lord like a servant', and fight without longing, possessiveness or sorrow.
Surrender all actions to me, the Lord who dwells in all beings as their inner self, with the knowledge of the self that scripture teaches, and do all your prescribed duties, such as fighting.
Lay all actions on me, setting aside the mistaken idea that the soul is their doer: it is the Lord who does all actions.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna promises freedom to those who follow his teaching on action with faith.
devanagari:
ये मे मतमिदं नित्यमनुतिष्ठन्ति मानवाः ।
श्रद्धावन्तोऽनसूयन्तो मुच्यन्ते तेऽपि कर्मभिः ॥
iast:
ye me matamidaṃ nityamanutiṣṭhanti mānavāḥ |
śraddhāvanto'nasūyanto mucyante te'pi karmabhiḥ ||
english: People who always follow this teaching of mine with faith and without finding fault are also freed from the bonds of action.

school_notes.note: Those who follow my teaching with faith, not finding fault with me, the supreme teacher, are freed from merit and demerit.
Not only those who practise this teaching, but those who have faith in it, and even those who merely do not find fault with it, are all freed.
Even those who act in this spirit are freed, through knowledge; how much more those with direct knowledge.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna warns of the confusion that comes from rejecting this teaching.
devanagari:
ये त्वेतदभ्यसूयन्तो नानुतिष्ठन्ति मे मतम् ।
सर्वज्ञानविमूढांस्तान्विद्धि नष्टानचेतसः ॥
iast:
ye tvetadabhyasūyanto nānutiṣṭhanti me matam |
sarvajñānavimūḍhāṃstānviddhi naṣṭānacetasaḥ ||
english: But those who find fault with my teaching and do not follow it, know them to be confused about all knowledge, lost and without understanding.

school_notes.note: Those who disparage my teaching and do not follow it are confused about all knowledge, ruined and without discernment.
Those who do not act knowing that everything is my body, sustained and directed by me, are confused about all knowledge and so are lost.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna acknowledges how strongly people are driven by their own nature and habits.
devanagari:
सदृशं चेष्टते स्वस्याः प्रकृतेर्ज्ञानवानपि ।
प्रकृतिं यान्ति भूतानि निग्रहः किं करिष्यति ॥
iast:
sadṛśaṃ ceṣṭate svasyāḥ prakṛterjñānavānapi |
prakṛtiṃ yānti bhūtāni nigrahaḥ kiṃ kariṣyati ||
english: Even a wise person acts according to their own nature. Beings follow their nature; what will suppression achieve?

school_notes.note: 'Nature' is the store of tendencies from past deeds, shown in this life; even the wise act according to it, let alone the foolish, so what can forced restraint do?
Even someone who knows from scripture that the self is distinct from nature keeps acting from old habit, since beings follow tendencies built up from beginningless time.
Explains why people do not follow the teaching: 'nature' is past conditioning.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna names attraction and aversion as the enemies to watch for in every experience.
devanagari:
इन्द्रियस्येन्द्रियस्यार्थे रागद्वेषौ व्यवस्थितौ ।
तयोर्न वशमागच्छेत्तौ ह्यस्य परिपन्थिनौ ॥
iast:
indriyasyendriyasyārthe rāgadveṣau vyavasthitau |
tayorna vaśamāgacchettau hyasya paripanthinau ||
english: Attraction and aversion lie in wait in the objects of every sense. Do not come under their control, for they are obstacles on a person's path.

school_notes.note: Attraction to the pleasant and aversion to the unpleasant arise with every sense object; this is where personal effort and scripture apply: do not fall under their sway in the first place.
Craving built up by old habits, and the aversion that follows when it is blocked, seize even someone who has restrained the senses and drive them into action.
Still, restrain them as far as you can: conditioning is strong, holding even Brahmā, yet it can be changed by great effort.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna teaches that one's own path, even imperfectly followed, is better than someone else's.
devanagari:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् ।
स्वधर्मे निधनं श्रेयः परधर्मो भयावहः ॥
iast:
śreyānsvadharmo viguṇaḥ paradharmātsvanuṣṭhitāt |
svadharme nidhanaṃ śreyaḥ paradharmo bhayāvahaḥ ||
english: Better your own duty done imperfectly than another's duty done well. Better to die in your own duty; another's duty is full of danger.

school_notes.note: One's own duty, even lacking in merit, is better than another's done perfectly; even death while doing one's own duty is better than living in another's, which brings fear of hell and the like.

Karma yoga, one's own duty because it comes easily to one bound up with nature, is better even when imperfect than the path of knowledge, which is hard and prone to lapses; dying in it before reaching the goal is still better, since progress continues in the next life.
Answers the objection that war is a terrible duty.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna asks what forces people to act wrongly against their own will, leading to Krishna's teaching on desire.
devanagari:
अथ केन प्रयुक्तोऽयं पापं चरति पूरुषः ।
अनिच्छन्नपि वार्ष्णेय बलादिव नियोजितः ॥
iast:
atha kena prayukto'yaṃ pāpaṃ carati pūruṣaḥ |
anicchannapi vārṣṇeya balādiva niyojitaḥ ||
english: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even without wanting to, as if forced?

school_notes.note: Arjuna asks what drives a person to sin, like a servant ordered by a king, even against their will.
Arjuna asks what makes someone on the path of knowledge pursue sense experience, the 'wrong' here, even without wanting to.
Of the many drivers of action, such as anger and desire, Arjuna asks which is strongest.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna names the enemy: desire, which turns into anger when frustrated (3.37-3.43).
devanagari:
काम एष क्रोध एष रजोगुणसमुद्भवः ।
महाशनो महापाप्मा विद्ध्येनमिह वैरिणम् ॥
iast:
kāma eṣa krodha eṣa rajoguṇasamudbhavaḥ |
mahāśano mahāpāpmā viddhyenamiha vairiṇam ||
english: It is desire; it is anger, born of the guna of rajas. All-devouring and deeply harmful, know it to be the enemy here.

school_notes.note: Desire for sense objects, born of rajas and past tendencies, is the great enemy; when blocked, it turns into anger at whoever obstructs it and drives one to harm others.
The strong driver is desire; anger is the same thing, since it is born of desire (2.62). Even anger at an insult to one's teacher stems from desire.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives three images for how desire covers wisdom.
devanagari:
धूमेनाव्रियते वह्निर्यथादर्शो मलेन च ।
यथोल्बेनावृतो गर्भस्तथा तेनेदमावृतम् ॥
iast:
dhūmenāvriyate vahniryathādarśo malena ca |
yatholbenāvṛto garbhastathā tenedamāvṛtam ||
english: As fire is covered by smoke, a mirror by dust, and an unborn child by the womb, so this is covered by desire.

school_notes.note: Fire by the smoke born with it, a mirror by dirt, an embryo by its membrane: in the same way 'this' is covered by desire.
In the same way, this whole range of beings is covered by desire.
As smoke hides fire, desire hides the Supreme Self; as dirt stops a mirror from reflecting, desire stops the mind from revealing the Supreme; as the womb binds an embryo, desire binds the soul.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes desire as a fire that can never be satisfied.
devanagari:
आवृतं ज्ञानमेतेन ज्ञानिनो नित्यवैरिणा ।
कामरूपेण कौन्तेय दुष्पूरेणानलेन च ॥
iast:
āvṛtaṃ jñānametena jñānino nityavairiṇā |
kāmarūpeṇa kaunteya duṣpūreṇānalena ca ||
english: Wisdom is covered by this constant enemy of the wise, son of Kunti: by desire, which is as hard to satisfy as fire.

school_notes.note: Desire is the constant enemy of the wise in particular: the wise know beforehand that it leads to harm, while the fool sees it as a friend until the suffering comes.
Desire covers the self's knowledge by producing infatuation with objects, and it can never be satisfied.
Even knowledge gained from scripture fails to reveal the Supreme directly when covered by desire; desire is hard to fill and never says 'enough'.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna locates where desire lives: in the senses, mind and intellect.
devanagari:
इन्द्रियाणि मनो बुद्धिरस्याधिष्ठानमुच्यते ।
एतैर्विमोहयत्येष ज्ञानमावृत्य देहिनम् ॥
iast:
indriyāṇi mano buddhirasyādhiṣṭhānamucyate |
etairvimohayatyeṣa jñānamāvṛtya dehinam ||
english: The senses, the mind and the intellect are said to be its seat. Through them it clouds wisdom and deludes the embodied self.

school_notes.note: Senses, mind and intellect are desire's base; through them it covers knowledge and deludes the embodied self.
Desire controls a person through the senses, mind and intellect, turning them towards objects and away from the self.
The enemy's seat is named so it can be destroyed: an enemy whose base is taken falls.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives the method: begin by mastering the senses, then overcome desire.
devanagari:
तस्मात्त्वमिन्द्रियाण्यादौ नियम्य भरतर्षभ ।
पाप्मानं प्रजहि ह्येनं ज्ञानविज्ञाननाशनम् ॥
iast:
tasmāttvamindriyāṇyādau niyamya bharatarṣabha |
pāpmānaṃ prajahi hyenaṃ jñānavijñānanāśanam ||
english: So, best of the Bharatas, first bring your senses under control, and then strike down this evil thing that destroys knowledge and wisdom.

school_notes.note: Control the senses first, then cast off desire, which destroys both knowledge learned from scripture and teachers and its direct experience.
Since desire turns one away from the self, begin, at the very start of the path to liberation, by restraining the senses through karma yoga.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna sets out an inner hierarchy of senses, mind, intellect and what lies beyond, to show where strength lies.
devanagari:
इन्द्रियाणि पराण्याहुरिन्द्रियेभ्यः परं मनः ।
मनसस्तु परा बुद्धिर्यो बुद्धेः परतस्तु सः ॥
iast:
indriyāṇi parāṇyāhurindriyebhyaḥ paraṃ manaḥ |
manasastu parā buddhiryo buddheḥ paratastu saḥ ||
english: The senses are said to be high; higher than the senses is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; and higher than the intellect is he.

school_notes.note: The senses are subtler and more inward than the body; the mind, which deliberates, is higher; the intellect, which decides, is higher still; and beyond the intellect is the embodied self.

Ranks these as obstacles to self-knowledge: busy senses block it; even when they rest, a restless mind blocks it; even when the mind rests, an intellect set on wrong conclusions blocks it. 'He' beyond the intellect is desire itself (see 3.43).
This knowledge is the weapon for killing the enemy; he cites the Kaṭha Upaniṣad that the Person is beyond even the unmanifest.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna ends chapter 3 urging Arjuna to master himself and overcome desire, the hardest enemy.
devanagari:
एवं बुद्धेः परं बुद्ध्वा संस्तभ्यात्मानमात्मना ।
जहि शत्रुं महाबाहो कामरूपं दुरासदम् ॥
iast:
evaṃ buddheḥ paraṃ buddhvā saṃstabhyātmānamātmanā |
jahi śatruṃ mahābāho kāmarūpaṃ durāsadam ||
english: So, knowing what is higher than the intellect, and steadying yourself by yourself, mighty-armed one, strike down this enemy in the form of desire, so hard to overcome.

school_notes.note: Knowing the self beyond the intellect, and steadying the mind through the self, slay this enemy, desire, so hard to grasp.
Knowing desire, the enemy of knowledge, to be stronger even than the intellect, fix your mind on karma yoga with your intellect and destroy this enemy.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna reveals that the yoga he teaches is ancient, passed down from the sun to the first kings (4.1-4.3).
devanagari:
इमं विवस्वते योगं प्रोक्तवानहमव्ययम् ।
विवस्वान्मनवे प्राह मनुरिक्ष्वाकवेऽब्रवीत् ॥
iast:
imaṃ vivasvate yogaṃ proktavānahamavyayam |
vivasvānmanave prāha manurikṣvākave'bravīt ||
english: I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat, the sun; Vivasvat taught it to Manu, and Manu passed it on to Ikshvaku.

school_notes.note: This yoga, taught in the last two chapters, I gave to the sun at the beginning of creation, to strengthen the rulers who protect the world. It is imperishable because its fruit, liberation, is imperishable.

Do not think this yoga was taught now just to spur you to fight: at the dawn of the age I taught it to Vivasvat as the means to liberation for the whole world, and it came down through a line of teachers.
This chapter teaches the Lord's greatness, the kinds of action and the greatness of knowledge; this verse shows the teaching was practised long before.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that the teaching passed through a line of royal sages and was eventually lost.
devanagari:
एवं परम्पराप्राप्तमिमं राजर्षयो विदुः ।
स कालेनेह महता योगो नष्टः परन्तप ॥
iast:
evaṃ paramparāprāptamimaṃ rājarṣayo viduḥ |
sa kāleneha mahatā yogo naṣṭaḥ parantapa ||
english: Handed down in this way, the royal sages knew it. But over a long span of time, scorcher of enemies, this yoga was lost here.

school_notes.note: Royal sages, both kings and sages, knew it through this succession; over a long time the line of teaching was broken.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna tells Arjuna he is receiving this ancient teaching because of their friendship and his devotion.
devanagari:
स एवायं मया तेऽद्य योगः प्रोक्तः पुरातनः ।
भक्तोऽसि मे सखा चेति रहस्यं ह्येतदुत्तमम् ॥
iast:
sa evāyaṃ mayā te'dya yogaḥ proktaḥ purātanaḥ |
bhakto'si me sakhā ceti rahasyaṃ hyetaduttamam ||
english: This same ancient yoga I have taught to you today, because you are my devotee and my friend; for this is the highest secret.

school_notes.note: Because you are my devotee and my friend, I have taught you this ancient yoga, the supreme secret, which is knowledge.
I taught it to you in full because you came to me in friendship and great devotion; no one but me could know or tell it, since it is the supreme secret taught in the Vedānta.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna is puzzled how Krishna, born in his own time, could have taught the sun at the beginning of the world.
devanagari:
अपरं भवतो जन्म परं जन्म विवस्वतः ।
कथमेतद्विजानीयां त्वमादौ प्रोक्तवानिति ॥
iast:
aparaṃ bhavato janma paraṃ janma vivasvataḥ |
kathametadvijānīyāṃ tvamādau proktavāniti ||
english: Your birth was recent, and Vivasvat's birth was long ago. How am I to understand that you taught it in the beginning?

school_notes.note: You were born recently in Vasudeva's house, and the sun at creation; how can you have taught it first? Krishna's answer removes the doubt, held by the foolish, that Vāsudeva is not the all-knowing Lord.
Arjuna asks how this can really be so, given the vast span of time between Vivasvat's birth and Krishna's.
Having heard 'surrender all actions to me' (3.30), Arjuna asks in order to learn Krishna's greatness from the beginning.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna answers that he and Arjuna have both lived many lives, but only he remembers them.
devanagari:
बहूनि मे व्यतीतानि जन्मानि तव चार्जुन ।
तान्यहं वेद सर्वाणि न त्वं वेत्थ परन्तप ॥
iast:
bahūni me vyatītāni janmāni tava cārjuna |
tānyahaṃ veda sarvāṇi na tvaṃ vettha parantapa ||
english: Many births of mine have passed, Arjuna, and many of yours too. I know them all; you do not, scorcher of enemies.

school_notes.note: You do not know your past births because your power of knowing is blocked by merit and demerit; I know mine because I am by nature eternally pure, awake and free.
This shows that Krishna's births are real: he says 'many births of mine have passed' and compares them with Arjuna's.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains how he, the unborn Lord, takes birth: by his own power, not by force of karma.
devanagari:
अजोऽपि सन्नव्ययात्मा भूतानामीश्वरोऽपि सन् ।
प्रकृतिं स्वामधिष्ठाय संभवाम्यात्ममायया ॥
iast:
ajo'pi sannavyayātmā bhūtānāmīśvaro'pi san |
prakṛtiṃ svāmadhiṣṭhāya saṃbhavāmyātmamāyayā ||
english: Though I am unborn and my self is imperishable, though I am the Lord of all beings, I come into being by my own power, taking charge of my own nature.

school_notes.note: Though unborn, imperishable and Lord of all, I come into being by governing my own prakṛti, the three-guna māyā of Viṣṇu, which holds the whole world in its power and keeps it from knowing me, Vāsudeva, as its own self.
Without giving up any divine quality, such as being unborn, imperishable and Lord of all, I come into being in my own form by my own will; 'prakṛti' here means my own nature.
Even the Lord's body is imperishable; citing the Bhāgavata, he is the imperishable source of many incarnations.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains why he takes birth: whenever dharma declines (4.7-4.8).
devanagari:
यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत ।
अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥
iast:
yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānirbhavati bhārata |
abhyutthānamadharmasya tadātmānaṃ sṛjāmyaham ||
english: Whenever there is a decline of dharma, Arjuna, and a rise of adharma, then I bring myself forth.

school_notes.note: Dharma here is the order of varnas and life-stages that brings beings prosperity and liberation; whenever it declines and adharma rises, I bring myself forth through māyā.
There is no fixed time for my coming: whenever the dharma taught by the Vedas declines and its opposite rises, I take birth by my own will.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives the purpose of his coming: to protect the good, end evil and re-establish dharma.
devanagari:
परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् ।
धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे ॥
iast:
paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṃ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām |
dharmasaṃsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
english: To protect the good, to destroy those who do evil, and to establish dharma firmly, I come into being age after age.

school_notes.note: To protect those on the good path, to destroy wrongdoers and to establish dharma fully, I come into being in every age.
'The good' are the foremost devotees, who cannot bear a moment without seeing him; he comes to sustain them by letting them see him, hear him and speak with him.
He is not compelled to be born in order to protect; he acts freely, in play, like a child at games, as the Brahma Sūtra says.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna promises freedom from rebirth to anyone who truly understands his divine birth and actions.
devanagari:
जन्म कर्म च मे दिव्यमेवं यो वेत्ति तत्त्वतः ।
त्यक्त्वा देहं पुनर्जन्म नैति मामेति सोऽर्जुन ॥
iast:
janma karma ca me divyamevaṃ yo vetti tattvataḥ |
tyaktvā dehaṃ punarjanma naiti māmeti so'rjuna ||
english: One who truly knows my divine birth and actions in this way is not born again on leaving the body, Arjuna, but comes to me.

school_notes.note: My birth is through māyā and my acts, such as protecting the good, are divine; whoever knows this truly is not reborn but comes to me, liberated.
Whoever truly knows that my birth and acts are not those of a karma-bound being but divine, undertaken only to protect those who take refuge in me, reaches me on leaving this body.
Knowing this is not by itself liberation: one who knows and constantly worships me reaches me.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says many have already reached him by overcoming passion, fear and anger through knowledge.
devanagari:
वीतरागभयक्रोधा मन्मया मामुपाश्रिताः ।
बहवो ज्ञानतपसा पूता मद्भावमागताः ॥
iast:
vītarāgabhayakrodhā manmayā māmupāśritāḥ |
bahavo jñānatapasā pūtā madbhāvamāgatāḥ ||
english: Free from passion, fear and anger, absorbed in me, taking refuge in me, many people, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have come to my state of being.

school_notes.note: Those who see no difference between themselves and the Lord, devoted to knowledge alone and purified by knowledge as their austerity, have reached the state of the Lord: liberation.
Many have been purified by the austerity of knowing the truth of my birth and acts, and have reached this state.
There are such liberated souls; 'absorbed in me' means they see nothing anywhere without me.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says he meets people in the way they approach him, since all paths lead to him.
devanagari:
ये यथा मां प्रपद्यन्ते तांस्तथैव भजाम्यहम् ।
मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः ॥
iast:
ye yathā māṃ prapadyante tāṃstathaiva bhajāmyaham |
mama vartmānuvartante manuṣyāḥ pārtha sarvaśaḥ ||
english: However people approach me, so I receive them. Everywhere, son of Pritha, people follow my path.

school_notes.note: I favour people in the way they seek me: to those who want results I give results. One cannot seek liberation and results at the same time.
However devotees conceive of me and take refuge, I show myself to them in that way; all people long to follow me, and I let even their ordinary eyes see my nature.
Even those who worship other gods follow my path, since I am the doer and enjoyer of all actions, as 9.23 says.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna observes that most people worship for quick worldly success.
devanagari:
काङ्क्षन्तः कर्मणां सिद्धिं यजन्त इह देवताः ।
क्षिप्रं हि मानुषे लोके सिद्धिर्भवति कर्मजा ॥
iast:
kāṅkṣantaḥ karmaṇāṃ siddhiṃ yajanta iha devatāḥ |
kṣipraṃ hi mānuṣe loke siddhirbhavati karmajā ||
english: Wanting success from their actions, people here worship the gods, because in the human world success born of action comes quickly.

school_notes.note: Wanting results, people worship gods such as Indra and Agni; he quotes the Upanishad that one who worships a god as other than oneself does not know.
People seek rewards by worshipping Indra and the others, not me, the self of those gods and enjoyer of all sacrifice, because rewards such as sons, cattle and food come quickly.
This is why they follow my path: through it, results come quickly.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says he created the four varnas according to qualities and actions, yet remains untouched as a non-doer.
devanagari:
चातुर्वर्ण्यं मया सृष्टं गुणकर्मविभागशः ।
तस्य कर्तारमपि मां विद्ध्यकर्तारमव्ययम् ॥
iast:
cāturvarṇyaṃ mayā sṛṣṭaṃ guṇakarmavibhāgaśaḥ |
tasya kartāramapi māṃ viddhyakartāramavyayam ||
english: The four varnas were created by me according to the division of qualities and actions. Though I am their maker, know me as the non-doer, the unchanging.

school_notes.note: The four varnas were created according to the gunas and their duties: the sattva-dominant brahmin has duties such as calm and self-control, the kshatriya, in whom rajas dominates, has others, and so on.

Reads the verse as about the whole world, from Brahmā to a blade of grass, headed by the four varnas and divided by gunas and their duties; Krishna creates, sustains and withdraws it, yet is not its doer.
Assigns the gunas: the brahmin is sattvic, the kshatriya sattvic-rajasic, the vaishya rajasic-tamasic, the shudra tamasic; their duties are listed at 18.42.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that action does not bind him because he has no desire for its fruit.
devanagari:

इति मां योऽभिजानाति कर्मभिर्न स बध्यते ॥

english: Actions do not stain me, and I have no longing for their fruit. Whoever knows me this way is not bound by actions.

school_notes.note: Actions do not stain me because I have no ego and no thirst for their fruit; whoever knows me, or anyone else, as the self in this way is not bound.
The variety of creation follows from beings' own good and bad karma, not from me, so in that sense I am not its doer.
The Lord has will but no clinging; his 'desire' is simply his knowledge.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna urges Arjuna to act as the wise of old did, knowing that action need not bind.

english: Knowing this, the seekers of liberation of old also acted. So you too should act, as those before you did long ago.

Purified by this knowledge of me, do the ancient action that Vivasvat, Manu and the others did.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna begins to explain the subtle difference between action and inaction (4.16-4.23).
devanagari:

english: What is action? What is inaction? Even the wise are confused about this. I will explain action to you; knowing it, you will be freed from harm.

school_notes.note: Even the wise are confused about action and inaction; knowing them, you will be freed from worldly existence. Do not think action is simply bodily movement and inaction simply sitting still.
'Inaction' here means the knowledge of the true self that must be present within the action; even the learned do not rightly know the nature of the action and the knowledge within it.
Action is hard to understand rightly.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna stresses that understanding right action, wrong action and inaction is difficult but necessary.
devanagari:

अकर्मणश्च बोद्धव्यं गहना कर्मणो गतिः ॥

english: One must understand what action is, understand what wrong action is, and understand what inaction is; the way of action is hard to fathom.

school_notes.note: One must understand prescribed action, forbidden action and not acting; the true nature of all three is hard to know.
Takes 'vikarma' here to mean action in its varied forms (regular, occasional and desire-driven rites, and earning the means for them), not wrong action.
Action, inaction (failing to do what is prescribed) and wrong action (what is forbidden, which binds) must be told apart, since without knowing them there is no liberation.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives the riddle of seeing inaction in action, a key to acting without bondage.
devanagari:

iast:
karmaṇyakarma yaḥ paśyedakarmaṇi ca karma yaḥ |
sa buddhimānmanuṣyeṣu sa yuktaḥ kṛtsnakarmakṛt ||
english: One who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise among people; such a person is disciplined and does all that is to be done.

school_notes.note: One who sees that the self does not act even in action, and that not acting still depends on a doer and so is action, sees rightly; all talk of doers and deeds belongs to the realm of ignorance.
'Inaction' is self-knowledge: one sees the action being done as taking the form of knowledge, and sees that knowledge as present within the action.
While acting, one sees that it is Viṣṇu's action, not one's own as a mere reflection; and when not acting, as in sleep, one sees that the Lord is always acting.

context: Krishna describes the wise person whose actions, free of selfish desire, are consumed by knowledge (4.19-4.23).

english: One whose undertakings are all free of desire and of the intentions behind it, whose actions are burned up in the fire of knowledge, is called learned by the wise.

school_notes.note: Such a person acts without desire: for the world's welfare if engaged in action, or just to sustain life if withdrawn. Their actions are burned up in the fire of knowledge.
A seeker of liberation whose actions are free of desire for results and of identifying the self with prakṛti is called wise.
This and the next four verses expand on the previous one.

context: Krishna adds that one free of attachment to results does nothing at all, even while fully active.

karmaṇyabhipravṛtto'pi naiva kiṃcitkaroti saḥ ||
english: Giving up attachment to the fruits of action, always content and depending on nothing, such a person does nothing at all, even while fully engaged in action.

school_notes.note: Action done by one who knows the actionless self is, in truth, no action at all.
Though engaged in action, such a person is really practising knowledge in the form of action.
Such a person knows, 'I resemble the Lord, ever content and independent.'

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes someone who acts only as the body requires, without expectation or possessiveness.

nirāśīryatacittātmā tyaktasarvaparigrahaḥ |
śārīraṃ kevalaṃ karma kurvannāpnoti kilbiṣam ||
english: Without expectations, with mind and body controlled, having given up all possessions, doing only what the body requires, one incurs no fault.

school_notes.note: One who has given up all possessions does only what keeps the body alive, without even ego in that, and incurs no sin.
Without desire for results, with mind controlled, free of 'mine' towards material things, and doing only bodily action throughout life, one sees the self through karma yoga alone.
Explains 'does nothing at all' (4.20): such a person incurs no sin.

context: Krishna continues: one content with what comes, free of envy and even in success or failure, is not bound by action.

iast:

english: Content with whatever comes unsought, beyond the pairs of opposites, free of envy, the same in success and failure, such a person is not bound even when acting.

school_notes.note: Content with what comes unasked, unshaken by heat and cold, without enmity, and even-minded whether food comes or not, such a renunciant is not bound.

Content with what comes to sustain the body, bearing heat and cold, without resentment towards others since misfortune comes from one's own karma, and even in victory or defeat, one is not bound even without the path of knowledge.
These are the marks of one whose mind is controlled.

context: Krishna concludes that action done as sacrifice, by one grounded in knowledge, leaves no trace.

english: For one who is free of attachment, liberated, with a mind established in knowledge, acting only as sacrifice, all action dissolves completely.

school_notes.note: The action of such a person, together with its fruit, is wholly destroyed.
All the old karma that causes bondage is wholly destroyed for such a person.
'Liberated' means not identifying with the body; 'established in knowledge' means knowing the Lord.

english: The act of offering is Brahman, the offering is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. Brahman is reached by one who sees Brahman in every action.

Everything in the rite is Brahman because it is Brahman's effect and has Brahman as its self; one who meditates on this reaches Brahman.
All this is called Brahman because its existence and activity depend on Brahman, not because it is Brahman's very nature; he cites the Padma Purāṇa.

context: Krishna begins listing the many forms that sacrifice can take (4.25-4.30).

Some practitioners of karma yoga devote themselves to worshipping the gods; others offer oblations, themselves Brahman, into the fire that is Brahman.
For some renunciants, worship of the Lord is itself their sacrifice.

english: Some offer hearing and the other senses into the fires of restraint; others offer sound and the other objects of the senses into the fires of the senses.

school_notes.note: Some practise restraint of the senses; others take in only objects that are not forbidden, and treat that as their offering.
Some strive to restrain the senses; others strive to stop the senses from chasing their objects.

english: Others offer all the actions of the senses and of the breath into the fire of the yoga of self-control, kindled by knowledge.

school_notes.note: They offer the activities of the senses and the vital breath into the fire of self-restraint, lit by discernment as a lamp is lit by oil.
Others, through the mind, strive to stop the senses and breath from turning to activity.
Self-restraint is the means, the fire.

Some practitioners of karma yoga worship with rightly earned wealth, through charity, rites and offerings; others devote themselves to fasting and austerity; others to visiting holy places.
Each offers their austerity or other practice into the Lord as an act of worship.

Some practise the three kinds of breath control, inhaling, exhaling and holding, together with a regulated diet.
They remain in breath retention.

All action, with all its parts such as worship, has knowledge as its fruit.

api cedasi pāpebhyaḥ sarvebhyaḥ pāpakṛttamaḥ |
sarvaṃ jñānaplavenaiva vṛjinaṃ santariṣyasi ||
english: Even if you were the worst wrongdoer of all, you would cross over all wrongdoing by the boat of knowledge alone.

school_notes.note: Even the worst sinner crosses the ocean of sin on the raft of knowledge; for a seeker of liberation, even merit counts as sin here.
Even the greatest sinner crosses the whole ocean of past sin on the raft of self-knowledge.
This and the next two verses praise knowledge.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna compares knowledge to a fire that consumes the effects of all past actions.
devanagari:

ज्ञानाग्निः सर्वकर्माणि भस्मसात्कुरुते तथा ॥

yathaidhāṃsi samiddho'gnirbhasmasātkurute'rjuna |
jñānāgniḥ sarvakarmāṇi bhasmasātkurute tathā ||
english: As a blazing fire turns firewood to ash, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge turns all actions to ash.

school_notes.note: Knowledge does not literally burn actions like fuel: right vision makes all actions seedless, unable to bear fruit.
The fire of self-knowledge burns up the store of karma accumulated since beginningless time.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna praises knowledge as the greatest purifier, found within through steady practice.
devanagari:
न हि ज्ञानेन सदृशं पवित्रमिह विद्यते ।
तत्स्वयं योगसंसिद्धः कालेनात्मनि विन्दति ॥
iast:
na hi jñānena sadṛśaṃ pavitramiha vidyate |
tatsvayaṃ yogasaṃsiddhaḥ kālenātmani vindati ||
english: Nothing in this world purifies like knowledge. One who is perfected in yoga finds it, in time, within oneself.

school_notes.note: A seeker made ready by karma yoga and meditation finds this knowledge within after a long time.
Nothing purifies like self-knowledge; one perfected by daily karma yoga practised as knowledge finds it within, in time.
The following verses give its means and what opposes it.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna names the qualities that lead to knowledge and peace: faith, dedication and self-control.
devanagari:

iast:

jñānaṃ labdhvā parāṃ śāntimacireṇādhigacchati ||
english: One who has faith, who is devoted to it and has mastered the senses, gains knowledge; having gained knowledge, one soon reaches supreme peace.

school_notes.note: Faith alone may be slow, so add dedication to the means, such as serving a teacher, and control of the senses; one with all three surely gains knowledge and soon reaches liberation.
One with faith in growing the knowledge taught, focused on it and restraining the senses, soon gains mature knowledge and the supreme peace, nirvāṇa.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna warns of the cost of doubt and lack of faith.
devanagari:

iast:
ajñaścāśraddadhānaśca saṃśayātmā vinaśyati |
nāyaṃ loko'sti na paro na sukhaṃ saṃśayātmanaḥ ||
english: But the ignorant, the faithless and the doubting perish; for one who doubts, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness.

school_notes.note: The ignorant and the faithless perish, but not as surely as the doubter, the worst of all, who has neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness, since doubt arises even there.
One without this knowledge, without eagerness to grow it, or doubting it, is lost: they gain neither the ordinary goals of life nor liberation.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the one who is free: acting through yoga, with doubts cut away by knowledge.
devanagari:

yogasaṃnyastakarmāṇaṃ jñānasaṃchinnasaṃśayam |
ātmavantaṃ na karmāṇi nibadhnanti dhanaṃjaya ||
english: Actions do not bind one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubts are cut away by knowledge, and who is self-possessed, Arjuna.

school_notes.note: Through yoga, here the vision of the highest truth, such a person has renounced merit and demerit, and their doubt is cut by knowledge of the oneness of the self and the Lord.
One whose action has taken the form of knowledge through this yoga, whose doubts about the self are cut away, and whose mind is firm, is not bound by past karma.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna ends chapter 4 urging Arjuna to cut through doubt with knowledge and rise to act.
devanagari:

chittvainaṃ saṃśayaṃ yogamātiṣṭhottiṣṭha bhārata ||
english: So, with the sword of knowledge, cut away this doubt about the self, born of ignorance and lodged in your heart; take up yoga, and stand up, Arjuna.

school_notes.note: Cut this doubt, born of lack of discernment and lodged in the intellect, with the sword of right knowledge, which removes grief and delusion; the doubt is 'about the self' because it concerns your own self.
Cut the doubt about the self, born of beginningless ignorance, with the sword of the self-knowledge I have taught; take up the karma yoga I have taught, and stand up for it.

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna asks Krishna to settle which is better, renouncing action or acting with discipline, opening chapter 5.
devanagari:
संन्यासं कर्मणां कृष्ण पुनर्योगं च शंससि ।
यच्छ्रेय एतयोरेकं तन्मे ब्रूहि सुनिश्चितम् ॥
iast:
saṃnyāsaṃ karmaṇāṃ kṛṣṇa punaryogaṃ ca śaṃsasi |
yacchreya etayorekaṃ tanme brūhi suniścitam ||
english: Krishna, you praise renouncing action, and then again the yoga of action. Tell me decisively which one of the two is better.

school_notes.note: Arjuna is unsure because Krishna praises both giving up prescribed actions and performing them: which is better, doing them or giving them up?
Arjuna asks because chapter 2 put karma yoga first and the path of knowledge after it, while chapters 3-4 praised karma yoga even for those fit for knowledge.
This chapter expands the karma yoga of chapter 3, covering both renunciation (4.22) and action (4.15); he explains 'Krishna' as the one who draws the whole world by governing it.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna answers that both paths lead to freedom, but disciplined action is the better of the two.

तयोस्तु कर्मसंन्यासात्कर्मयोगो विशिष्यते ॥
iast:
saṃnyāsaḥ karmayogaśca niḥśreyasakarāvubhau |
tayostu karmasaṃnyāsātkarmayogo viśiṣyate ||
english: Renunciation and the yoga of action both lead to the highest good; but of the two, the yoga of action is better than renouncing action.

school_notes.note: Both lead to liberation by giving rise to knowledge, but here performing action is praised above mere renunciation of action.
Even for one capable of the path of knowledge, both work on their own to bring the highest good, but karma yoga is better.
This renunciation is not the monastic stage of life; he cites a text that worship of the Lord is greater than renunciation understood as giving up the opposites.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna redefines the renunciant as one free of hatred and craving, whatever their outward life.

iast:
jñeyaḥ sa nityasaṃnyāsī yo na dveṣṭi na kāṅkṣati |
nirdvandvo hi mahābāho sukhaṃ bandhātpramucyate ||
english: Know that one who neither hates nor craves is always a renunciant; free of the pairs of opposites, mighty-armed one, such a person is easily released from bondage.

school_notes.note: A person of action who neither hates nor craves is to be known as always a renunciant, even while acting, and is freed without effort.
A karma yogi content in experiencing the self wants nothing else and so hates nothing; such a person is always established in knowledge, and is easily freed because karma yoga is easy to practise.
Explains what the word 'renunciation' means, to show why it leads to the highest good.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says the paths of knowledge and action are not truly separate.
devanagari:

एकमप्यास्थितः सम्यगुभयोर्विन्दते फलम् ॥
iast:
sāṃkhyayogau pṛthagbālāḥ pravadanti na paṇḍitāḥ |
ekamapyāsthitaḥ samyagubhayorvindate phalam ||

school_notes.note: Only the childish say they have different, opposed results; the wise know both lead to the same highest good.
Those who say the two differ in their fruit, karma yoga leading to knowledge and knowledge alone to seeing the self, are not wise: both have the one fruit of seeing the self.
Both are inner aids to knowledge, so they do not conflict.

context: Krishna continues: both paths reach the same goal, and seeing this is true understanding.

iast:
yatsāṃkhyaiḥ prāpyate sthānaṃ tadyogairapi gamyate |
ekaṃ sāṃkhyaṃ ca yogaṃ ca yaḥ paśyati sa: paśyati ||
english: The state reached by the followers of Sankhya is reached by the followers of yoga as well. One who sees Sankhya and yoga as one truly sees.

school_notes.note: The liberation reached by renunciants devoted to knowledge is reached by yogis too, who act for the Lord without seeking results, by way of gaining knowledge and renunciation.
The vision of the self reached by those devoted to knowledge is reached by karma yogis too; one who sees them as one in their fruit sees rightly.
Yogis too reach the fruit of knowledge, by way of knowledge.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains why action is better: renunciation without disciplined action is hard to achieve.

योगयुक्तो मुनिर्ब्रह्म नचिरेणाधिगच्छति ॥
iast:
saṃnyāsastu mahābāho duḥkhamāptumayogataḥ |
yogayukto munirbrahma nacireṇādhigacchati ||
english: But renunciation is hard to attain without yoga, mighty-armed one; the sage disciplined in yoga soon reaches Brahman.

school_notes.note: True renunciation is hard to reach without karma yoga; the sage disciplined in action offered to the Lord soon reaches Brahman, here meaning renunciation grounded in knowledge.
The path of knowledge cannot be reached without karma yoga; one who practises karma yoga reaches the self easily and soon, while one on the path of knowledge reaches it with great difficulty.
Without yoga, renunciation brings only the hardship of conquering desire and the like, not its real fruit, liberation.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the disciplined person who acts in the world without being stained by it.

iast:
yogayukto viśuddhātmā vijitātmā jitendriyaḥ |
sarvabhūtātmabhūtātmā kurvannapi na lipyate ||
english: One disciplined in yoga, pure in heart, self-controlled, with senses mastered, whose self has become the self of all beings, is not stained even while acting.

school_notes.note: One whose self is the self of all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, sees rightly; acting for the world's welfare, they are not stained.
One who practises karma yoga as worship of the Supreme is purified by it, easily masters the mind and senses, and sees the selves of all beings as alike with their own.
'The self of all beings' is the Supreme Lord.

पश्यञ्श्रृण्वन्स्पृशञ्जिघ्रन्नश्नन्‌गच्छन्स्वपञ्श्वसन् ॥
iast:
naiva kiṃcitkaromīti yukto manyeta tattvavit |
paśyañśrṛṇvanspṛśañjighrannaśnangacchansvapañśvasan ||
english: "I do nothing at all," thinks the disciplined knower of truth, while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, breathing,

school_notes.note: The knower of truth, composed, regards themselves as doing nothing at all, whatever the body and senses are doing.
Knowing that the senses and breath act on their objects, one thinks 'I do nothing'; the self, whose nature is knowledge alone, is a doer only through its karma-born link with the senses.
These two verses clarify what renunciation means.

इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेषु वर्तन्त इति धारयन् ॥
iast:
pralapanvisṛjangṛhṇannunmiṣannimiṣannapi |
indriyāṇīndriyārtheṣu vartanta iti dhārayan ||
english: speaking, letting go, holding, opening and closing the eyes, holding firmly that it is only the senses moving among the objects of the senses.

context: Krishna gives the image of the lotus leaf for acting without being stained.

english: One who acts placing all actions in Brahman and giving up attachment is not stained by wrongdoing, as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.

school_notes.note: Placing all actions in the Lord, as a servant acts for his master, and unattached even to liberation, one is untouched by sin; the only fruit of such action is purity of mind.
'Brahman' here means prakṛti, as in 14.3: placing actions in prakṛti, present as the senses, and thinking 'I do nothing', one is untouched by sin.
Only one who has both renunciation and yoga is unstained by action; the result is repeated to show the means is essential.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that the disciplined act only to purify themselves.

english: Yogis act with the body, the mind, the intellect, or even the senses alone, giving up attachment, for the purification of the self.

school_notes.note: With body, mind, intellect and senses free of 'mine', thinking 'I act for the Lord, not for my own reward', they act to purify the mind.
Giving up attachment to rewards like heaven, they act to destroy the old karma that binds the self.
This is how such people conduct themselves.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna contrasts the peace of those who give up results with the bondage of those driven by desire.
devanagari:

अयुक्तः कामकारेण फले सक्तो निबध्यते ॥
iast:

ayuktaḥ kāmakāreṇa phale sakto nibadhyate ||
english: The disciplined, giving up the fruit of action, attain lasting peace; the undisciplined, driven by desire and attached to the fruit, are bound.

school_notes.note: One who acts for the Lord, not for reward, gives up the fruit and reaches the peace called liberation, step by step; one driven by desire is bound.
One focused on the self alone acts for its purification and reaches steady peace in experiencing it; one restless for other rewards, attached to the fruit, is bound.
States the results of being disciplined or not, to establish the rule.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna pictures the body as a city of nine gates in which the self rests, untouched by action.
devanagari:

iast:
sarvakarmāṇi manasā saṃnyasyāste sukhaṃ vaśī |
navadvāre pure dehī naiva kurvanna kārayan ||
english: Renouncing all actions in the mind, the self-controlled embodied one dwells happily in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action.

school_notes.note: Renouncing all actions with the discerning mind, by seeing inaction in action, the embodied one rests happily in the body, the city with nine gates.
Knowing that being a doer comes from the body, a result of past karma, and not from the self's own nature, one rests happily, neither driving the body nor acting through it.
'In the mind' means giving up the pride of being the doer.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that the self does not create action or its consequences; nature does (5.14-5.15).
devanagari:

na karmaphalasaṃyogaṃ svabhāvastu pravartate ||
english: The Lord does not create agency or actions for people, nor the link between action and its fruit; it is nature that does this.

'The Lord' here is the self in its natural state, free of karma: it does not produce the doership, acts and fruits peculiar to gods, humans and others; these come from tendencies born of contact with prakṛti.
The soul does not truly act; it is called 'lord' only relative to inert matter.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna adds that people are deluded because ignorance covers their knowledge.
devanagari:
नादत्ते कस्यचित्पापं न चैव सुकृतं विभुः ।

nādatte kasyacitpāpaṃ na caiva sukṛtaṃ vibhuḥ |

english: The all-pervading one does not take on anyone's wrongdoing or good deeds. Knowledge is covered by ignorance, and so beings are deluded.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna compares knowledge to the sun, which reveals the truth once ignorance is cleared.
devanagari:

teṣāmādityavajjñānaṃ prakāśayati tatparam ||
english: But for those whose ignorance is destroyed by knowledge of the self, that knowledge, like the sun, reveals the supreme.

school_notes.note: For those whose ignorance is destroyed by discerning knowledge of the self, knowledge reveals the highest truth as the sun reveals all forms.
When ignorance, the beginningless karma that covers the self, is destroyed by self-knowledge, the self's own unlimited knowledge shines like the sun.
Knowledge alone destroys ignorance; the first knowledge mentioned is indirect knowledge.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes those wholly devoted to the supreme, who reach freedom from rebirth.

gacchantyapunarāvṛttiṃ jñānanirdhūtakalmaṣāḥ ||
english: Their minds on That, their selves in That, established in That, devoted to That, their impurities shaken off by knowledge, they reach the state from which there is no return.

Resolved on seeing the self, minds set on it, devoted to its practice, their past impurities shaken off, they reach the self in the state from which there is no return.
This is the immediate means to direct knowledge.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the equal vision of the wise, who see the same self in every being.
devanagari:
विद्याविनयसंपन्ने ब्राह्मणे गवि हस्तिनि ।
शुनि चैव श्वपाके च पण्डिताः समदर्शिनः ॥

śuni caiva śvapāke ca paṇḍitāḥ samadarśinaḥ ||
english: The wise see the same in a brahmin rich in learning and humility, in a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste who eats dogs.

school_notes.note: The wise see the one Brahman equally in a learned and humble brahmin, the most refined, and in a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste.
Those who know the self see it as the same everywhere, of the nature of knowledge alone; inequality belongs to prakṛti, not to the self.
Seeing the Lord's forms as equal everywhere is a means to direct knowledge.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says those who see all beings equally have overcome rebirth in this very life.
devanagari:
इहैव तैर्जितः सर्गो येषां साम्ये स्थितं मनः ।
निर्दोषं हि समं ब्रह्म तस्माद्ब्रह्मणि ते स्थिताः ॥
iast:

english: Even here, rebirth is overcome by those whose minds are established in sameness; for Brahman is flawless and the same in all, so they are established in Brahman.

school_notes.note: The deluded think Brahman is tainted by the faults of an outcaste, but it is untouched by them, flawless and the same; those whose minds rest in this sameness have conquered birth while still living.
Even while still practising, those whose minds rest in the sameness of all selves have conquered rebirth: the self, free of prakṛti's flaws, is Brahman, and resting in it is that victory.
Praises this equal vision.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the one established in Brahman as unmoved by the pleasant and the unpleasant.
devanagari:
न प्रहृष्येत्प्रियं प्राप्य नोद्विजेत्प्राप्य चाप्रियम् ।
स्थिरबुद्धिरसंमूढो ब्रह्मविद्ब्रह्मणि स्थितः ॥
iast:
na prahṛṣyetpriyaṃ prāpya nodvijetprāpya cāpriyam |
sthirabuddhirasaṃmūḍho brahmavidbrahmaṇi sthitaḥ ||
english: One who does not rejoice at getting what is pleasant, nor recoil at getting what is unpleasant, steady in mind and undeluded, knows Brahman and is established in Brahman.

school_notes.note: Only those who take the body for the self rejoice or grieve at the pleasant and unpleasant; one who sees the self alone does not meet with them at all.
Whatever pleasant or unpleasant things come through past karma, one should neither rejoice nor be shaken, keeping the mind on the steady self and free of confusing it with the changing body.
The rest of the chapter brings renunciation, yoga and knowledge together.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna contrasts outward pleasures with the lasting happiness found within (5.21-5.22).
devanagari:
बाह्यस्पर्शेष्वसक्तात्मा विन्दत्यात्मनि यत् सुखम् ।
स ब्रह्मयोगयुक्तात्मा सुखमक्षयमश्नुते ॥
iast:
bāhyasparśeṣvasaktātmā vindatyātmani yat sukham |
sa brahmayogayuktātmā sukhamakṣayamaśnute ||
english: One unattached to outer contacts finds the happiness that is in the self; joined in yoga with Brahman, such a person enjoys happiness that never fades.

school_notes.note: With the mind not attached to outer sense objects, one finds the happiness that lies in the self, and, joined to Brahman in meditation, enjoys undying happiness.
Unattached to experiences other than the self, one finds happiness within, and through the practice of Brahman gains the undying happiness of experiencing it.
Only one joined in meditation on Brahman gains the undying happiness of the self, not otherwise.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains why the wise do not delight in sense pleasures: they begin, end and bring sorrow.
devanagari:
ये हि संस्पर्शजा भोगा दुःखयोनय एव ते ।
आद्यन्तवन्तः कौन्तेय न तेषु रमते बुधः ॥
iast:
ye hi saṃsparśajā bhogā duḥkhayonaya eva te |
ādyantavantaḥ kaunteya na teṣu ramate budhaḥ ||
english: Pleasures born of contact are nothing but sources of sorrow; they have a beginning and an end, son of Kunti, and the wise do not delight in them.

school_notes.note: Pleasures born of contact with objects are wombs of pain, in this world and the next; knowing that not a trace of happiness is found in worldly existence, the wise turn their senses away.
Pleasures from contact between the senses and objects end in sorrow and last only a short time; one who knows their true nature takes no delight in them.
Criticises pleasures of desire in order to encourage renunciation.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says that withstanding the pull of desire and anger in this life is the mark of a happy, disciplined person.
devanagari:
शक्नोतीहैव यः सोढुं प्राक्शरीरविमोक्षणात् ।
कामक्रोधोद्भवं वेगं स युक्तः स सुखी नरः ॥
iast:
śaknotīhaiva yaḥ soḍhuṃ prākśarīravimokṣaṇāt |
kāmakrodhodbhavaṃ vegaṃ sa yuktaḥ sa sukhī naraḥ ||
english: One who can withstand the surge of desire and anger here, before leaving the body, is disciplined; that person is happy.

school_notes.note: The surge of desire and anger can arise at any moment while one lives, so one must never relax one's guard until death; one who can withstand it is disciplined and happy.
One who, through the joy of experiencing the self, can hold back the surge of desire and anger while still practising is fit for that experience.
Desire is easiest to master in a human body; higher worlds such as Brahmā's are reached only by those who have conquered desire.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the yogi whose happiness, joy and light are all within.

english: One whose happiness is within, whose joy is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

school_notes.note: Such a yogi becomes Brahman while still alive and reaches liberation, the peace of Brahman.
Giving up all outward experience, finding joy only in the self and knowing only the self, the yogi attains the bliss of experiencing the self.
Their joy comes from seeing the Supreme Self, and their inner light is the self-luminous Lord made manifest.

छिन्नद्वैधा यतात्मानः सर्वभूतहिते रताः ॥
iast:

english: Sages whose wrongs are worn away, whose doubts are cut through, who are self-controlled and delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the peace of Brahman.

school_notes.note: Renunciants of right vision, sinless and free of doubt, self-restrained and devoted to the good of all beings, which is to say non-violent, attain liberation.
Free of the opposites, minds fixed on the self, devoted to the welfare of all beings as to their own, these seers attain the bliss of Brahman.
'Doubts cut through' means doubt and error removed; he cites a verse that one should cut them with the sword of knowledge.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says the peace of Brahman is close at hand for those free of desire and anger.
devanagari:

iast:
kāmakrodhaviyuktānāṃ yatīnāṃ yatacetasām |
abhito brahmanirvāṇaṃ vartate viditātmanām ||
english: For ascetics who are free of desire and anger, who have controlled their minds and know the self, the peace of Brahman is near on every side.

school_notes.note: For renunciants free of desire and anger who know the self, liberation is present on both sides: while living and after death.
For those who strive, free of desire and anger and with minds mastered, the bliss of Brahman is already in their hands.
Brahman is easily reached by them, on every side.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives a brief instruction in meditation, previewing chapter 6 (5.27-5.28).

स्पर्शान्कृत्वा बहिर्बाह्यांश्चक्षुश्चैवान्तरे भ्रुवोः ।
प्राणापानौ समौ कृत्वा नासाभ्यन्तरचारिणौ ॥
iast:
sparśānkṛtvā bahirbāhyāṃścakṣuścaivāntare bhruvoḥ |
prāṇāpānau samau kṛtvā nāsābhyantaracāriṇau ||
english: Shutting out outer contacts, fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, making the in-breath and the out-breath even as they move within the nostrils,

school_notes.note: By not dwelling on the sounds and other objects the senses have brought in, one keeps them outside; then one fixes the gaze between the brows and evens the breath.
Withdrawing the senses, sitting upright in a posture suited to yoga, resting the gaze on the tip of the nose and evening the breath, one turns the mind only to the self.
Describes the method of meditation: fixing the gaze between the brows (a text also allows the tip of the nose) and resting in breath retention.

विगतेच्छाभयक्रोधो यः सदा मुक्त एव सः ॥

yatendriyamanobuddhirmunirmokṣaparāyaṇaḥ |
vigatecchābhayakrodho yaḥ sadā mukta eva saḥ ||
english: with senses, mind and intellect controlled, the sage intent on liberation, free of desire, fear and anger, is truly free for ever.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna closes chapter 5: knowing him as the friend of all beings brings peace.
devanagari:
भोक्तारं यज्ञतपसां सर्वलोकमहेश्वरम् ।
