english: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.

school_notes.note: Know me as the enjoyer of all sacrifices and austerities, the great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, who helps without expecting anything in return and dwells in every heart; knowing me, one attains peace.
Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifice, Lord even of the lords of the worlds, and friend of all, one finds happiness in the very doing of karma yoga.
This is the one who is to be meditated upon.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna opens chapter 6, on meditation, by redefining the true renunciant as one who acts without depending on results.
devanagari:
अनाश्रितः कर्मफलं कार्यं कर्म करोति यः ।

sa saṃnyāsī ca yogī ca na niragnirna cākriyaḥ ||
english: One who does the work that should be done, without depending on its fruit, is a renunciant and a yogi; not one who merely gives up the sacred fire, nor one who gives up action.

school_notes.note: One who does their regular duty without thirst for its fruit is both renunciant and yogi; not merely someone who has given up the sacred fires and rites.
One who acts, not for rewards like heaven, but because worshipping the Supreme Person, our friend, is itself the goal, is both a renunciant (devoted to knowledge) and a yogi (devoted to action).
This chapter teaches the yoga of meditation, close to knowledge. Even monks have their 'fire' and rites: Brahman and its worship.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says renunciation and yoga are the same at heart: both require giving up selfish intentions.
devanagari:
यं संन्यासमिति प्राहुर्योगं तं विद्धि पाण्डव ।
न ह्यसंन्यस्तसंकल्पो योगी भवति कश्चन ॥
iast:
yaṃ saṃnyāsamiti prāhuryogaṃ taṃ viddhi pāṇḍava |

english: What they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, son of Pandu; for no one becomes a yogi without renouncing selfish intentions.

school_notes.note: The true renunciation known to scripture, giving up all actions and their fruits, is likened to the yoga of action because no one becomes a yogi without giving up intentions.
What they call the path of knowledge, know to be karma yoga itself: through reflecting on the true self, one gives up the intention of taking prakṛti to be the self.
Renunciation is contained within yoga: without giving up desire and intention, how could anyone have the means?

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that action is the way into yoga, and calm is the way once yoga is reached.
devanagari:
आरुरुक्षोर्मुनेर्योगं कर्म कारणमुच्यते ।
योगारूढस्य तस्यैव शमः कारणमुच्यते ॥
iast:
ārurukṣormuneryogaṃ karma kāraṇamucyate |
yogārūḍhasya tasyaiva śamaḥ kāraṇamucyate ||
english: For the sage who wants to rise to yoga, action is said to be the means; for the same sage, once risen to yoga, calm is said to be the means.

school_notes.note: For one who cannot yet stay in meditation, action is the means; once established in it, calm, the ceasing of all actions, is the means.
Karma yoga is the means for one seeking the vision of the self; only for one firmly established is ceasing from action the means. Action must be done until liberation is reached.
For one who has completed the means and has direct knowledge, calm in absorption is the cause of supreme happiness.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the one who has risen to yoga: free of attachment to pleasures and to action itself.
devanagari:
यदा हि नेन्द्रियार्थेषु न कर्मस्वनुषज्जते ।
सर्वसंकल्पसंन्यासी योगारूढस्तदोच्यते ॥
iast:
yadā hi nendriyārtheṣu na karmasvanuṣajjate |
sarvasaṃkalpasaṃnyāsī yogārūḍhastadocyate ||
english: When a person is not attached to the objects of the senses or to actions, and has renounced all selfish intentions, they are said to have risen to yoga.

school_notes.note: When the meditating yogi, seeing no purpose in them, clings neither to sense objects nor to any kind of action, and has given up all intentions, they are said to have risen to yoga.

When the yogi, by nature experiencing only the self, clings neither to material objects nor to related actions, they have risen to yoga; until then, karma yoga, the practice of not clinging, is the means.
Gives the mark of one risen to yoga: for them faults dissolve by themselves, for others only through effort.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: In the chapter on meditation, Krishna says self-mastery must come before steady practice, and calls Arjuna to rely on his own effort.
devanagari:
उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् ।
आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥
iast:
uddharedātmanātmānaṃ nātmānamavasādayet |
ātmaiva hyātmano bandhurātmaiva ripurātmanaḥ ||
english: Lift yourself up by your own effort, and do not let yourself sink. You alone are your own friend, and you alone are your own enemy.

school_notes.note: Raise yourself out of the ocean of worldly existence to steadiness in yoga. Even a loving relative can be a tie rather than a help toward liberation, so the self alone is the true friend; and any outside enemy is ultimately of one's own making.
Reads 'self' here as the mind: a mind not attached to sense objects lifts a person up, while an attached mind drags them down. The mind alone is friend or enemy.
A brief note: the ascent to yoga has to be made by one's own effort.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains when the self is friend and when it is enemy: it depends on self-mastery.
devanagari:
बन्धुरात्मात्मनस्तस्य येनात्मैवात्मना जितः ।
अनात्मनस्तु शत्रुत्वे वर्तेतात्मैव शत्रुवत् ॥
iast:
bandhurātmātmanastasya yenātmaivātmanā jitaḥ |
anātmanastu śatrutve vartetātmaiva śatruvat ||
english: For one who has conquered themselves, the self is a friend; but for one who has not, the self acts with hostility, like an enemy.

school_notes.note: The self is a friend to one who has mastered body and senses; for one who has not, it behaves like an outside enemy.

Whoever has won their mind back from sense objects has that mind as a friend; for one who has not, their own mind works against their good like an enemy. He quotes Parāśara: the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation.
'Self' here is the mind, which is friend or enemy to the soul; he quotes the saying that the mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the self-mastered person as steady through comfort and hardship, praise and insult.
devanagari:
जितात्मनः प्रशान्तस्य परमात्मा समाहितः ।
शीतोष्णसुखदुःखेषु तथा मानापमानयोः ॥
iast:
jitātmanaḥ praśāntasya paramātmā samāhitaḥ |
śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkheṣu tathā mānāpamānayoḥ ||
english: For one who has conquered themselves and is at peace, the supreme self stays steady in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour.

school_notes.note: For the self-mastered renunciant whose mind is serene, the Supreme Self is present as their very self; such a person stays even in heat and cold, honour and insult.
'Supreme self' here means the individual self in its own nature, called supreme relative to earlier states; it is firmly settled in a mind unchanged by heat, cold, honour and dishonour.
For the self-mastered, the mind seldom goes out to objects, so the Supreme Self is present in the heart: such a person has direct knowledge.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the disciplined yogi, content with wisdom and indifferent to wealth.
devanagari:
ज्ञानविज्ञानतृप्तात्मा कूटस्थो विजितेन्द्रियः ।
युक्त इत्युच्यते योगी समलोष्टाश्मकाञ्चनः ॥
iast:
jñānavijñānatṛptātmā kūṭastho vijitendriyaḥ |
yukta ityucyate yogī samaloṣṭāśmakāñcanaḥ ||
english: The yogi who is satisfied with knowledge and wisdom, unshakable, with senses mastered, to whom a lump of earth, a stone and gold are the same, is called disciplined.

school_notes.note: Knowledge is understanding what scripture teaches; wisdom is making it one's own experience. Satisfied by both, the yogi becomes unshakable.
Satisfied with knowledge of the self and of how it differs from prakṛti, and steady in the self that is the same through every state, such a person sees earth, stone and gold alike.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna praises the even-minded person who regards friend and enemy, good and bad, alike.
devanagari:
सुहृन्मित्रार्युदासीनमध्यस्थद्वेष्यबन्धुषु ।
साधुष्वपि च पापेषु समबुद्धिर्विशिष्यते ॥
iast:
suhṛnmitrāryudāsīnamadhyasthadveṣyabandhuṣu |
sādhuṣvapi ca pāpeṣu samabuddhirviśiṣyate ||
english: One who has the same regard for well-wishers, friends and enemies, the neutral and the impartial, the hateful and relatives, the good and even the wicked, stands out.

school_notes.note: Defines each: a well-wisher helps without expecting a return; a friend has affection; the neutral takes no side; the impartial wishes well to both sides of a quarrel.

Distinguishes them by age and motive (well-wishers of any age, friends of one's own age, enemies for some cause, those hostile or kind from birth), and says the yogi regards all of them equally as selves.
All souls are alike in being conscious; differences come from the mind, and whatever goodness beings have is the Lord's doing, not their own.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna begins detailed instructions for meditation: practise alone, in a quiet place, free of possessiveness (6.10-6.17).
devanagari:
योगी युञ्जीत सततमात्मानं रहसि स्थितः ।
एकाकी यतचित्तात्मा निराशीरपरिग्रहः ॥
iast:
yogī yuñjīta satatamātmānaṃ rahasi sthitaḥ |
ekākī yatacittātmā nirāśīraparigrahaḥ ||
english: The yogi should constantly practise concentration, staying in a secluded place, alone, with mind and body controlled, without expectations and without possessions.

school_notes.note: Meditate in a solitary place such as a mountain cave, alone, which implies having renounced, with mind and body controlled.
The practitioner of karma yoga should, during the time set for yoga each day, make the mind steady in seeing the self, in a quiet place free of people, alone.
This begins the method of the yoga of meditation.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes how to prepare a place and a seat for meditation.
devanagari:
शुचौ देशे प्रतिष्ठाप्य स्थिरमासनमात्मनः ।
नात्युच्छ्रितं नातिनीचं चैलाजिनकुशोत्तरम् ॥
iast:
śucau deśe pratiṣṭhāpya sthiramāsanamātmanaḥ |
nātyucchritaṃ nātinīcaṃ cailājinakuśottaram ||
english: In a clean place, setting up a firm seat for oneself, neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, a deerskin and kusha grass,

school_notes.note: A clean place, pure by nature or made pure; a steady seat with cloth, skin and kusha grass, laid in the reverse of the order named.
A pure place, untouched by impure people or things; a seat of wood or the like, neither too high nor too low, with a back support and pleasing to the mind.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna continues: seated, with mind focused and senses quiet, one practises for inner purification.
devanagari:
तत्रैकाग्रं मनः कृत्वा यतचित्तेन्द्रियक्रियः ।
उपविश्यासने युञ्ज्याद्योगमात्मविशुद्धये ॥
iast:
tatraikāgraṃ manaḥ kṛtvā yatacittendriyakriyaḥ |
upaviśyāsane yuñjyādyogamātmaviśuddhaye ||
english: sitting there on the seat, making the mind one-pointed, with the activity of mind and senses controlled, one should practise yoga to purify oneself.

school_notes.note: Withdrawing the mind from every object and making it one-pointed, one should practise yoga to purify the inner self.
This is the yoga of absorption.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives the posture for meditation: body upright, gaze steady, not looking around.
devanagari:
समं कायशिरोग्रीवं धारयन्नचलं स्थिरः ।
सम्प्रेक्ष्य नासिकाग्रं स्वं दिशश्चानवलोकयन् ॥
iast:
samaṃ kāyaśirogrīvaṃ dhārayannacalaṃ sthiraḥ |
samprekṣya nāsikāgraṃ svaṃ diśaścānavalokayan ||
english: holding the body, head and neck straight and still, steady, gazing at the tip of one's nose and not looking around,

school_notes.note: Holding body, head and neck erect and still, one gazes as if at the tip of the nose; 'as if', because the aim is to fix the mind on the self, not on the nose.
Sitting supported and steady, eyes on the tip of the nose, calm, fearless, celibate, the mind controlled and fixed on me, one should sit thinking only of me (6.13-6.14).

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the inner attitude for meditation: calm, fearless, self-restrained and focused on him.
devanagari:
प्रशान्तात्मा विगतभीर्ब्रह्मचारिव्रते स्थितः ।
मनः संयम्य मच्चित्तो युक्त आसीत मत्परः ॥
iast:
praśāntātmā vigatabhīrbrahmacārivrate sthitaḥ |
manaḥ saṃyamya maccitto yukta āsīta matparaḥ ||
english: calm and fearless, firm in the vow of celibacy, controlling the mind and thinking of me, one should sit disciplined, intent on me.

school_notes.note: Fearless, keeping the student's vow (celibacy, serving the teacher, living on alms), with the mind withdrawn and fixed on me, the Supreme Lord.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the goal of meditation: a peace that rests in him.
devanagari:
युञ्जन्नेवं सदात्मानं योगी नियतमानसः ।
शान्तिं निर्वाणपरमां मत्संस्थामधिगच्छति ॥
iast:
yuñjannevaṃ sadātmānaṃ yogī niyatamānasaḥ |
śāntiṃ nirvāṇaparamāṃ matsaṃsthāmadhigacchati ||
english: Always practising in this way, with mind controlled, the yogi reaches peace, the supreme nirvana that rests in me.

school_notes.note: Practising this way, the yogi reaches the peace that culminates in liberation and abides in me.
Always fixing the mind on me, the Supreme Brahman and the mind's auspicious support, the yogi's mind, purified by contact with me, becomes still and reaches the peace that rests in me.
'Supreme nirvana' is what follows after leaving the body.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna advises moderation: extremes of eating and sleeping obstruct yoga.
devanagari:
नात्यश्नतस्तु योगोऽस्ति न चैकान्तमनश्नतः ।
न चाति स्वप्नशीलस्य जाग्रतो नैव चार्जुन ॥
iast:
nātyaśnatastu yogo'sti na caikāntamanaśnataḥ |
na cāti svapnaśīlasya jāgrato naiva cārjuna ||
english: Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all; not for one who sleeps too much, Arjuna, nor for one who stays awake too long.

school_notes.note: Not for one who eats beyond their measure, nor one who fasts entirely; he quotes scripture that food in one's own measure protects, more harms, and less does not sustain.
Overeating and fasting, too much and too little activity, too much sleep and too much waking, and overexertion and idleness all obstruct yoga.
The warning against fasting and the like is for those not strong enough for it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the balanced life in which yoga can end sorrow.
devanagari:
युक्ताहारविहारस्य युक्तचेष्टस्य कर्मसु ।
युक्तस्वप्नावबोधस्य योगो भवति दुःखहा ॥
iast:
yuktāhāravihārasya yuktaceṣṭasya karmasu |
yuktasvapnāvabodhasya yogo bhavati duḥkhahā ||
english: For one who is moderate in eating and recreation, measured in effort at work, and moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.

school_notes.note: Measured in food and in walking, measured in action, keeping set times for sleep and waking: for such a person, yoga ends all sorrow.
For one moderate in food, recreation, effort, sleep and waking, the yoga that ends all sorrow and bondage is achieved.
As much food and rest as keeps fatigue away.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the sign of success in meditation: a mind resting in the self, free of craving.
devanagari:
यदा विनियतं चित्तमात्मन्येवावतिष्ठते ।
निःस्पृहः सर्वकामेभ्यो युक्त इत्युच्यते तदा ॥
iast:
yadā viniyataṃ cittamātmanyevāvatiṣṭhate |
niḥspṛhaḥ sarvakāmebhyo yukta ityucyate tadā ||
english: When the well-controlled mind rests in the self alone, free of longing for any desire, one is said to be disciplined in yoga.

school_notes.note: When the controlled mind gives up thoughts of outer things and rests in the self alone, free of thirst for any object seen or unseen, one is called absorbed.
When the mind, finding the self to be the highest goal, rests fixed and still there, one is free of all desire and called fit for yoga.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives the image of a lamp sheltered from wind for the steady mind in meditation.
devanagari:
यथा दीपो निवातस्थो नेङ्गते सोपमा स्मृता ।
योगिनो यतचित्तस्य युञ्जतो योगमात्मनः ॥
iast:
yathā dīpo nivātastho neṅgate sopamā smṛtā |
yogino yatacittasya yuñjato yogamātmanaḥ ||
english: "A lamp in a windless place does not flicker": that is the comparison used for the yogi of controlled mind, practising the yoga of the self.

school_notes.note: Those who know yoga use this image of a lamp in a windless place for the controlled mind of one practising meditation.
The image is for the self itself: with every other activity of the mind stilled, the self stands unwavering and shining with knowledge, like a flame out of the wind.
'The yoga of the self' means yoga directed towards the Lord.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna begins describing the fulfilment of meditation (6.20-6.23).
devanagari:
यत्रोपरमते चित्तं निरुद्धं योगसेवया ।
यत्र चैवात्मनात्मानं पश्यन्नात्मनि तुष्यति ॥
iast:
yatroparamate cittaṃ niruddhaṃ yogasevayā |
yatra caivātmanātmānaṃ paśyannātmani tuṣyati ||
english: When the mind, restrained by the practice of yoga, comes to rest, and when, seeing the self through the self, one is content in the self,

school_notes.note: When the restrained mind comes to rest, and one sees the supreme light of consciousness with a mind purified by absorption, one is content in one's own self.
When the mind delights in yoga as the highest happiness, and, seeing the self with the mind, one is content in the self, needing nothing else.
With the mind, one sees the Lord, the true self, within the body.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna continues describing the boundless happiness found in meditation, which keeps the yogi steady.
devanagari:
सुखमात्यन्तिकं यत्तद् बुद्धिग्राह्यमतीन्द्रियम् ।
वेत्ति यत्र न चैवायं स्थितश्चलति तत्त्वतः ॥
iast:
sukhamātyantikaṃ yattad buddhigrāhyamatīndriyam |
vetti yatra na caivāyaṃ sthitaścalati tattvataḥ ||
english: when one knows that boundless happiness, grasped by the intellect and beyond the senses, and, established there, never moves away from the truth,

school_notes.note: This happiness is endless, grasped by the intellect alone without the senses, not born of objects; established in it, one does not move from the truth.
Experiencing that boundless happiness, beyond the senses and grasped only by the intellect turned to the self, one does not move away from it.
'From the truth', because that happiness is the Lord's own nature.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna continues: the one established in this state is not shaken even by great sorrow.
devanagari:
यं लब्ध्वा चापरं लाभं मन्यते नाधिकं ततः ।
यस्मिन्स्थितो न दुःखेन गुरुणापि विचाल्यते ॥
iast:
yaṃ labdhvā cāparaṃ lābhaṃ manyate nādhikaṃ tataḥ |
yasminsthito na duḥkhena guruṇāpi vicālyate ||
english: having gained which one thinks no other gain greater, and established in which one is not shaken even by great sorrow,

school_notes.note: Having gained the self, one thinks no gain greater; established in it, one is not moved even by great pain, such as being struck by weapons.
Once out of meditation, one longs only for it; while in it, one is not shaken even by great sorrow, such as the loss of a virtuous son.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna defines yoga as freedom from sorrow and urges practising it without discouragement.
devanagari:
तं विद्याद्‌दुःखसंयोगवियोगं योगसंज्ञितम् ।
स निश्चयेन योक्तव्यो योगोऽनिर्विण्णचेतसा ॥
iast:
taṃ vidyādduḥkhasaṃyogaviyogaṃ yogasaṃjñitam |
sa niścayena yoktavyo yogo'nirviṇṇacetasā ||
english: know that this release from union with sorrow is called yoga. This yoga should be practised with determination and without discouragement.

school_notes.note: Yoga is named by its opposite: it is disconnection from contact with sorrow. It must be practised with firm resolve and a mind that does not despair.
Know that knowledge opposed to contact with sorrow is what 'yoga' means; at the start, practise it resolutely and with a glad heart.
It not only ends sorrow that has arisen but stops it arising at all; whoever wishes to thrive must practise it.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives further meditation instruction: let go of desires and gather in the senses (6.24-6.26).
devanagari:
संकल्पप्रभवान्कामांस्त्यक्त्वा सर्वानशेषतः ।
मनसैवेन्द्रियग्रामं विनियम्य समन्ततः ॥
iast:
saṃkalpaprabhavānkāmāṃstyaktvā sarvānaśeṣataḥ |
manasaivendriyagrāmaṃ viniyamya samantataḥ ||
english: Giving up completely all desires born of selfish intention, and restraining the whole range of the senses on every side by the mind alone,

school_notes.note: Give up every desire born of intention without residue, and control the whole range of senses on all sides with the discerning mind.

Desires are of two kinds: born of contact (heat, cold) and born of intention (sons, grandsons, land). The second can be given up entirely by the mind; for the first, which cannot be avoided, give up the joy or distress they bring.
Not even a small, occasional desire for any object should be kept, and only the mind can restrain them.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna teaches patience: settle the mind gradually in the self and let all thoughts go.
devanagari:
शनैः शनैरुपरमेद्‌बुद्ध्या धृतिगृहीतया ।
आत्मसंस्थं मनः कृत्वा न किंचिदपि चिन्तयेत् ॥
iast:
śanaiḥ śanairuparamedbuddhyā dhṛtigṛhītayā |
ātmasaṃsthaṃ manaḥ kṛtvā na kiṃcidapi cintayet ||
english: one should gradually come to rest, with the intellect held firm by steadiness; making the mind abide in the self, one should think of nothing at all.

school_notes.note: Gradually, not suddenly, with an intellect held by patience, making the mind rest in the self with the conviction 'the self is all; there is nothing else', one should think of nothing.
The intellect is the means for restraining the mind and for delighting in the self.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna gives practical advice for a wandering mind: bring it back, each time it strays.
devanagari:
यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम् ।
ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
iast:
yato yato niścarati manaścañcalamasthiram |
tatastato niyamyaitadātmanyeva vaśaṃ nayet ||
english: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, one should rein it in from there and bring it back under the control of the self.

school_notes.note: Wherever the restless mind goes out, to sound or any other object, restrain it by seeing that object's true nature and by cultivating dispassion, and bring it back to the self.
Wherever the mind goes out, drawn by attraction to objects, restrain it with effort and bring it under control by contemplating the self as surpassing joy.
'Wherever' means in whatever direction it runs; bring it under control in the self alone.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the supreme happiness of the yogi whose mind has become calm (6.27-6.28).
devanagari:
प्रशान्तमनसं ह्येनं योगिनं सुखमुत्तमम् ।
उपैति शान्तरजसं ब्रह्मभूतमकल्मषम् ॥
iast:
praśāntamanasaṃ hyenaṃ yoginaṃ sukhamuttamam |
upaiti śāntarajasaṃ brahmabhūtamakalmaṣam ||
english: Supreme happiness comes to the yogi whose mind is at peace, whose passions are stilled, who is free of impurity and has become one with Brahman.

school_notes.note: Unsurpassed happiness comes to the yogi of tranquil mind, free of the passion of delusion and the like, liberated while living, firm in the conviction 'all is Brahman', and sinless.
The yogi whose mind is fixed on the self, all impurities burned and rajas destroyed, abides in their own nature and gains the highest happiness, the experience of the self.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna continues: the purified yogi easily comes to the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman.
devanagari:
युञ्जन्नेवं सदात्मानं योगी विगतकल्मषः ।
सुखेन ब्रह्मसंस्पर्शमत्यन्तं सुखमश्नुते ॥
iast:
yuñjannevaṃ sadātmānaṃ yogī vigatakalmaṣaḥ |
sukhena brahmasaṃsparśamatyantaṃ sukhamaśnute ||
english: Always practising in this way, the yogi, freed from impurity, easily attains the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman.

school_notes.note: Practising in this way, free of obstacles and sin, the yogi easily reaches unsurpassed happiness through contact with the supreme Brahman.
Practising this way, with all past impurities removed, the yogi always enjoys, without strain, the boundless happiness of experiencing Brahman; next come four stages of yoga's ripening.
Expands the previous verse.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the yogi's vision of oneness: the self in all beings and all beings in the self.
devanagari:
सर्वभूतस्थमात्मानं सर्वभूतानि चात्मनि ।
ईक्षते योगयुक्तात्मा सर्वत्र समदर्शनः ॥
iast:
sarvabhūtasthamātmānaṃ sarvabhūtāni cātmani |
īkṣate yogayuktātmā sarvatra samadarśanaḥ ||
english: One whose self is disciplined in yoga sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, seeing the same everywhere.

school_notes.note: Such a one sees their own self in all beings, and all beings, from Brahmā to a blade of grass, as one with the self; they see the one Brahman and self equally in all.
Selves free of prakṛti are all alike, being of the nature of knowledge, and difference belongs to prakṛti; so the yogi sees their own self in all beings and all beings in their self.
The self in all beings is the Supreme Lord, and all beings are in him; quoting the Bhāgavata, one sees him equally present in Brahmā and in a blade of grass.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna promises that one who sees him everywhere is never separated from him.
devanagari:
यो मां पश्यति सर्वत्र सर्वं च मयि पश्यति ।
तस्याहं न प्रणश्यामि स च मे न प्रणश्यति ॥
iast:
yo māṃ paśyati sarvatra sarvaṃ ca mayi paśyati |
tasyāhaṃ na praṇaśyāmi sa ca me na praṇaśyati ||
english: Whoever sees me everywhere and sees everything in me, I am never lost to them, and they are never lost to me.

school_notes.note: Whoever sees me, Vāsudeva, the self of all, in all beings, and all beings in me, never loses sight of me, nor I of them, since we share one self.
In the ripened stage, seeing every self, freed of merit and demerit, as like me, one sees me in all selves and all selves in me.
'I am never lost to them' means I always provide for their welfare; 'they are never lost to me' means they always remain my devotees.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says the yogi who worships him in all beings abides in him in every circumstance.
devanagari:
सर्वभूतस्थितं यो मां भजत्येकत्वमास्थितः ।
सर्वथा वर्तमानोऽपि स योगी मयि वर्तते ॥
iast:
sarvabhūtasthitaṃ yo māṃ bhajatyekatvamāsthitaḥ |
sarvathā vartamāno'pi sa yogī mayi vartate ||
english: The yogi who, established in oneness, worships me as dwelling in all beings, remains in me, however they may live.

school_notes.note: However the yogi of right vision lives, they abide in Viṣṇu's supreme state, always free; nothing obstructs their liberation.
Even when out of meditation and living in whatever way, such a yogi, seeing themselves and all beings, sees me.
Holding that the one Lord is everywhere, they abide in me in every condition; yet such a person rarely does wrong, and if they do, great suffering follows.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna names the highest yogi as one who feels others' joy and pain as their own.
devanagari:
आत्मौपम्येन सर्वत्र समं पश्यति योऽर्जुन ।
सुखं वा यदि वा दुःखं स योगी परमो मतः ॥
iast:
ātmaupamyena sarvatra samaṃ paśyati yo'rjuna |
sukhaṃ vā yadi vā duḥkhaṃ sa yogī paramo mataḥ ||
english: One who, by comparison with oneself, sees the same in all beings, Arjuna, whether it is pleasure or pain, is considered the highest yogi.

school_notes.note: As pleasure is welcome to me, it is welcome to every being; as pain is unwelcome to me, so it is to all; one who sees this sees equally.
Such a person regards the birth or death of another's son just as they would their own son's, since all selves are alike.
Explains equal vision in another way.

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna objects that the mind is too restless for the steady yoga Krishna describes (6.33-6.34).
devanagari:
योऽयं योगस्त्वया प्रोक्तः साम्येन मधुसूदन ।
एतस्याहं न पश्यामि चञ्चलत्वात्स्थितिं स्थिराम् ॥
iast:
yo'yaṃ yogastvayā proktaḥ sāmyena madhusūdana |
etasyāhaṃ na paśyāmi cañcalatvātsthitiṃ sthirām ||
english: Krishna, this yoga of evenness you have described, I do not see how it can last, because the mind is restless.

school_notes.note: Because the mind is restless, Arjuna does not see this yoga of evenness becoming stable.
Arjuna finds it hard to see all selves, long experienced as utterly different, as equal to one another and to the Lord, because the mind is so restless.
Because the mind is restless, the yoga cannot stand firm.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna compares controlling the mind to controlling the wind.
devanagari:
चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्‌दृढम् ।
तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
iast:
cañcalaṃ hi manaḥ kṛṣṇa pramāthi balavaddṛḍham |
tasyāhaṃ nigrahaṃ manye vāyoriva suduṣkaram ||
english: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, strong and stubborn. I think controlling it is as hard as controlling the wind.

school_notes.note: The mind not only wanders but churns up the body and senses and overpowers them; restraining it is as hard as holding back the wind.
Even with familiar things the mind will not stay put; holding it on the self, so unlike its usual objects, is like fanning against a gale.
He cites Vyāsa: because the mind is restless, steadiness in yoga is impossible without practice or dispassion.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna agrees the mind is hard to control but gives the remedy: practice and detachment.
devanagari:
असंशयं महाबाहो मनो दुर्निग्रहं चलम् ।
अभ्यासेन तु कौन्तेय वैराग्येण च गृह्यते ॥
iast:
asaṃśayaṃ mahābāho mano durnigrahaṃ calam |
abhyāsena tu kaunteya vairāgyeṇa ca gṛhyate ||
english: Without doubt, mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to control; but it can be held, son of Kunti, through practice and detachment.

school_notes.note: Practice is the mind's repeated return to the same object; detachment is freedom from thirst for pleasures, seen and unseen, by repeatedly seeing their flaws.
The mind is indeed hard to hold, but it can be held somehow: by turning towards the self through practice, and by losing thirst for other things through seeing their flaws.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna adds that yoga is difficult without self-control but achievable with steady effort.
devanagari:
असंयतात्मना योगो दुष्प्राप इति मे मतिः ।
वश्यात्मना तु यतता शक्योऽवाप्तुमुपायतः ॥
iast:
asaṃyatātmanā yogo duṣprāpa iti me matiḥ |
vaśyātmanā tu yatatā śakyo'vāptumupāyataḥ ||
english: Yoga is hard to reach for one who lacks self-control; that is my view. But one who is self-controlled and keeps striving can reach it by the right means.

school_notes.note: For one whose mind is not controlled through practice and detachment, yoga is hard to gain; one who masters the mind that way and keeps striving can reach it.
Without mastery of the mind, yoga is hard to gain however great the effort; with the mind won over through karma yoga, worship of me, and continued striving, this yoga of equal vision can be reached.
The mind never controls itself on its own; he cites a text that liberation is not for those without good intent.

context: Arjuna asks what happens to someone who sets out on the path in faith but falls short (6.37-6.39).

अयतिः श्रद्धयोपेतो योगाच्चलितमानसः ।
अप्राप्य योगसंसिद्धिं कां गतिं कृष्ण गच्छति ॥

english: Krishna, what becomes of one who has faith but does not strive enough, whose mind strays from yoga, and who fails to reach perfection in yoga?

school_notes.note: Arjuna asks about one with faith but little effort, whose mind strays from yoga, even at the time of death, and so fails to reach right vision.
Arjuna asks about one who began yoga with faith but whose practice faltered for lack of firm effort.
'Does not strive enough' means makes no effort.

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna fears that someone who falls short may lose both worldly and spiritual goals.

कच्चिन्नोभयविभ्रष्टश्छिन्नाभ्रमिव नश्यति ।
अप्रतिष्ठो महाबाहो विमूढो ब्रह्मणः पथि ॥

kaccinnobhayavibhraṣṭaśchinnābhramiva naśyati |

english: Fallen from both, does such a person not perish like a scattered cloud, without support, mighty-armed one, lost on the path to Brahman?

school_notes.note: Fallen from both the path of action and the path of yoga, without support and confused on the path to Brahman, does such a person vanish like a torn cloud?
Like a piece of cloud torn from one great cloud that never reaches another, does such a person, having left the means to heaven and not reached Brahman, perish in between?

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna asks Krishna to resolve his doubt about the one who falls short.

एतन्मे संशयं कृष्ण छेत्तुमर्हस्यशेषतः ।
त्वदन्यः संशयस्यास्य छेत्ता न ह्युपपद्यते ॥
iast:
etanme saṃśayaṃ kṛṣṇa chettumarhasyaśeṣataḥ |
tvadanyaḥ saṃśayasyāsya chettā na hyupapadyate ||
english: Krishna, please dispel this doubt of mine completely; no one but you can dispel it.

school_notes.note: No sage or god other than you can remove this doubt, so you alone should.
No one but you, who see everything directly and always, can cut this doubt.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna reassures Arjuna that no sincere effort for good is ever lost (6.40-6.45).
devanagari:
पार्थ नैवेह नामुत्र विनाशस्तस्य विद्यते ।
न हि कल्याणकृत्कश्चिद्‌दुर्गतिं तात गच्छति ॥

pārtha naiveha nāmutra vināśastasya vidyate |
na hi kalyāṇakṛtkaściddurgatiṃ tāta gacchati ||
english: Son of Pritha, there is no destruction for such a person, neither in this world nor in the next; for no one who does good, my friend, ever comes to a bad end.

school_notes.note: Destruction here means a birth lower than before, which does not happen to one fallen from yoga. Krishna calls Arjuna 'tāta', a word for a son, since a father extends himself in his son.
For one who began yoga with faith and fell away, there is no loss in either world: neither failure to gain what was desired nor meeting with harm.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the next life of one who fell short in yoga: rest in higher worlds, then birth in a good family.
devanagari:
प्राप्य पुण्यकृतां लोकानुषित्वा शाश्वतीः समाः ।

iast:
prāpya puṇyakṛtāṃ lokānuṣitvā śāśvatīḥ samāḥ |
śucīnāṃ śrīmatāṃ gehe yogabhraṣṭo'bhijāyate ||
english: Having reached the worlds of those who do good and lived there for countless years, one who fell from yoga is born into the home of the pure and prosperous.

school_notes.note: The renunciant fallen from yoga reaches the worlds of those who performed great sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice, and after enjoying them is born into a pure and prosperous family.

Fallen from yoga out of desire for some pleasure, they enjoy that kind of pleasure in the worlds of the very meritorious, by the power of yoga, until the craving is spent, and are then born into a pure, prosperous home.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says one who was further along may be born directly into a family of yogis, a rarer birth.
devanagari:
अथवा योगिनामेव कुले भवति धीमताम् ।

iast:
athavā yogināmeva kule bhavati dhīmatām |
etaddhi durlabhataraṃ loke janma yadīdṛśam ||
english: Or they are born into a family of wise yogis; but a birth like this is harder to gain in this world.

school_notes.note: Or they are born into a poor family of wise yogis, a birth harder to gain than the one just described.
If their yoga had ripened before they strayed, they are born into a family of wise yogis who teach yoga; both kinds of birth are rare for ordinary people and come from the greatness of yoga.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that past spiritual progress carries over into the next life.

english: There they regain the understanding they had in their former body, and from there they strive again for perfection, joy of the Kurus.

school_notes.note: In that family they regain the understanding of their former body and, from those impressions, strive even harder for perfection.
In that birth they regain their earlier understanding of yoga and, like someone waking from sleep, strive again so that no obstacle stops them.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says past practice carries a person forward, and even the wish to know yoga lifts one beyond ritual.
devanagari:
पूर्वाभ्यासेन तेनैव ह्रियते ह्यवशोऽपि सः ।

pūrvābhyāsena tenaiva hriyate hyavaśo'pi saḥ |
jijñāsurapi yogasya śabdabrahmātivartate ||
english: By that earlier practice they are carried forward even without wanting to; even one who merely wishes to know yoga goes beyond the Veda, Brahman in the form of words.

school_notes.note: The earlier practice draws them on toward perfection, unless they have done some stronger wrong in the meantime; even one who only wants to know yoga goes beyond the results of Vedic rites.

Carried by earlier practice, the one who fell from yoga is drawn back into yoga even against their will; even one who had only begun to inquire, then strayed, regains that inquiry and takes up karma yoga again.
Even one who longs intensely to know yoga goes beyond the Veda and reaches the Supreme Brahman.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says that steady effort across many lives brings the yogi to the highest goal.
devanagari:

अनेकजन्मसंसिद्धस्ततो याति परां गतिम् ॥
iast:
prayatnādyatamānastu yogī saṃśuddhakilbiṣaḥ |
anekajanmasaṃsiddhastato yāti parāṃ gatim ||
english: But the yogi who strives with effort, cleansed of wrongdoing and perfected over many births, then reaches the highest goal.

school_notes.note: Striving harder, purified of sin and gathering impressions little by little over many births, the yogi gains right vision and reaches the highest goal.
Purified by merit gathered over many births, the yogi who strives with effort, even after straying, surely reaches the highest goal.
Not in one birth: by knowing, meditating and seeing over many births one enters Nārāyaṇa, as a text he cites says.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna urges Arjuna to become a yogi, ranking yoga above austerity, learning and ritual.
devanagari:

कर्मिभ्यश्चाधिको योगी तस्माद्योगी भवार्जुन ॥

english: The yogi is greater than ascetics, greater even than people of learning, and greater than people of ritual action. So be a yogi, Arjuna.

school_notes.note: 'People of learning' here means those learned in scripture, and 'people of action' those who perform rites like the fire offering; the yogi surpasses them all.
Yoga leads to a greater goal than austerity alone, than knowledge other than self-knowledge, or than rites like the horse sacrifice; so the yogi surpasses them all.
Citing the Garuḍa Purāṇa: meditation on Hari surpasses austerity and sacrifice, and even meditation on other gods.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna closes chapter 6: the greatest yogi is the one devoted to him with faith, preparing the theme of devotion.

śraddhāvān bhajate yo māṃ sa me yuktatamo mataḥ ||
english: And of all yogis, the one who worships me with faith, with their inner self absorbed in me, I consider the most disciplined of all.

school_notes.note: Even among yogis who meditate on Rudra, the Ādityas and others, the one who worships me, Vāsudeva, with faith and a mind fixed on me, is the most disciplined.
Reads 'of all yogis' as 'than all yogis': this devotee is not one of the four kinds of yogi described earlier, but surpasses them and the ascetics and the rest.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna opens chapter 7, on knowledge of his nature, promising Arjuna complete understanding of him.
devanagari:
मय्यासक्तमनाः पार्थ योगं युञ्जन्मदाश्रयः ।
असंशयं समग्रं मां यथा ज्ञास्यसि तच्छृणु ॥

mayyāsaktamanāḥ pārtha yogaṃ yuñjanmadāśrayaḥ |
asaṃśayaṃ samagraṃ māṃ yathā jñāsyasi tacchṛṇu ||
english: Hear, son of Pritha, how, with your mind attached to me, practising yoga and relying on me, you will know me completely, without doubt.

school_notes.note: With your mind attached to me, the Supreme Lord, practising yoga and relying on me alone, unlike those who rely on rites or austerity for some goal, hear how you will know me fully.
With a mind bound fast to me in intense love, so that you would fall apart if separated from my nature, qualities and deeds, and depending on me alone, hear how you will know me.
The earlier chapters stressed the means; the next six stress the greatness of the Lord.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna promises a complete teaching about himself, after which nothing more needs to be known.
devanagari:

यज्ज्ञात्वा नेह भूयोऽन्यज्ज्ञातव्यमवशिष्यते ॥

english: I will teach you this knowledge in full, together with realised wisdom; once you know it, nothing more here remains to be known.

school_notes.note: Knowledge 'with wisdom' means with one's own direct experience; knowing it, nothing further remains to be known as a means to life's goal.
'Wisdom' (vijñāna) is knowledge of what sets me apart from all conscious and non-conscious things: free of every flaw and full of countless auspicious qualities.
This knowledge is about me; 'wisdom' is knowledge of the particulars.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna notes how rare true knowledge of him is.
devanagari:
मनुष्याणां सहस्रेषु कश्चिद्यतति सिद्धये ।
यततामपि सिद्धानां कश्चिन्मां वेत्ति तत्त्वतः ॥

yatatāmapi siddhānāṃ kaścinmāṃ vetti tattvataḥ ||
english: Among thousands of people, hardly one strives for perfection; and among those who strive and succeed, hardly one knows me as I truly am.

school_notes.note: Among thousands, one strives for perfection; and of those who strive, who are already accomplished in a sense, only one knows me truly.
Among thousands fit for scripture, few strive all the way to perfection; among those, few know me and strive through me; and among thousands who know me, hardly one knows me as I truly am.
Shows how rare this knowledge is.

english: Earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego: this is my nature, divided eightfold.

This eightfold prakṛti, which takes the form of the world's objects, instruments and places of enjoyment, belongs to me.
Ego is included within the great principle.

The higher nature is Śrī, consciousness itself, who sustains the life of beings; he cites a text on the Lord's two natures, one inert and one conscious.

english: Understand that all beings have these two as their source. I am the origin of the whole world, and its dissolution.

school_notes.note: All beings arise from these two natures, the field and the knower of the field; since my two natures are their cause, I am the origin and the end of the whole world.

english: There is nothing higher than me, Arjuna. All this is strung on me, like pearls on a thread.

I am higher than all, as the cause of both natures and the master of everything conscious and non-conscious; no one else has greater knowledge, power or strength.
I alone am the highest; there is nothing at all higher than me.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna begins describing how he is present in the essence of everything (7.8-7.11).

english: I am the taste in water, son of Kunti; I am the light of the moon and the sun; I am Om in all the Vedas, sound in space, and the vigour in human beings.

This is the detailed knowledge: the Lord alone governs the natural qualities of things, such as taste in water; those qualities do not depend on water and the rest.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna calls himself the eternal seed of all beings and the source of intelligence and brilliance.

english: Know me, son of Pritha, as the eternal seed of all beings. I am the intelligence of the intelligent and the brilliance of the brilliant.

school_notes.note: I am the seed from which all beings sprout; I am the discerning power of the discerning and the boldness of the bold.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says he is present even in desire, so long as it does not go against dharma.
devanagari:

english: Of the strong, I am the strength that is free of desire and passion; in all beings, I am desire that is not against dharma, best of the Bharatas.

school_notes.note: I am the strength free of craving for absent things and passion for present ones, the strength that simply sustains the body, not the strength that feeds the thirst of worldly people.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says the three qualities of nature come from him, yet he is not bound by them.
devanagari:
ये चैव सात्त्विका भावा राजसास्तामसाश्च ये ।
मत्त एवेति तान्विद्धि न त्वहं तेषु ते मयि ॥

ye caiva sāttvikā bhāvā rājasāstāmasāśca ye |
matta eveti tānviddhi na tvahaṃ teṣu te mayi ||
english: Whatever states of being there are, whether of sattva, rajas or tamas, know that they come from me alone; but I am not in them, they are in me.

school_notes.note: Though they come from me, I am not under their control as worldly beings are; rather, they are under mine.
All states of sattva, rajas and tamas, as objects, bodies, senses and their causes, arise from me and rest in me as my body; I never depend on them.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains why the world fails to recognise him: it is bewildered by the play of the three gunas.
devanagari:
त्रिभिर्गुणमयैर्भावैरेभिः सर्वमिदं जगत् ।
मोहितं नाभिजानाति मामेभ्यः परमव्ययम् ॥
iast:
tribhirguṇamayairbhāvairebhiḥ sarvamidaṃ jagat |
mohitaṃ nābhijānāti māmebhyaḥ paramavyayam ||
english: Deluded by these states made of the three gunas, this whole world does not recognise me, who am beyond them and imperishable.

school_notes.note: Deluded by the gunas' products, attraction, aversion, delusion and the like, beings lose discernment and do not know me as distinct from the gunas and imperishable.
The whole world, conscious and non-conscious, arises from me, rests in me as my body and dissolves into me; yet, deluded by the gunas, beings do not know me.
'Made of' the gunas expresses identity, not product: māyā itself is not a product of the gunas.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says the illusion woven by the gunas is hard to cross, except by taking refuge in him.
devanagari:
दैवी ह्येषा गुणमयी मम माया दुरत्यया ।
मामेव ये प्रपद्यन्ते मायामेतां तरन्ति ते ॥
iast:
daivī hyeṣā guṇamayī mama māyā duratyayā |
māmeva ye prapadyante māyāmetāṃ taranti te ||
english: This divine māyā of mine, made of the gunas, is hard to get past; but those who take refuge in me alone cross beyond this māyā.

school_notes.note: This māyā of the Lord Viṣṇu, made of the three gunas, is hard to overcome; those who give up everything else and take refuge in me alone, their own self, cross the māyā that deludes all beings.
This māyā of the three gunas is 'divine' because I made it in play; it is called māyā because it produces wondrous effects, like the magical weapons of asuras in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Māyā deludes; belonging to the God who creates and plays, it is immensely powerful and hard to cross. He derives 'divine' from the root 'div', to play.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes those who do not turn to him, deluded and drawn to a demonic nature.
devanagari:
न मां दुष्कृतिनो मूढाः प्रपद्यन्ते नराधमाः ।
माययापहृतज्ञाना आसुरं भावमाश्रिताः ॥
iast:
na māṃ duṣkṛtino mūḍhāḥ prapadyante narādhamāḥ |
māyayāpahṛtajñānā āsuraṃ bhāvamāśritāḥ ||
english: Evildoers, the deluded, the lowest of people, whose knowledge is stolen by māyā and who have taken on a demonic nature, do not take refuge in me.

school_notes.note: Sinners, the deluded, the lowest of people, robbed of knowledge by māyā, take on the demonic nature marked by violence, falsehood and the like.
Those who do not take refuge in me are of four kinds, according to the degree of their sin; the 'deluded' misunderstand my nature and cling to material things.
The demonic nature is described from 16.7 onwards.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna names four kinds of people who turn to him: the distressed, the curious, those seeking gain, and the wise.
devanagari:
चतुर्विधा भजन्ते मां जनाः सुकृतिनोऽर्जुन ।
आर्तो जिज्ञासुरर्थार्थी ज्ञानी च भरतर्षभ ॥
iast:
caturvidhā bhajante māṃ janāḥ sukṛtino'rjuna |
ārto jijñāsurarthārthī jñānī ca bharatarṣabha ||
english: Four kinds of virtuous people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

school_notes.note: The distressed are those beset by thieves, tigers, disease and the like; the seeker wants to know the truth of the Lord; the seeker of wealth wants riches; the wise know the truth of Viṣṇu.
The distressed have lost position and wealth and want them back; the seeker of wealth wants riches not yet gained. They are ranked by the merit behind them, each higher than the last.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna singles out the wise devotee, who loves him for his own sake, as dearest to him.
devanagari:
तेषां ज्ञानी नित्ययुक्त एकभक्तिर्विशिष्यते ।
प्रियो हि ज्ञानिनोऽत्यर्थमहं स च मम प्रियः ॥
iast:
teṣāṃ jñānī nityayukta ekabhaktirviśiṣyate |
priyo hi jñānino'tyarthamahaṃ sa ca mama priyaḥ ||
english: Of these, the wise one, always disciplined and devoted to the One alone, stands out; for I am exceedingly dear to the wise, and they are dear to me.

school_notes.note: The wise, knowing the truth, are always absorbed and devoted to one alone, since they see nothing else to worship; I am their very self, so I am supremely dear to them.
The wise one's union with me is constant, since I alone am their goal; the others are joined to me only until they get what they want.
'Devoted to the One alone' means devotion to me and to no other, as the Garuḍa Purāṇa says.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says all four kinds of devotees are noble, but the wise one is his very self.
devanagari:
उदाराः सर्व एवैते ज्ञानी त्वात्मैव मे मतम् ।
आस्थितः स हि युक्तात्मा मामेवानुत्तमां गतिम् ॥
iast:
udārāḥ sarva evaite jñānī tvātmaiva me matam |
āsthitaḥ sa hi yuktātmā māmevānuttamāṃ gatim ||
english: All of these are noble, but I consider the wise one to be my very self; for, wholly disciplined, they rely on me alone as the highest goal.

school_notes.note: All are dear to me, for no devotee of mine is not dear; but the wise one is my very self, not other than me.
All are generous, since even those who seek small things from me are giving me everything. But I hold that I depend on the wise one to sustain myself, since they cannot sustain themselves without me.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna describes the rare great soul who, after many lives, sees him in everything.
devanagari:
बहूनां जन्मनामन्ते ज्ञानवान्मां प्रपद्यते ।
वासुदेवः सर्वमिति स महात्मा सुदुर्लभः ॥
iast:
bahūnāṃ janmanāmante jñānavānmāṃ prapadyate |
vāsudevaḥ sarvamiti sa mahātmā sudurlabhaḥ ||
english: At the end of many births, the wise one comes to me, knowing "Vāsudeva is all." Such a great soul is very rare.

school_notes.note: At the end of many births, with mature knowledge, one directly realises me, Vāsudeva, the inner self, as everything; no one equals such a great soul.
After many births of merit, one knows that they exist only for Vāsudeva and depend on him, and that he is their goal, their means, and everything they desire.
One becomes wise only at the end of many births, as the Brahma Purāṇa says.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains that people driven by desires worship other gods for what they want (7.20-7.23).

तं तं नियममास्थाय प्रकृत्या नियताः स्वया ॥
iast:
kāmaistaistairhṛtajñānāḥ prapadyante'nyadevatāḥ |
taṃ taṃ niyamamāsthāya prakṛtyā niyatāḥ svayā ||
english: Those whose knowledge is carried away by various desires turn to other gods, following one rule or another, driven by their own nature.

school_notes.note: Robbed of discernment by desires for sons, cattle, heaven and the like, they turn to gods other than Vāsudeva, following the rules of each, driven by tendencies from past lives.
Driven by sinful tendencies bound up with the gunas, worldly people, their knowledge of me stolen by desires, worship Indra and other gods alone to fulfil those desires.
'Nature' here means conditioning, impressions, tendencies.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says he strengthens each person's faith in whatever form they choose to worship.

तस्य तस्याचलां श्रद्धां तामेव विदधाम्यहम् ॥
iast:

tasya tasyācalāṃ śraddhāṃ tāmeva vidadhāmyaham ||
english: Whatever form any devotee wishes to worship with faith, I make that very faith of theirs unwavering.

school_notes.note: Whatever divine form a desire-driven devotee wishes to worship with faith, I make that faith steady.
Those gods are my bodies, as the Upanishad says of the sun; even one who does not know this, worshipping such a form with faith, receives steady faith from me.
Devotees of Brahmā and other gods reach a limit, while devotees of Viṣṇu reach the endless, as a Nārada text he cites says.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says that even worship of other gods bears fruit only because he grants it.

लभते च ततः कामान्मयैव विहितान्हि तान् ॥
iast:
sa tayā śraddhayā yuktastasyārādhanamīhate |
labhate ca tataḥ kāmānmayaiva vihitānhi tān ||
english: Endowed with that faith, they seek to worship that form, and from it they gain their desires, which are in fact granted by me alone.

school_notes.note: With the faith I give them, they worship that deity and gain their desires, which are in fact arranged by me, the all-knowing Lord who apportions the fruits of action.
Worshipping Indra and the others, who are my body, they gain the desires I grant, though they do not know that this worship is really worship of me.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna contrasts the limited fruit of worshipping lesser gods with coming to him.

iast:
antavattu phalaṃ teṣāṃ tadbhavatyalpamedhasām |
devāndevayajo yānti madbhaktā yānti māmapi ||
english: But the fruit gained by these people of small understanding comes to an end. Worshippers of the gods go to the gods; my devotees come to me.

school_notes.note: Their fruit perishes; with the same effort they could have gained endless fruit by coming to me. Krishna voices compassion for them.
Those who worship only Indra and the like reach those gods, whose enjoyments and lifespans are limited, and so they fall again along with them.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says the unwise mistake his appearance in human form for an ordinary birth (7.24-7.26).

iast:
avyaktaṃ vyaktimāpannaṃ manyante māmabuddhayaḥ |
paraṃ bhāvamajānanto mamāvyayamanuttamam ||
english: The unwise think of me, the unmanifest, as having become manifest, not knowing my higher nature, which is imperishable and supreme.

school_notes.note: The undiscerning think I, the eternal Lord, have only now become manifest, not knowing my supreme nature as the Supreme Self.
Out of supreme compassion I was born as Vasudeva's son without giving up my nature, so that all could approach me; the unwise take me for an ordinary prince.
The unwise think the Lord, who has no body made of matter, has taken on such a body; citing scripture, his body is bliss itself.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says his divine nature is hidden by his own power, so the world fails to see him.
devanagari:
नाहं प्रकाशः सर्वस्य योगमायासमावृतः ।
मूढोऽयं नाभिजानाति लोको मामजमव्ययम् ॥
iast:
nāhaṃ prakāśaḥ sarvasya yogamāyāsamāvṛtaḥ |
mūḍho'yaṃ nābhijānāti loko māmajamavyayam ||
english: Veiled by my yoga-māyā, I am not revealed to everyone. This deluded world does not know me as unborn and imperishable.

school_notes.note: I am revealed only to some, my devotees; veiled by yoga-māyā, the joining of the gunas, I am not known to the deluded world.
Veiled by the 'māyā' of a human form like any other being's, I am not seen by all; seeing only my human shape, the world does not know me as the Lord, though my deeds surpass those of wind and Indra.
This not-knowing is by my will: through my power and my māyā I hide myself and bind the world's mind, as the Padma Purāṇa says.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says he knows all beings in all times, though none of them truly knows him.

भविष्याणि च भूतानि मां तु वेद न कश्चन ॥
iast:
vedāhaṃ samatītāni vartamānāni cārjuna |
bhaviṣyāṇi ca bhūtāni māṃ tu veda na kaścana ||
english: I know the beings of the past, the present and the future, Arjuna, but no one knows me.

school_notes.note: No one knows me except the devotee who takes refuge in me; for lack of knowing my truth, people do not worship me.
Among all beings of the three times that I watch over, I find hardly anyone who knows me as Vāsudeva, come down to be the refuge of all, and takes refuge in me.
Māyā does not bind me; no one, however powerful, knows me by their own power.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains how desire and aversion confuse all beings from birth (7.27-7.28).

सर्वभूतानि संमोहं सर्गे यान्ति परन्तप ॥
iast:
icchādveṣasamutthena dvandvamohena bhārata |
sarvabhūtāni saṃmohaṃ sarge yānti parantapa ||
english: Through the delusion of the opposites, which arises from desire and aversion, all beings fall into confusion at birth, scorcher of enemies.

school_notes.note: Desire and aversion, opposed to each other like heat and cold, give rise to the delusion of the opposites, and through it all beings are confused from the moment they come into being.
Because of desire and aversion practised in earlier births towards pleasure and pain, beings are deluded by the opposites at the very moment of birth.
When desire and aversion grow strong, nothing can be known; they arise once there is a body.

context: Krishna describes those who, freed from desire and aversion, turn to him steadfastly.

ते द्वन्द्वमोहनिर्मुक्ता भजन्ते मां दृढव्रताः ॥

english: But people of good deeds, whose wrongdoing has come to an end, freed from the delusion of the opposites, worship me with firm resolve.

Those whose beginningless sin, which turns them away from me, is destroyed by merit gathered over many births take refuge in me and are freed from delusion.

Those who strive, relying on me, to see the self free of prakṛti come to know that Brahman, the whole of the inner self, and all action.
'For freedom from old age and death' praises the longing for liberation rather than commanding it; he cites texts that the single-minded devotee who does not even seek liberation is greater.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna begins answering: he defines Brahman, the inner self and action (8.3-8.4).
devanagari:

भूतभावोद्भवकरो विसर्गः कर्मसंज्ञितः ॥

akṣaraṃ brahma paramaṃ svabhāvo'dhyātmamucyate |
bhūtabhāvodbhavakaro visargaḥ karmasaṃjñitaḥ ||
english: Brahman is the supreme Imperishable; one's own essential nature is called the inner self; and the creative offering that brings beings into existence is called action.

school_notes.note: 'The Imperishable' is the Supreme Self, as in the Upanishad's 'at the command of this Imperishable', not the syllable Om, which 8.13 calls 'the one-syllable Brahman'.
Takes 'the supreme Imperishable' here to be the individual self in its pure form, free of prakṛti, rather than the Supreme Lord.
'Supreme' rules out reading 'the Imperishable' as the Veda; the 'inner self' is the soul's own enduring nature.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna completes his definitions, naming himself as the lord of sacrifice within the body.
devanagari:

english: The realm of beings is perishable existence; the realm of the gods is the cosmic Person; and the lord of sacrifice is I myself, here in the body, best of the embodied.

school_notes.note: The realm of beings is whatever is born and perishes; the realm of the gods is the Person, Hiraṇyagarbha within the sun, who supports the senses of all beings; the lord of sacrifice is the Lord within the body.
For seekers of power, the 'realm of beings' means the refined objects of sense (sound, touch and the rest) found in the elements, which they seek and meditate on.
The realm of beings concerns embodied souls: perishable effects. Even the unmanifest undergoes a kind of change.

'My state' means existence in me, free of sorrow and full of unsurpassed bliss.

'Sustainer' means the one who supports and nourishes; he cites texts for 'Seer' meaning all-knowing.

Withdrawing the senses and holding the mind on me, the Imperishable, in the lotus of the heart, one remains steady in yogic concentration.

english: For one who remembers me constantly, day after day, with a mind that turns to nothing else, I am easy to reach, son of Pritha, for that ever-disciplined yogi.

For one who, out of great love, cannot bear to live without remembering me, I am easy to reach; it is I myself, not just my state, that they attain.
'Ever-disciplined' means always using the means; 'yogi' means one whose yoga is complete.

Great souls who know me truly and, out of love, cannot sustain themselves without me, having reached me do not return to birth, the home of all sorrow.

Those who know the order of days and nights, set by my will for all beings from humans to four-faced Brahmā, know that Brahmā's day lasts a thousand cycles of the four ages.

Knowing these paths, the yogi is not confused at death but goes by the path of the gods; so be absorbed every day in contemplating the path of light.
Knowing the paths with their means, and practising them, one is not deluded, as the Skanda Purāṇa says.

This chapter clarifies what chapter 7 taught.

english: All this world is pervaded by me in my unmanifest form. All beings dwell in me, but I do not dwell in them.

school_notes.note: My supreme nature, beyond the reach of the senses, pervades the world; beings dwell in me, the unmanifest, but I am not in them as something contained.
I pervade this whole world, unseen, as its inner controller, to sustain and govern it, as the Upanishad says: 'who dwells in the earth, whom the earth does not know'.
If he pervades everything, why is he not seen? Because his form is unmanifest.

context: Krishna completes the paradox, calling it a sign of his divine power.

english: And yet beings do not dwell in me: see my divine power! My self sustains all beings and brings them into being, yet does not dwell in them.

school_notes.note: The self is unattached, as the Upanishad says: 'it is unattached, it clings to nothing'. This is my divine yoga.
Beings do not rest in me as water rests in a pot; I hold them by my will alone. I support all beings, yet receive no support from them.
They are in him, yet not in contact with him the way things touch the earth; his very body sustains beings.

As a great wind moves everywhere in space with no support, held only by me, so all beings rest in me and are held by me.
Wind resting in space does not take on the qualities of space.

english: At the end of a cosmic age, son of Kunti, all beings return to my nature; at the beginning of an age, I send them forth again.

school_notes.note: At dissolution all beings enter my lower, three-guna nature; at creation I send them forth again as before.
At the end of Brahmā's life, by my will, beings enter my prakṛti, which is my body and is called 'darkness'; at the start of the next age I send them forth again, as Manu says.

context: Krishna says beings arise again and again, carried by the power of nature that he governs.

english: Taking hold of my own nature, I send forth again and again this whole multitude of beings, helpless under the power of nature.

Shaping my prakṛti eightfold, I send forth the four kinds of beings (gods, animals, humans and plants), helpless under the spell of prakṛti.
He leans on prakṛti the way a capable person might lean on a stick while walking, in play.

Unequal creation does not make me cruel or partial, since the differences come from beings' own past karma, as the Brahma Sūtra says.
'As if indifferent', but not truly indifferent: whatever exists exists by his favour and ceases by his neglect, as the Bhāgavata says.

school_notes.note: With me as witness, unchanging awareness, my māyā produces the moving and unmoving world, as the Upanishad says: 'the one God hidden in all beings'.
Overseen by me, whose will is always fulfilled, my prakṛti brings forth the world according to beings' karma; this shows my lordship and my freedom from cruelty.
If he is 'as if indifferent', does prakṛti produce by itself? No: I alone oversee and bring about prakṛti's production.

Nothing that those hostile to the Lord hope for is gained, and their rites and knowledge are futile.

context: Krishna promises to provide for and protect those devoted to him alone.
devanagari:

तेषां नित्याभियुक्तानां योगक्षेमं वहाम्यहम् ॥
iast:
ananyāścintayanto māṃ ye janāḥ paryupāsate |
teṣāṃ nityābhiyuktānāṃ yogakṣemaṃ vahāmyaham ||
english: Those who think of no one else and worship me, always disciplined, I bring them what they lack and protect what they have.

school_notes.note: For renunciants who know the supreme God as their own self and worship him constantly, I provide what they lack and protect what they have.
For those who cannot live without thinking of me and worship me fully, I myself bring about their union with me, from which there is no return, and keep it secure.
'Thinking of no one else' means thinking of nothing other than him, as the Gautama supplements say.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says worship of other gods ultimately reaches him, though without true understanding (9.23-9.25).
devanagari:

तेऽपि मामेव कौन्तेय यजन्त्यविधिपूर्वकम् ॥
iast:
ye'pyanyadevatābhaktā yajante śraddhayānvitāḥ |

english: Even those devoted to other gods, who worship them with faith, are really worshipping me, son of Kunti, though not in the proper way.

school_notes.note: Those devoted to other gods worship me, but 'not in the proper way', which means out of ignorance.
Worshippers of Indra and others really worship me, since all are my body and their names ultimately refer to me; but they do not know this.
Otherwise 'I am the ritual' (9.16) would be untrue.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna explains why such worship falls short: he is the real recipient of every sacrifice.
devanagari:
अहं हि सर्वयज्ञानां भोक्ता च प्रभुरेव च ।
न तु मामभिजानन्ति तत्त्वेनातश्च्यवन्ति ते ॥
iast:
ahaṃ hi sarvayajñānāṃ bhoktā ca prabhureva ca |
na tu māmabhijānanti tattvenātaścyavanti te ||
english: For I am the enjoyer and the lord of all sacrifices; but they do not know me as I truly am, and so they fall.

school_notes.note: I am the enjoyer of all sacrifices as their deity, and their lord, as 8.4 said; not knowing me truly, they worship wrongly and fall.
How remarkable that within the same rite, a mere difference of intention makes some gain small, fleeting fruits and others the boundless joy of reaching the Supreme Person.
Gives the reason why worship is properly directed to him.

context: Krishna says people reach whatever they devote themselves to.

english: Those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship spirits go to the spirits; and those who worship me come to me.

school_notes.note: Those devoted to the gods reach the gods; those devoted to ancestral rites reach the ancestors; worshippers of spirits reach the spirits; my worshippers reach me.
'Devoted' here means having the intention: those who resolve to worship Indra and the rest reach them.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says even the simplest offering, given with love, is accepted by him.

english: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from one whose heart is pure, I accept.

school_notes.note: Whoever offers me a leaf, flower, fruit or water with devotion, I accept it from that person of pure mind.
Even something anyone can obtain, a leaf or a flower, offered by one who out of love cannot live without giving it, I receive as if it were something I had never had.
Answers the worry that the weak cannot worship one so great: he is pleased by devotion alone; but offering what is not permitted is a fault.

context: Krishna teaches turning every part of life into an offering (9.27-9.28).

yatkaroṣi yadaśnāsi yajjuhoṣi dadāsi yat |

english: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever austerity you practise, son of Kunti, do it as an offering to me.

school_notes.note: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, offer, give to brahmins and others, or practise as austerity, do it as an offering to me.
Offer all ordinary and Vedic actions to me, giving up the sense of being their doer and enjoyer.

context: Krishna says offering every act to him frees one from karma's bonds.

śubhāśubhaphalairevaṃ mokṣyase karmabandhanaiḥ |
saṃnyāsayogayuktātmā vimukto māmupaiṣyasi ||
english: In this way you will be freed from the bonds of action, with their good and bad results; with your self joined in the yoga of renunciation, you will be set free and come to me.

school_notes.note: Offering everything to me frees you from actions with good and bad results; this offering is called the yoga of renunciation.
Knowing yourself as existing for me and governed by me, and all action as my worship, you will be freed from the endless bonds of past karma and come to me.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says he is impartial to all, yet especially close to those who love him.
devanagari:
समोऽहं सर्वभूतेषु न मे द्वेष्योऽस्ति न प्रियः ।
ये भजन्ति तु मां भक्त्या मयि ते तेषु चाप्यहम् ॥
iast:
samo'haṃ sarvabhūteṣu na me dveṣyo'sti na priyaḥ |
ye bhajanti tu māṃ bhaktyā mayi te teṣu cāpyaham ||
english: I am the same to all beings; no one is hateful to me and no one is dear. But those who worship me with devotion are in me, and I am in them.

school_notes.note: Like fire, which takes away the cold only for those who come near it, I favour my devotees and not others; they are in me by their very nature.
Among all beings, however high or low by birth, form, nature or knowledge, I am equally the refuge; no one is rejected as too low to approach me.
Those who worship me are under my care and I am under theirs, as the Paiṅgi supplements say.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna says devotion counts for more than a person's past conduct (9.30-9.31).

साधुरेव स मन्तव्यः सम्यग्व्यवसितो हि सः ॥
iast:
api cetsudurācāro bhajate māmananyabhāk |
sādhureva sa mantavyaḥ samyagvyavasito hi saḥ ||
english: Even if a person of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, they should be regarded as good, for they have resolved rightly.

school_notes.note: Even one of very bad conduct who worships me alone should be considered good, since their resolve is right.
Even one who has broken the conduct proper to their birth, if they worship me for its own sake, is to be honoured as a foremost Vaiṣṇava, equal to those described before.
A devotee is rarely of very bad conduct; but if, by great merit, such a person becomes a devotee, they should be considered good.

context: Krishna promises that his devotee is never lost.

कौन्तेय प्रति जानीहि न मे भक्तः प्रणश्यति ॥

kṣipraṃ bhavati dharmātmā śaśvacchāntiṃ nigacchati |
kaunteya prati jānīhi na me bhaktaḥ praṇaśyati ||
english: They quickly become righteous and attain lasting peace. Know this for certain, son of Kunti: my devotee never perishes.

school_notes.note: Make this firm promise, Arjuna: my devotee, whose inner self is offered to me, never perishes.
With sins removed by devotion and rajas and tamas uprooted, they quickly become wholly given to worship and reach lasting peace.
Such complete devotion arises in gods and their portions; he cites the Śāṇḍilya branch of the Sāmaveda.

english: For those who take refuge in me, son of Pritha, even those of sinful birth, women, vaishyas and shudras, they too reach the highest goal.

school_notes.note: 'Of sinful birth': who are they? Women, vaishyas and shudras; they too reach the highest goal.
Women, vaishyas and shudras, though of sinful birth, reach the highest goal by taking refuge in me.

english: How much more, then, holy brahmins and devoted royal sages! Having come to this impermanent, joyless world, worship me.

How much more brahmins of meritorious birth and royal sages; so you, a royal sage, living in this unstable world struck by threefold suffering, should worship me.

english: Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, worship me, bow down to me. Disciplining yourself in this way, with me as your goal, you will come to me.

Fix your mind on me, the Lord of all, free of every flaw and full of every auspicious quality, with eyes like lotus petals, dark as a rain cloud and radiant as a thousand suns.

Even the gods and sages, who see beyond the senses, do not know my names, deeds, nature and qualities, because their very knowledge and power come from me.

'Beginningless' means he is the mover and the beginning of everything.

Understanding is deciding what should and should not be done; calm is being established in the Supreme.

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna responds by acknowledging Krishna as the supreme Brahman (10.12-10.15).

school_notes.note: Sages like Vasiṣṭha, the divine sage Nārada, Asita, Devala and Vyāsa say this, and you yourself tell me so.

पश्यामि त्वां दीप्तहुताशवक्त्रं ।

दृष्ट्वाद्भुतं रूपमुग्रं तवेदं ।

context: Arjuna sees gods and sages entering and praising the cosmic form.

अमी हि त्वां सुरसंघा विशन्ति ।

स्वस्तीत्युक्त्वा महर्षिसिद्धसंघाः ।

amī hi tvāṃ surasaṃghā viśanti |

रूपं महत्ते बहुवक्त्रनेत्रं ।

बहूदरं बहुदंष्ट्राकरालं ।
दृष्ट्वा लोकाः प्रव्यथितास्तथाहम् ॥

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna, overwhelmed, begs Krishna for grace.
devanagari:
दंष्ट्राकरालानि च ते मुखानि ।
दृष्ट्वैव कालानलसन्निभानि ।
दिशो न जाने न लभे च शर्म ।
प्रसीद देवेश जगन्निवास ॥

english: Seeing your mouths, terrible with tusks and blazing like the fire at the end of time, I lose all sense of direction and find no comfort. Be gracious, lord of gods, refuge of the world.

Seeing your mouths set on destroying everything, I find no comfort; be gracious to me, so that I may return to my normal state.

सहास्मदीयैरपि योधमुख्यैः ॥

These, along with some of our own chief warriors, rush into your terrible mouths to their destruction.

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna describes warriors being crushed in the cosmic form's jaws.

केचिद्विलग्ना दशनान्तरेषु ।
संदृश्यन्ते चूर्णितैरुत्तमाङ्गैः ॥

विशन्ति वक्त्राण्यभिविज्वलन्ति ॥

speaker: Arjuna

ल्लोकान्समग्रान्वदनैर्ज्वलद्भिः ।
तेजोभिरापूर्य जगत्समग्रं ।

Devouring the hosts of kings with your blazing mouths in fury, you lick your lips again and again.

speaker: Arjuna
context: Arjuna, frightened, asks the terrible form who it is and what it intends.
devanagari:
आख्याहि मे को भवानुग्ररूपो ।
नमोऽस्तु ते देववर प्रसीद ।
विज्ञातुमिच्छामि भवन्तमाद्यं ।
न हि प्रजानामि तव प्रवृत्तिम् ॥

ākhyāhi me ko bhavānugrarūpo |

english: Tell me who you are, in this terrible form. I bow to you, best of gods; be gracious. I want to know you, the first of all, for I do not understand what you are doing.

school_notes.note: Tell me who you are, so fierce in form; I want to know you, the first, for I do not understand your purpose.
Who are you, in this terrible form, and what have you set out to do? I do not know your intention.
Arjuna asks 'who are you?' to learn another aspect of him, as one may know someone's name and still ask what they are; otherwise he could not have just called him Viṣṇu.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna answers that he is Time, the destroyer, and the warriors' end is already set (11.32-11.34).

कालोऽस्मि लोकक्षयकृत्प्रवृद्धो ।
लोकान्समाहर्तुमिह प्रवृत्तः ।
ऋतेऽपि त्वां न भविष्यन्ति सर्वे ।
येऽवस्थिताः प्रत्यनीकेषु योधाः ॥

kālo'smi lokakṣayakṛtpravṛddho |

ṛte'pi tvāṃ na bhaviṣyanti sarve |
ye'vasthitāḥ pratyanīkeṣu yodhāḥ ||
english: I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of worlds, now set on annihilating the worlds here. Even without you, none of the warriors drawn up in the opposing armies will survive.

school_notes.note: I am Time, grown great to destroy the worlds; even without you, Bhishma, Drona, Karna and the others will not live.
'Time' is the one who counts out the lifespans of Duryodhana and the other kings; I have come in this fearsome form to destroy them.
'Time' (kāla) names the Lord's powers to bind, to cut the bonds of the world, and to know, from the senses of the root.

licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikisource text); underlying Sanskrit work is public domain

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna tells Arjuna the outcome is already decided and that he is only the instrument.

तस्मात्त्वमुत्तिष्ठ यशो लभस्व ।

मयैवैते निहताः पूर्वमेव ।
निमित्तमात्रं भव सव्यसाचिन् ॥

nimittamātraṃ bhava savyasācin ||
english: So stand up and win glory; conquer your enemies and enjoy a prosperous kingdom. They have already been slain by me; be merely the instrument, Arjuna.

Rise to fight and win a righteous kingdom; these men have already been slain by me for their wrongs, and you are merely the instrument of their killing.

speaker: Krishna
context: Krishna names the great warriors Arjuna fears and tells him not to be distressed but to fight.

द्रोणं च भीष्मं च जयद्रथं च ।

मया हतांस्त्वं जहि मा व्यथिष्ठा ।
युध्यस्व जेतासि रणे सपत्नान् ॥

school_notes.note: Krishna names each warrior Arjuna feared: Drona, his own teacher, master of divine weapons; Bhishma; Jayadratha; and Karna.
Do not be distressed, thinking 'how can I kill my teachers and kin?'; I have appointed them for death for their wrongs.
Jayadratha is named because of his father's boon that whoever made his head fall to the ground would have their own head shattered; Karna because of the spear he had from Indra.
